item.title: [bolavip.com] NY Yankees clear up confusion around Aaron Judge with reassuring update
item.dc:creator: Federico O'donnell

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees sparked confusion around Aaron Judge during player introductions ahead of Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. While several non-roster players were announced to the fans at Yankee Stadium, Judge, the franchise player, wasn’t.
Immediately, the fanbase in The Bronx started panicking over what it might mean not only for the 2026 MLB Postseason but looking ahead to the offseason, too. However, before Yankees fans could run away with all sorts of theories, manager Aaron Boone explained the real reason Judge wasn’t introduced along with the rest of his clubhouse teammates.
“Aaron Judge missed the pregame intros because he was receiving treatment, Aaron Boone said,” as reported by Bryan Hoch of MLB.com on X. “Judge is in Somerset today taking live at-bats.“
Positive news for NY Yankees
Although every fan in The Bronx will agree Judge should take any chance he can to get treatment and rehab for his calf strain, some didn’t appreciate the fact that Judge wasn’t out on the field with the rest of the team for player introductions before the series against Boston. “He couldn’t take a break, pause or start it later?” a fan replied to the update.
Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees walks back to the dugout.
Still, the majority of the fanbase was pleased to learn there were no sketchy things happening inside the clubhouse and that it was simply a bad-timing issue. Many feared Judge missing the player introductions was related to Boone’s explanation of Judge’s absence for the Wild Card against the Red Sox and that there might be some sort of rift inside the locker room. That appears to be out of the question.
Judge prioritizes his return
Instead, it’s an encouraging sign to learn Judge is still making progress and getting himself ready to return at some point in the 2026 MLB Postseason. In order to do so, however, the Yankees must defeat the Red Sox, and they already know what will happen if they win, tie, or lose in Game 2 of the Wild Card.
Any buzz of a divide between Judge and the rest of the team should be put to rest. In fact, Judge was in the dugout to watch the action and cheer on his teammates during Game 1’s statement 9-0 victory for the home team.
Key takeaways
- Aaron Judge missed pregame intros because he was receiving treatment for a calf strain.
- The franchise player was in Somerset taking live at-bats to prepare his return.
- He remained in the dugout to support the Yankees during their 9-0 victory in Game 1.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the New York Yankees will play the second game of their series with the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx.
The Yankees will look to close out the series (and advance to the ALDS) with a victory.
They most recently won by a score of 9-0 on Tuesday.
Michael Kay Makes Statement About Chisholm Jr.’s Future
Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not play in Tuesday’s game (Anthony Volpe got the start at second base).
Ahead of Tuesday’s game, Michael Kay spoke about Chisholm Jr. (via ESPN New York).
Kay: “The thing that Boone has to do, he has to manage this guy now, because last year he didn’t start the first game against Garrett Crochet and he was very, very upset, and he gets pouty as well. Now, I don’t think the Yankees have to worry about that long-term because I don’t know if he’s going to be back. My guess is he probably isn’t going to be back, but you’re going to need him for this run. The guy’s got an immense amount of talent, and if he does get locked in, he’s a really, really difference-maker sort of player.”
Chisholm Jr. is back in the lineup on Wednesday.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/30 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF L. García Jr. 1B S. Jones RF G. Lombard Jr. SS J. Chisholm Jr. 2B T. Grisham CF A. Wells C R. McMahon 3B M. Fried SP”
Looking At Jazz
Chisholm Jr. is in the middle of his 7th season at the MLB level.
He had spent the first part of his career with the Miami Marlins.
The Marlins then traded Chisholm Jr. to the Yankees during the middle of the 2024 season (and he helped them reach the World Series).
The Yankees wrote (via X) on July 27, 2024: “The New York Yankees today announced that they have acquired infielder/outfielder Jazz Chisholm Jr. from the Miami Marlins in exchange for minor league catcher Agustín Ramírez, infielder Jared Serna and infielder Abrahan Ramírez.”
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees are looking to win their first World Series since the 2009 season.
Whoever wins the series will play the Tampa Bay Rays in the next round.

item.content:encoded:
New MLB Rumors Update Don Mattingly, Joe Espada Hot Seat Buzz Amid Phillies, Astros Playoff Series
The Philadelphia Phillies and Houston Astros could reportedly be searching for new managers if they aren't able to go on lengthy postseason runs.
According to Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is "likely to be replaced" unless the team can advance deep into the playoffs.
Astros owner Jim Crane also won't hesitate to fire manager Joe Espada if the team can't advance beyond the Wild Card round or only lasts "a round or two" in the postseason, per Rosenthal.
Philadelphia is currently tied 1-1 through two games in its National League Wild Card Series matchup with the Atlanta Braves, while Houston faced a 1-0 series deficit against the Chicago White Sox in the American League Wild Card round heading into Wednesday's action.
Mattingly has operated as the Phillies' interim manager since Rob Thomson was fired on April 28. Philadelphia opened the season with a 9-19 record before Thomson was let go, but was able to advance to the playoffs with an 88-74 overall mark.
While the turnaround has been impressive, the Phillies could still look in a different direction for their next full-time manager if they suffer an early playoff elimination.
As for Houston, Espada's future became particularly murky after the team parted ways with general manager Dana Brown on Aug. 24.
The Astros still won the AL West this year, but finished at just 81-81. It represented their lowest win total in a 162-game season since 2014.
After Houston missed the playoffs entirely in 2025, a Wild Card exit will likely cause a change at manager.

item.title: [New York Daily News] It’s ‘too early’ to know if Yankees will have Aaron Judge for potential ALDS
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: With the Yankees one win away from advancing to the ALDS, Aaron Boone wasn’t sure if he would have Aaron Judge for the potential showdown with the Rays. “Probably too early to tell,” Boone said Wednesday when asked if Judge could return should the Yankees pick up another Wild Card win over the Red Sox. Judge, recovering from a moderate right calf strain that he suffered on Sept. 16, went to Double-A Somerset to face live pitching on Tuesday. Boone, speaking before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series,
item.content:encoded:
With the Yankees one win away from advancing to the ALDS, Aaron Boone wasn’t sure if he would have Aaron Judge for the potential showdown with the Rays.
“Probably too early to tell,” Boone said Wednesday when asked if Judge could return should the Yankees pick up another Wild Card win over the Red Sox.
Judge, recovering from a moderate right calf strain that he suffered on Sept. 16, went to Double-A Somerset to face live pitching on Tuesday. Boone, speaking before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, wasn’t sure who threw to Judge. The manager said the potential options included Luis Gil, Eli Morgan and Justin Topa.
Boone also wasn’t sure what, if any, running Judge did on Wednesday. On Tuesday, the skipper said that Judge would have to run the bases before he could be “a full player” for the Yankees.
On Wednesday, Boone also didn’t rule out the idea that the Rays’ home could impact whether the Yankees roster Judge for the ALDS. Tropicana Field has a turf field, the type of surface that isn’t kind to lower-body and leg injuries. Even when Judge is healthy, Boone tries to get him a DH day or two at The Trop when possible.
“I guess that could [make an impact],” Boone said, “but we’ll see where we are in hopefully making that decision in a couple days.”
In addition to baserunning — Judge did do some light running and agility work in the outfield at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday — the back-to-back MVP still needs to do defensive work. Judge did face live pitching during Monday’s pre-postseason workout, too.
“He had to check a lot of boxes for the trainers and the strength guys to say, ‘OK, you’re ready for that, you can go do that,’” Boone said. “I feel like in the couple weeks since the injury, he’s made real strides and significant improvements. Hopefully, we’re in a position to make another decision in a couple of days.”
Aside from Judge’s rehab plans, Boone also addressed the slugger’s absence from pregame introductions on Tuesday. Judge’s name noticeably wasn’t called as the Yankees took to the first base line — others left off the Wild Card roster participated — but Boone indicated he was getting treatment.
“I didn’t even know until it happened,” Boone said. “But I think a couple of the injured guys weren’t involved in it. But I think he was getting treatment stuff.”

item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Aaron Judge Takes Swings in Double-A Park, Eyes Postseason Return
Yankees captain Aaron Judge went to Somerset, New Jersey, for live batting practice Wednesday as he tries to work his way back from a leg injury to be available later in the postseason should New York advance.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge was not included on the roster for the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. He did not join teammates along the first-base line for introductions before the Yankees' 9-0 win in Tuesday's opener of the best-of-three series.
"I think he was getting treatment," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge ran in the outfield before Tuesday night's game and on Wednesday went to the ballpark of the Yankees' Double-A farm team to hit. He was due back at Yankee Stadium to watch Game 2 on Wednesday night.
Aaron Judge has been sidelined since Sept. 16 with a strained right calf, Judge was not included on the roster for the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
If New York advances to a best-of-five Division Series against Tampa Bay, it would start Saturday.
"Probably too early to tell," Boone said of Judge's potential availability.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge was limited to 66 games this season. The 34-year-old slugger hit .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs in September.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers, sidelined with a left forearm flexor strain since Aug. 22, was to throw a bullpen at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday.
Boone said right-hander Clarke Schmidt won't pitch again this year. The 30-year-old relieved on Sept. 16 at Minnesota in his first big league appearance since Tommy John surgery on July 11, 2025, then was put on the injured list with right biceps inflammation.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.content:encoded:
MLB postseason frustration boiled over for Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong during an 8-0 loss to the San Diego Padres in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series.
Crow-Armstrong was visibly upset after being called out on a check swing by third-base umpire Bill Miller in the top of the eighth inning. The 24-year-old center fielder took his bat toward Miller in an apparent attempt to demonstrate that he had not followed through with his swing.
Miller stood by the call and did not eject Crow-Armstrong, who continued to voice his disagreement before returning to the dugout.
Crow-Armstrong disputes second check-swing call
The eighth-inning call was actually the second time Crow-Armstrong was ruled out on a check swing during the game. Miller made a similar call in the sixth inning, adding to the frustration for the Cubs star.
Despite his objections, the calls stood, and Crow-Armstrong finished the game 0-for-3 with a walk as Chicago struggled to generate offense against San Diego.
The Cubs were held scoreless throughout the game, falling behind in the best-of-three Wild Card Series and putting themselves in a difficult position heading into Game 2.
MVP-caliber season comes under spotlight
Crow-Armstrong’s frustration came after one of the best seasons of his young career. The 24-year-old enjoyed a spectacular 2026 regular season, tying Kyle Schwarber for the MLB home run lead with 45.
He also finished fourth in the league with 107 RBI and tied Jazz Chisholm Jr. for fourth with 41 stolen bases over 162 games. Crow-Armstrong finished the regular season with a .280 batting average and a .810 OPS, numbers that have placed him firmly in the National League MVP conversation.
Now, however, the focus shifts entirely to the Cubs’ postseason survival.
Chicago and San Diego will meet again Wednesday for Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. With the Cubs trailing 1-0, another loss would end their season and send the Padres into the next round.
After a frustrating opening game, Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs will need to quickly move past the disputed calls and find a way to generate offense against San Diego’s pitching staff.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice, rare Ivy Leaguer in major leagues, had route to stardom that was anything but routine
Posted/updated on: September 30, 2026 at 2:54 pm
NEW YORK (AP) — Ben Rice’s route to stardom with the New York Yankees was anything but routine, even though he is a creature of habit.
A rare Ivy League graduate playing big league baseball, the baby-faced 27-year-old has filled the offensive void created by Aaron Judge’s injury-filled season. Rice had a night to remember in the AL Wild Card Series opener, hitting a grand slam with six RBIs and four hits in a 9-0 rout of the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
He tied the Yankees RBIs record for a postseason game, matching Bobby Richardson, Bernie Williams, Hideki Matsui and Robinson Canó.
“Ben is Mr. Consistency, on top of being a Ivy League graduate,” teammate Spencer Jones said. “He’s incredibly smart. He doesn’t take himself too seriously.”
A 12th-round pick in the 2021 amateur draft from Dartmouth, Rice played just 30 college games over three years due to the coronavirus pandemic. He grew up in Cohasset, Massachusetts, less than an hour’s drive south of Fenway Park.
He was a Yankees fan surrounded by Red Sox Nation, idolizing New York captain Derek Jeter.
“I was always playing with the Yankees on MLB 2K6 when I was a little guy. What a team to root for. They’re always so good. Pretty cool,” he said.
Rice thought back to his youth at Joseph Osgood Elementary School.
D
“Definitely wearing the Yankees jersey to the first-grade picture day probably got some weird looks,” he said.
Rice was a 10-year-old in Massachusetts when he watched the Yankees win their last title in 2009.
“It’s probably a little hazy for me,” he said. “I was pretty young.”
Rice is likely to get MVP votes after leading the Yankees with 41 homers, 97 RBIs and 105 runs while hitting .264 in his second full big league season.
“Count on one hand, one of the best hitters in the league,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
New York struggled when Judge was out with a toe injury in 2023 and had difficulty generating offense this year when their captain missed most of the season with a broken rib. Rice became the key cog, living up to the “Benny Barrels” nickname given to him by Yankees broadcaster David Cone.
Rice was hitting .306 through May, then batted .196 in June. An 18-for-58 (.119) slide after the All-Star break dropped his season average to .248 on Aug. 22 but he hit .327 (37 for 113) over the remainder.
“For as great a year as he had, he had a stretch there for a month where it was a grind and a struggle,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “But he kind of got himself out of it. Really finished the last month with a flurry, and obviously carried it in here the first game of the postseason.”
When Rice debuted with the Yankees two years ago, he joined Yankees coach Brad Ausmus, Kyle Hendricks and Jim Beattie as Dartmouth graduates in the major leagues. Rice’s degree is in psychology.
“He’s a Dartmouth grad — he’s an intelligent guy,” Ausmus said when Rice first made it to the big leagues.
Before heading to Yankee Stadium, Rice makes sure to start every day with scrambled eggs and toast.
“Same breakfast every day. Same routine in the cage every day. The whole timeline of the day is the same. Really just everything,” he said. “Of course, you’ve got different pitchers on the mound, there’s different ways you prepare, but I think the consistency just leaves you asking yourself fewer questions throughout the day because you just go out there, OK, this is what I do, and this is how I’m going to go about my business and just be ready for whenever the game starts.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] CC Sabathia Makes Strong Statement on Cam Schlittler After 117-Pitch Outing
item.dc:creator: Cole Sullivan
item.description: The New York Yankees secured a dominant 9-0 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. Ben Rice led New York's offense with two home runs, four hits and six RBIs, while Cam Schlittler dominated Boston from the mound and never let the Red Sox threaten on the scoreboard. Schlittler threw 6.1 shutout innings, allowing just two hits, both of which were singles, and striking out 10 batters while throwing a career-high 117 pitches
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees secured a dominant 9-0 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.
Ben Rice led New York's offense with two home runs, four hits and six RBIs, while Cam Schlittler dominated Boston from the mound and never let the Red Sox threaten on the scoreboard.
Schlittler threw 6.1 shutout innings, allowing just two hits, both of which were singles, and striking out 10 batters while throwing a career-high 117 pitches.
He threw the most pitches by a Yankees starter in the playoffs since 2012, when legend CC Sabathia threw 121 pitches.
Sabathia Makes Statement on Schlittler
Sabathia tuned into the game after recently having his number retired by the Yankees this past weekend.
He praised Schlittler for his dominant performance, which helped catapult the Yankees to a 1-0 series lead.
"117! Incredible tone-setting performance, Cam. AL Cy Young in the bag," Sabathia posted on X.
Schlittler Makes Playoff History Against Red Sox
While his pitch count was certainly a major topic of discussion, Schlittler also made MLB postseason history with his dominant performance.
He became the first player in Yankees history with multiple postseason outings of 10+ strikeouts and zero runs allowed. Both of those outings came against the Red Sox.
After the game, Schlittler made it clear that he wants to become a legend in the league, and he knows he has to perform in the playoffs when it matters most.
"It's very well known that if you want to be a legend, which is obviously the goal, you've got to do it in the postseason," Schlittler said. "Go out there and have dominant starts and put the team in the position to win."
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post CC Sabathia Makes Strong Statement on Cam Schlittler After 117-Pitch Outing appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [districtondeck.com] The eye-popping Statcast data behind James Wood's strong 2026 campaign

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB season has come and gone. It was an eventful year for the Washington Nationals, with Luis García Jr. hitting over 20 home runs before being traded at the deadline, CJ Abrams logging easily the best season of his career, and Cade Cavalli posting All-MLB-caliber numbers. In fact, you can vote for Cavalli and his Nationals teammates to be selected to the 2026 All-MLB teams from now every day until the 9th of October.
Nationals' James Wood was a Statcast monster this year
One Nat stood head and shoulders above the rest in 2026, and that was right fielder James Wood. Posting his second straight 30 HR season, Wood not only cranked up his walk rate this season, but also cut down on the strikeout rate that had him brushing up against the single-season record in 2025 (that was then surpassed by the White Sox' Colson Montgomery this year). Under the hood, there's no reason to be worried that he can't repeat this success. It's worth looking into the numbers that made the 6'6" slugger such a beast in 2026.
There's a couple more traditional stats that Wood was notable in before we look at his Statcast numbers. Despite missing nearly a month of play on the injured list, James still finished second in the National League in runs scored. His National League-leading walk rate of 16.4% contributed to an MLB fourth-best on-base percentage of .3884. And his weighted on-base average (wOBA), the primary informing component of wRC+, was second in the National League only to the inevitable MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong.
It could have gotten even better. Wood's expected slugging clip according to Statcast was .548, 45 points above his actual number. The only hitter in the NL above him in that regard was Shohei Ohtani, who, in case you forgot, just won the National League MVP award two years in a row. That also juiced his expected wOBA to .403, tops in the NL and second only in MLB to Astros MVP favorite Yordan Álvarez.
The batted ball data is even more eye-popping. When Wood made contact with a ball in 2026, he squared it up with a high bat speed (what Statcast refers to as a "blast") more often than any other hitter in the majors. It's the most valuable type of swing, and likely feeds into his NL-best xwOBA. His barrel rate, both per plate appearance and per batted ball, was also best in the National League.
Raw exit velo? We've got that too: his 90th-percentile exit velocity of 110.9 MPH was second in baseball only to freak athlete Oneil Cruz, and his EV50 (the average exit velo of the hardest 50% of his batted balls) is tops in MLB at 106.5 MPH. A 99th-percentile walk rate and 100th percentile barrel rate are freakish, and give some credence to the idea that maybe--just maybe--the Nationals should pay this guy.
Other standouts
James Wood wasn't the only National to exceed expectations this year. After three straight seasons of below-replacement level production from backstop Keibert Ruiz, the 2026 campaign for the Venezuelan was a shocking but welcome departure from career norms.
Despite only playing 105 games as Nationals manager Blake Butera had Harry Ford starting against lefties for much of the second half, Ruiz posted 1.9 FanGraphs WAR in 2026, the best mark of his major league career. After miserable framing numbers his entire career, Keibert was worth +3 framing runs this year. At the plate, he rebounded from back-to-back seasons under a 70 wRC+ to end up above-average for the first time in his career in a full season.
That juice, a .443 slugging clip with the highest ISO (SLG - AVG) of his career at .163, was largely powered by a pull-air rate of 33.9% across his batted balls. The only hitter in baseball to pull the baseball in the air more than Ruiz this year was Pete Crow-Armstrong, who continued to defy early-career game power concerns by swatting 40 bombs en route to a 10 WAR season.
Ruiz was near the middle of the pack in barrel rates, but was still able to transfer near bottom-of-the-barrel bat speed into a top-25 hard-hit rate when he swung the bat. All that came without sacrificing his typically low K rate, which he kept under 11%--the 11th-lowest mark in the majors among hitters with at least 350 plate appearances.
The Nationals might also have something special on their hands in unheralded 27-year-old lefty reliever Erik Tolman. Tolman was having a tough year at Triple-A Rochester--through mid-August, he was running a 5.23 ERA in 32 appearances. Despite good stuff and strikeout rates, he was getting hit hard and walking too many guys to be effective. Still, his contract was selected on August 19. 15 appearances and five weeks later, Tolman's first ride in the major leagues ends with a whole lot of red on his TJStats page. He's still walking guys, but actually did so at a lower rate than he did at Triple-A.
The stuff is electric--among pitchers with at least 10 innings thrown, Tolman had the second-highest Stuff+ rating (136) of all changeups thrown in the big leagues in 2026, and his aggregate Stuff+ was 16th best in MLB, minimum 10 IP. Tolman, for all he's been through, has the skills to succeed in the major leagues, and looks like he might be joining the ranks of coveted lefty relievers held by the Nationals in recent years alongside Robert Garcia and José A. Ferrer.
It's gonna be a long offseason. It might be even longer depending on how CBA negotiations go in the coming months. But stick with District on Deck for the analysis you need through the winter months.

What It Means
Bellinger is hitting for a .264 BA, .338 OBP and .429 SLG with a 15.8% strikeout rate and a 10.5% walk rate. His OPS is .768 and he has scored 73 runs. In 562 plate appearances, he has hit 17 home runs and driven in 73 runs. Bellinger has recorded 12 steals on 18 attempts. In his last game he had a one-hit performance (1-for-4) against the Red Sox.
Sonny Gray (18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and 149 strikeouts in 169 2/3 innings pitched) makes the start for the Red Sox, his 30th of the season.

item.content:encoded:
Happy 39th birthday to four-time MLB All-Star, two-time National League Hoffman Reliever of the Year and 2020 World Series champion, Kenley Jansen!
Jansen made his Major League debut with the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2010, and he was a staple of their bullpen for more than a decade. He spent 12 years coming out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, where he posted three 40-save seasons and led the National League with 41 in 2017. Known for his nasty stuff, Jansen racked up 1,022 K’s in 705 innings, but didn’t get his ring until the COVID-shortened 2020 season.
Jansen departed Los Angeles after the 2021 campaign and just completed his 17th MLB season and his first as a Detroit Tiger. He recorded another 22 saves in 50 appearances this year to give him 498 in his career, good for the active lead and third all-time behind just Mariano Rivera and Trevor Hoffman.
Which brings us to today’s quiz. While he isn’t participating in the playoffs this season, Jansen sits second all-time in MLB Postseason saves with 20 in his career. With that being said, can you name the MLB pitchers with at least five playoff-saves to their credit?
Good luck!

item.dc:creator: Dan Martin

It was a highlight in a rocky season for the one-time shortstop of the future for the Yankees, who bounced from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre to The Bronx and all around the infield in a wild season.

item.content:encoded:
Anthony Volpe sure looked comfortable in his first playoff start at second base while delivering a key hit and sacrifice bunt in a 9-0 win over Boston in Game 1 of the wild card series at the Stadium.
It was a highlight in a rocky season for the one-time shortstop of the future for the Yankees, who bounced from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre to The Bronx and all around the infield in a wild season.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Now he looks like he could be a key piece to a potential playoff run.
“I’m just in the moment and ready to go,’’ Volpe said. “Everything that happened, happened. … It’s all hands on deck.”
His path to Game 1 included offseason surgery to repair his left shoulder a little less than a year ago, followed by a minor league rehab assignment that began in April before he was optioned to the minors when he failed to show enough to merit a trip back to The Bronx at short.
When he finally got back to the majors, it came because José Caballero, who replaced Volpe at short, was hurt.
And after more than one trip back to the minors, Volpe didn’t play his first major league game at second base until this month.
“It was frustrating,’’ Volpe said. “As bad as it was, it was a good opportunity.”
“Credit to him,’’ Aaron Boone said prior to the game. “It was an incredibly difficult situation, but that’s why I always [say], we live in the moment so much. It’s a snapshot in such a long grind of the season. There’s gonna be good times, bad times, twists and turns. A lot of times, the cream usually rises to the top.”
The Yankees went with Volpe over lefty-swinging Jazz Chisholm Jr. against Boston left-hander Payton Tolle, with Volpe having started at second just 11 times in the majors before Tuesday night.
Still, infield coach Dan Fiorito expressed confidence that Volpe would be solid wherever he was asked to play.
“I know he’s ready,’’ Fiorito said before the game. “He’s got some games there going back to the minors.”
And Fiorito said Volpe’s knowledge of the game has helped with the transition.
Shop Yankees Merch
“He doesn’t have the same experience as he does at shortstop, but he’s a baseball player,’’ Fiorito said. “He knows all his responsibilities. He’s looked good out there so far.”
Prior to this season, Volpe had appeared in just two games as a pro at second base, as the Yankees prepared him throughout his career to be the shortstop for the foreseeable future.
But his offense stalled and his defense regressed and when he played through the shoulder injury last season, it took a toll.
Many scouts have long believed that, despite the Gold Glove he won as a rookie, Volpe was better suited as a second baseman and with George Lombard Jr. so far looking the part, the best chance Volpe has of sticking in The Bronx — and making a difference this postseason — is an ability to play second and perhaps third.
“Anthony is a competitor,” Fiorito said. “He’s dialed in. He knows where everybody’s got to be on the field at all times. And he’s in the right spot at the right time. That makes you feel good about him.”
And Fiorito has been most impressed with Volpe’s consistency at other parts of the infield.
“He’s made some really good plays there, but he’s also made the ones you expect him to and that’s what you need this time of year,’’ Fiorito said.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Austin Wells on experience catching Cam Schlittler's 117-pitch night appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees catcher Austin Wells reflected on the experience of guiding Cam Schlittler through a dominant Game 1 start against the Boston Red Sox in Tuesday's 9-0 victory at Yankee Stadium. Wells had a front-row view of Schlittler's command throughout the night, helping guide a game plan that kept the Red Sox scoreless and allowed the Pinstripes to seize control of Game 1.
Wells caught all 117 pitches as Schlittler worked 6 1/3 scoreless innings, allowing two hits and one walk while striking out 10. The outing helped New York take a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series. YES Network shared Wells' postgame interview with Meredith Marakovits on X, formerly Twitter, as the catcher reflected on the Cy Young candidate's performance against his hometown club.
"This one will probably be one of the more special ones of his career."@M_Marakovits caught up with Austin Wells after being behind the plate for Cam Schlittler's 117 pitch night. pic.twitter.com/ZVlqiq7qA6
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
— YES Network (@YESNetwork) September 30, 2026
Schlittler threw 77 strikes and generated 24 swings and misses while leaning heavily on his curveball. His 117 pitches marked a career high and the most by a Yankees postseason starter since CC Sabathia threw 121 in the 2012 AL Division Series.
The right-hander finished the regular season 14-6 with an American League-best 1.95 ERA, a 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts across 193 2/3 innings. His latest outing lowered his career ERA against Boston to 0.47 across six starts, including postseason play.
Wells contributed offensively as well. He delivered an RBI single in the second inning, singled again in the seventh and added a sacrifice fly during New York's five-run eighth. He finished with two hits and two RBIs.
Schlittler exited to a standing ovation from the sellout crowd after another elite postseason start vs. the Red Sox, while Wells helped guide the Yankees to within one victory of the AL Division Series.
Related: Yankees fans give Ben Rice his flowers after dominant win over Red Sox

item.title: [ktik.com] Cam Schlittler (10 K’s), Ben Rice (2 HRs) send Yankees to Game 1 rout
item.dc:creator: Cam Schlittler s; Ben Rice send Yankees
item.description: NEW YORK — Cam Schlittler fanned 10 in 6 1/3 dominant innings while Ben Rice homered twice and drove in six runs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-0 rout of the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of an American League wild-card series on Tuesday night. The Yankees can close out the best-of-three series on Wednesday when Max Fried pitches. Sonny Gray will try to extend Boston’s season to Game 3 on Thursday. Nearly a year after fanning 12 and allowing five hits in eight scoreless innings in Game 3
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Cam Schlittler fanned 10 in 6 1/3 dominant innings while Ben Rice homered twice and drove in six runs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-0 rout of the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of an American League wild-card series on Tuesday night.
The Yankees can close out the best-of-three series on Wednesday when Max Fried pitches. Sonny Gray will try to extend Boston’s season to Game 3 on Thursday.
Nearly a year after fanning 12 and allowing five hits in eight scoreless innings in Game 3 of last year’s wild-card series, Schlittler (1-0) was equally as sharp in his third career postseason start to help the Yankees get the upper hand.
Schlittler allowed just three baserunners, two singles and a walk. His 117 pitches were not only a career high but the most by a Yankee in a postseason game since CC Sabathia threw a 121-pitch complete game in Game 5 of the 2012 AL Division Series against the Baltimore Orioles.
Schlittler threw 77 pitches for strikes while going up against the team he grew up rooting for in Walpole, Mass.
A native of Cohasset, Mass., Rice hit a solo homer for a 2-0 lead in the fifth off left-handed reliever Erik Miller and added an RBI single in the seventh. He capped a five-run eighth by launching a grand slam off Brayan Bello over the right-center-field fence.
Rice went 4-for-5 and had New York’s first four-hit postseason game since Gleyber Torres accomplished the feat in Game 1 of the 2020 wild-card series at Cleveland.
Catcher Austin Wells helped Schlittler by winning an ABS challenge on Wilyer Abreu for a called third strike to end the first inning and hit an RBI single with two on in the second against Boston starter Payton Tolle.
Rookie George Lombard Jr. had three hits and two runs.
Tolle allowed one run on five hits in 4 2/3 innings. The left-hander struck out four, walked one and threw 58 of 83 pitches for strikes.
Paul Blackburn (1 2/3 innings) and John Schreiber (one inning) finished the Yankees’ three-hitter.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees flex homegrown muscle in Game 1 win vs. Red Sox: ‘All of us came up with one another in a way’
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell
item.description: The Yankees’ domestic scouting department is certainly giving itself a pat on the back after Tuesday night. The Bombers defeated the Boston Red Sox 9-0 in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series, and it was a homegrown victory in every sense. On top of Cam Schlittler’s continued dominance, the Yankees offense was carried by five of their own draft picks, one of which enters the postseason as the engine of their offense. Ben Rice continued his superb season into the playoffs, going 4-for-5
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ domestic scouting department is certainly giving itself a pat on the back after Tuesday night.
The Bombers defeated the Boston Red Sox 9-0 in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series, and it was a homegrown victory in every sense.
On top of Cam Schlittler’s continued dominance, the Yankees offense was carried by five of their own draft picks, one of which enters the postseason as the engine of their offense.
Ben Rice continued his superb season into the playoffs, going 4-for-5 with two homers and six RBIs. Rice’s first homer of the night came in the sixth inning off of reliever Erik Miller into Monument Park to extend the Bombers’ lead to 2-0 — although it felt much larger with the way Schlittler was dealing. His second shot sealed the deal with a grand slam in the bottom of the eighth to put the finishing touches on the Bo Sox.
“He pummeled pitches all night,” said manager Aaron Boone. “They went after him a little bit and he made them pay. I mean, some great left-on-left at-bats, the double to right-center smoke, the homer out the front door in Monument Park. And an exclamation point there at the end. Just a big-time night by a great hitter.”
It was the 27th multi-homer game in Yankees postseason history and in the absence of Aaron Judge, they’ll need more performances just like that. Rice slashed .264/.363/.534 with 41 homers and 97 RBI during the regular season, so offensive output was somewhat expected and crucial this postseason.
However, the same can’t be said for his fellow homegrown Yankees who ignited their offense in the second inning off of Red Sox starter Payton Tolle.
George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe and Austin Wells — all three being former first-round picks of the club — were at the center of a crucial rally to get the Yanks on the board in a game where offense was a premium.
Lombard started off the frame with a bloop single to center and was followed up by a bullet line drive into left-center by Anthony Volpe to set up first and second with one out.
While another of their former first-rounders, Spencer Jones, popped out, it set up Wells for a clutch two-out RBI single to give the Yanks a 1-0 lead that they carried all the way through to being just one win away from advancing to the ALDS.
“Yeah, it’s super fun,” said Rice about the homegrown guys’ contributions. “All of us came up with one another in a way. There was some overlap. Maybe a couple guys were ahead of others. But now we’re all here in the big leagues. And it’s been so cool seeing each guy have success and carve out their own role.
“Definitely a tight-knit group, and we take pride in that.”
It wasn’t exactly the smoothest season for any of the three players. Lombard. had a tough transition to the bigs, committing seven errors at shortstop and posting a .696 OPS, Volpe was up-and-down between Triple-A after losing his job as the Yankees shortstop and Wells had a brutal year batting .186 with a .624 OPS.
As they say, nothing matters when the playoff starts, and it seems the unexpected contributors took that as a fresh slate.
Lombard collected three singles while Volpe’s lone hit came in the second. Jones added a single of his own to leadoff the seventh that led to yet another rally that included a single from Wells and an RBI single from Rice to take a 3-0 lead.
All in all, their homegrown kids combined for 11 of their 12 hits on Tuesday night and the Bombers will need plenty of more contributions from their kids throughout the postseason, especially from Rice, Lombard, Wells and Jones, who are expected to start most games throughout their run.
Volpe, who started at second base, will likely take a seat for Jazz Chisholm Jr. in Game 2 with right-hander Sonny Gray on the mound, but still figures to have a vital role for this team in the postseason — especially against left-handed pitching.

item.title: [New York Post] Ben Rice delivers otherworldly night to carry Yankees’ offense in Game 1 win
item.dc:creator: Dan Martin
item.description:
For so much of this season that’s seen Aaron Judge sidelined with injuries, Ben Rice was the driving force of the Yankees lineup. So why should the first game of the playoffs, with Judge still out with a strained calf, be any different?
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. Try it free There was Rice, hitting second in the order
item.content:encoded:
For so much of this season that’s seen Aaron Judge sidelined with injuries, Ben Rice was the driving force of the Yankees lineup.
So why should the first game of the playoffs, with Judge still out with a strained calf, be any different?




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
There was Rice, hitting second in the order for Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Red Sox — even with left-hander Payton Tolle starting for the Red Sox — and putting up a line even Judge would be envious of.
Rice homered twice, had four hits and six RBIs as the Yankees pulled away with a 9-0 win. The six RBIs tied a franchise record for a postseason game.
Rice delivered first against Tolle and then against another lefty, Erik Miller, in the fifth, before providing more insurance against a third left-hander Alec Gamboa, with a run-scoring single in the seventh.
To cap his night, Rice hit a grand slam in the eighth.
“He pummeled pitches all night,” Aaron Boone said. “They went after him a little bit and he made them pay.”
Asked if it was his best game ever, Rice said, “I would say it’s definitely up there.”
And the Yankees needed it.
In a game that lacked offensive firepower early on, Rice came through with a one-out double off Tolle just two batters into the game.
The 110 mph shot seemingly set the Yankees up for an early lead, but he was stranded at second.
He came through again in the fifth.
This time, with the Yankees clinging to a 1-0 lead, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy went to the bullpen with two outs and no one on, removing Tolle — who’d pitched well after a shaky second — for Miller.
Rice greeted Miller by blasting a solo homer to dead center.
The 423-foot shot made it 2-0.
Then, with the bases loaded and no one out in the seventh, Rice smoked a 106 mph single to right for a three-run lead.
Shop Yankees Merch
On a night in which the Yankees got nothing from the rest of the top of the order — as Paul Goldschmidt went hitless and Heliot Ramos whiffed twice in the three spot — Rice’s presence made the difference.
It was a fitting way to open the playoffs for the lefty slugger, who found himself in the AL MVP conversation early in the season, before Judge went down with the fractured rib that cost him more than three months.
Rice, like most of the rest of the Yankee lineup, survived for the first few weeks of Judge’s absence before falling into a slump.
Eventually, a nearly five-week funk almost sank the Yankee lineup, but Rice finished the regular season strong, with a 1.023 OPS over his final 28 games and with 41 homers for the season.
“Just a big-time night by a big-time hitter,’’ Boone said.
It’s unclear how far the Yankees will be able to go if Judge isn’t able to return, but any chance rests on the bat of Rice. On Tuesday, he was up to the challenge.

item.title: [MLB.com] 'Locked-in' Lombard makes more history with 3-hit postseason debut
item.dc:creator: Matthew Ritchie
item.description: NEW YORK -- A little while after the Trade Deadline, George Lombard Jr.’s first career hit left his bat with an exit velocity of 100.2 mph, landed nearly 400 feet away in the left-center-field bleachers and made him the third-youngest player in Yankees history to homer in his MLB debut. It was among the most emphatic arrivals to the Majors that a player could picture for himself. On Tuesday night, Lombard’s latest entrance into the Yankees’ history books in Game 1 of the American League Wild Car
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- A little while after the Trade Deadline, George Lombard Jr.’s first career hit left his bat with an exit velocity of 100.2 mph, landed nearly 400 feet away in the left-center-field bleachers and made him the third-youngest player in Yankees history to homer in his MLB debut. It was among the most emphatic arrivals to the Majors that a player could picture for himself.
On Tuesday night, Lombard’s latest entrance into the Yankees’ history books in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series was a tad quieter -- a bloop single that lilted softly into shallow center field. But his second-inning knock, the catalyst for New York’s 9-0 win over Boston at Yankee Stadium, likely felt just as sweet as any titanic blast could.
And even if there was a touch of nervousness in the young shortstop’s chest, it was hard to tell once the first pitch was thrown.
“I think those ‘excitement butterflies’ were there a little bit, like during the intros, and going out there,” Lombard said. “But once the game started, I was just kind of locked in and having fun.”
At 21 years and 119 days old, Lombard singled to become the youngest player in Yankees history to record a hit in his postseason debut, winning a seven-pitch battle against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle. After a pair of singles, punctuated by Austin Wells’ two-out RBI knock, Lombard came around to score to get New York on the board early, giving starter Cam Schlittler all the cushion he would need.
In his next at-bat, Lombard poked a grounder between the third baseman and shortstop for an infield single. The fourth-inning knock then made him the second-youngest player in postseason history with a hit in each of his first two plate appearances. The dream start would have been cemented with another positive ending to his trip around the bases; however, Lombard wandered too far off second base on Spencer Jones’ lineout to the third baseman and was doubled off.
Lombard’s last at-bat in the eighth inning produced the loudest contact of the night. He crushed a 3-1 fastball off the right-center-field wall with an exit velocity of 108.6 mph for a long single, his third hit of the game. With that, he also became the second-youngest player in postseason history with three hits in his postseason debut, with only Gregg Jefferies (21 years, 64 days) ahead of him in Game 1 of the 1988 NL Championship Series.
Lombard finished the evening 3-for-4 with two runs scored, and he made the play on every fielding opportunity he had, each feeling routine as one would like.
Since Lombard burst into the big leagues with a loud blast and dazzling defense, his age has been a constant source of intrigue. He already grabbed the title of becoming the youngest player to start at shortstop for the Yankees in a postseason game when he stepped onto the field (breaking a 94-year record held by Frankie Crosetti from the 1932 World Series). When he made his debut back on Aug. 4, the only shortstop more fresh-faced than him to play the position in New York was Derek Jeter in 1995.
“It’s definitely an honor, and I have to pinch myself every now and then,” Lombard said. “But we know what the goal is, and what we’re all trying to do as a group. So it’s easy to focus on that and continue to get my work in and compete every day.”
But Lombard’s regular-season cameo was far from smooth sailing. There was the stretch from Aug. 21-27 when he made an error in six consecutive contests. He hit only .219 in September, a bit of a dip from the .253 average he notched in his debut month (though his OPS was 54 points higher during that September run).
Still, there didn’t seem to be a time when Lombard felt out of place or overwhelmed, or a reason to quell the excitement around the 21-year-old. He was building up a tolerance to the big leagues, one that seems to have prepared him for the entropy of the postseason excitement.
“Just watching him go through it all this couple of months, how he's handled himself, how he's handled success and fallen down,” manager Aaron Boone said on Monday’s off-day workout. “I feel like he's totally equipped for it.”
“I mean, that’s the name of the game up here, being able to bounce back, being resilient -- whatever happens,” Lombard said. “Obviously, you never know what can happen on the field, the goods and the bads, especially when there’s a lot of eyes on you every single day. So just lean on your teammates, lean on the guys in the clubhouse, lean on your circle, and just be resilient. Go out there every day and do your job.”

item.title: [New York Post] Austin Wells did more than reward the Yankees’ belief in him with huge Game 1
item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
If Brian Cashman had acted as most expected him to act at the trade deadline, Austin Wells would not have taken his second-inning at-bat.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. Try it free Facing lefty Payton Tolle, this was a game reserved for a righty-hitting catcher. Maybe Ryan Jeffers, who might as well have been looking for
item.content:encoded:
If Brian Cashman had acted as most expected him to act at the trade deadline, Austin Wells would not have taken his second-inning at-bat.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Facing lefty Payton Tolle, this was a game reserved for a righty-hitting catcher. Maybe Ryan Jeffers, who might as well have been looking for a New York apartment considering the months of speculation. Or maybe the switch-hitting Adley Rutschman, another potential Yankees target who was behind the plate Tuesday because he was redirected instead to the Red Sox, who overwhelmed the Orioles with their trade package.
But Cashman did not pull the trigger on finding another catcher, even a complement, and so Wells — who had been among the worst hitters in baseball at that point — only saw his stranglehold on the starting job strengthen.
That move — or rather lack of move — sure looked smart when Wells took that second-inning at-bat and drove in the only run the Yankees would need.
The Yankees’ starting catcher (and with all due respect to Ali Sánchez, their only catcher) breathed even more life into his revitalized season in the Yankees’ 9-0 statement of a victory over Boston in The Bronx to move one win from an ALDS date with the Rays.
“By no means was it surprising,” Ben Rice said of Wells, who went from virtually unplayable to a catcher the Yankees will ride for as long as this postseason run lasts.
Before the Yankees ran away late in the game, their offense had started with promise but only promise: Prior to Wells stepping up for his first at-bat, the club had gone 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and was threatening to waste another opportunity. In the frame, George Lombard Jr. singled, moved to second on a one-out knock from Anthony Volpe and then watched as Spencer Jones fouled out for the second out.
But the lefty-hitting Wells — who batted .122 with a .436 OPS against southpaws this season — ripped a hit through the right side of the infield, giving the Yankees a lead they only padded from there.
Wells added a second single off a lefty — Alec Gamboa in the seventh inning, plus a sacrifice fly in the eighth against Brayan Bello — to make it two hits off southpaws in the postseason, which is remarkable for a player who had 11 hits (in 99 plate appearances) against such pitching all season.
“I think just overall I’m feeling better, seeing the ball well and just competing up there,” said Wells, who has been a different hitter since a stint on the injured list in June with cervical headaches.
Those 15 days sidelined, when he could heal, refresh his mind and tweak his swing, may have saved his job and Yankees future.
“In the moment, [I] didn’t realize how much it was affecting me,” Wells said of the headaches, “but taking the time and getting back and feeling healthy, I feel like I can see the ball a lot better.”
He felt better on the other side of the injured list, but the results did not arrive immediately. And his inability against pitching of all types through the middle of July ensured the Yankees at least tested the trade market. He was hitting .152 with a .501 OPS on July 19. As much as they valued his rapport with pitchers and his defense, he had nearly become unplayable.
And yet Wells kept playing, made steady progress and showed enough in late July and early August to dissuade Cashman from overpaying in prospects.
Shop Yankees Merch
At a time when catchers typically are wearing down, in August and September, Wells posted his two best months of the year.
And even though the date read Sept. 29, he showed Tuesday why October may further his revival.

item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
El manager de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Boone, confirmó a los medios este martes que Aaron Judge «aún no está listo» en su proceso de recuperación por la distensión en la pantorrilla, según reportó Bryan Hoch de MLB.com, motivo por el cual quedó oficialmente fuera del roster del equipo para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana.
La decisión definitiva se tomó tras una reunión del cuerpo técnico con el equipo de preparadores físicos, luego de evaluar la respuesta física del capitán neoyorquino durante una sesión de práctica de bateo en vivo realizada el lunes en el Yankee Stadium.
Aunque el tres veces Jugador Más Valioso del nuevo circuito había expresado la semana pasada su firme intención de estar disponible para el inicio de la postemporada, el panorama médico siempre lució complejo debido a la naturaleza de la lesión en la pantorrilla sufrida el pasado 16 de septiembre.
El tiempo de recuperación habitual para este tipo de molestias musculares hizo que su presencia en esta primera etapa de octubre resultara poco realista, a pesar de los esfuerzos del toletero por acelerar su rehabilitación.
Muy probable que regrese si avanzan
No obstante, el panorama a corto plazo no es del todo desalentador para la organización. A pesar de su ausencia en esta trascendental primera ronda frente a los Medias Rojas de Boston, los reportes indican que existe una buena probabilidad de que el cañonero regrese a la alineación activa para la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, siempre y cuando Nueva York logre superar a sus históricos rivales en la llave de comodines.
Se espera que la gerencia y el cuerpo médico de los Bombarderos del Bronx ofrezcan mayores detalles y claridad sobre los próximos pasos en el cronograma de trabajo de Judge a lo largo de esta misma semana.
Sigue la cobertura por El Extrabase

item.title: [Excélsior] Revés a Yankees antes de jugar: Aaron Judge queda fuera del roster para la serie ante los Red Sox

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees, Aaron Judge, quedó fuera del roster para encarar la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana contra los Boston Red Sox, serie de primera ronda de playoffs que arranca este mismo martes por la noche.
 En contraste con la sensible baja del bombardero, el bateador designado Giancarlo Stanton —ausente desde el pasado 24 de abril debido a distensiones musculares crónicas en las pantorrillas— sí fue incluido de última hora en la nómina de la postemporada de la MLB junto al jardinero central Trent Grisham.
Sin tener actividad ofical desde el 16 de septiembre por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, Judge realizó una práctica de bateo en vivo este lunes en las instalaciones del Yankee Stadium en un intento desesperado por convencer al mánager Aaron Boone y al cuerpo médico del club.
 Durante dicha sesión frente a los lanzadores de ligas menores Ryan Weathers y Elmer Rodríguez, el patrullero recibió dos bases por bolas, conectó un rodado directo al montículo y se ponchó cantado, evidenciando una notable falta de ritmo en la caja de bateo.
El tres veces Jugador Más Valioso (JMV) del joven circuito recibió una inyección de plasma pobre en plaquetas el 21 de septiembre para acelerar su proceso de recuperación. El pelotero de 34 años de edad ya se había perdido gran parte del año entre el 31 de mayo y el 8 de septiembre debido a una fractura de costilla, logrando participar en apenas 66 compromisos de la campaña regular antes de sufrir esta última recaída muscular.
El retorno de Giancarlo Stanton y el panorama de Boston
La ofensiva de los Yankees dependerá ahora del regreso de Giancarlo Stanton. El toletero de 36 años comenzó la campaña registrando un promedio de .256 con tres cuadrangulares en 24 desafíos antes de ingresar a la lista de lesionados. Por su parte, Grisham superó una distensión en el isquiotibial derecho sufrida el 4 de septiembre para unirse al grupo de 15 jugadores de posición habilitados para la serie.
Por el lado de los Boston Red Sox, el mánager Alex Cora confirmó que el zurdo estelar Garrett Crochet estará disponible desde el bullpen de relevistas. Crochet no lanza desde el 25 de abril debido a una severa inflamación en el hombro izquierdo, pero cuenta con el antecedente de haber maniatado a la ofensiva neoyorquina en la postemporada anterior tras permitir solo una carrera en siete entradas de labor.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are set to take on the Boston Red Sox Tuesday night in Game 1 of their Wild Card Series matchup at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.
For the Yankees, right-handed ace and AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler will be on the mound, while the Red Sox will send out lefty Payton Tolle.
Ahead of the contest, Yankees manager Aaron Boone officially released his first postseason lineup card, and it featured some interesting decisions across the board.
Yankees Announce Luis Garcia Jr. Move
While many knew it was going to be a tall task to get the perfect starting lineup to please everybody, Tuesday night seemed like a fairly easy decision for Boone, as he prioritized right-handed hitters against the lefty pitcher.
With that, All-Star slugger Luis Garcia Jr. is not in the starting lineup for the series opener. Veteran Paul Goldschmidt will play first base in his place.
Here’s the full Yankees lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Yankees 9/29 P. Goldschmidt 1B B. Rice DH H. Ramos RF C. Bellinger LF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Rosario 3B A. Volpe 2B S. Jones CF A. Wells C C. Schlittler SP.”
Yankees 9/29
P. Goldschmidt 1B
B. Rice DH
H. Ramos RF
C. Bellinger LF
G. Lombard Jr. SS
A. Rosario 3B
A. Volpe 2B
S. Jones CF
A. Wells C
C. Schlittler SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 29, 2026
Garcia Jr.’s 2026 Season
It’s been a career year for Garcia Jr., who was traded from the Washington Nationals to the Yankees prior to the MLB trade deadline.
He’s hitting .277 across 516 at-bats and has recorded 143 hits, 30 home runs and 92 RBIs, while slugging .521 with a .831 OPS.
Against lefties, however, Garcia Jr. has appeared in 55 games and is hitting .235 with just two home runs and 10 RBIs across 81 at-bats, along with a .600 OPS. That helps explain why Boone decided to use him off the bench in Game 1.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: How Paul Goldschmidt can join Rickey Henderson vs. Red Sox appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Paul Goldschmidt could enter a remarkable group before the New York Yankees even take their first swing against the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
If New York bats him leadoff in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series, the 39-year-old will join a short list of players who have occupied the top lineup spot in a postseason game at his age or older.
MLB Network's Jon Morosi identified the previous members of that group: Justin Turner with the 2025 Cubs, Craig Biggio with the 2005 Astros, Rickey Henderson with the 2000 Mariners and 1999 Mets, Ozzie Smith with the 1996 Cardinals, Joe Morgan with the 1983 Phillies, and Pete Rose with the 1980 Phillies.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
It is an unusual piece of history for a player better known for driving in runs than setting the table.
The matchup gives Yankees manager Aaron Boone a reason to consider it. Boston is starting left-hander Payton Tolle, and Goldschmidt hit .299 with a .967 OPS against left-handed pitching during the regular season. He also has experience atop New York's order: in 147 at-bats from the leadoff spot, he collected 41 hits, nine home runs, and 23 RBIs while drawing 17 walks.
Those numbers suggest the decision would be about more than a historical footnote. Goldschmidt produced a .355 on-base percentage and .872 OPS when batting first this season. Against Tolle, Boone could use the veteran's right-handed bat to put an immediate runner on base or give New York an early lead with one swing.
The Yankees had not posted their Game 1 lineup as of Tuesday afternoon, so Goldschmidt's place in that group of legends remains conditional. Whenever the lineup arrives, New York's priority will be finding enough offense to beat its longtime rival. If Goldschmidt leads off, he will have a chance to make history and help the Yankees start the series on the right foot.
However, they must do so without their star Aaron Judge, who is not on the Wild Card roster.

item.content:encoded:
Get excited, New York Yankees fans! The MLB playoffs are here, and on Tuesday, September 29, the Yanks will go head-to-head with the Boston Red Sox in an anticipated three-game series in the AL Wild Card round.
Earlier on Tuesday, the Yankees revealed their 26-man roster, and one major omission is Aaron Judge, who has been left off the WC roster.
To that same breath, Trent Grisham and Giancarlo Stanton are both good to go for the Yankees.
Before the first game of the series on Tuesday night, the Yankees announced a notable Anthony Volpe lineup decision.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Reveal Ryan Weathers Roster Decision Ahead of Red Sox Series
Anthony Volpe Batting 7th; Playing 2B for Series Opener
In a bit of a surprising move, Anthony Volpe is in the New York Yankees batting order over Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Per the Yankees social media team, here is the full group:
Some quick lineup notes: Paul Goldschmidt gets the nod in the leadoff spot, George Lombard Jr. is making his postseason debut as a rookie, and Amed Rosario is batting sixth and playing third.
So with the Boston Red Sox opting to run out a southpaw starter, manager Aaron Boone is deploying several right-handed hitters.
Back to Anthony Volpe, his playoff status about a month ago was in serious limbo, but after an injury to Chisholm, Volpe has logged reps at second base, and he’s quietly been pretty solid at the plate.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Suddenly Cut Pitcher During Phillies NLWC Series
Anthony Volpe’s 2026 Season Thus Far
The 2026 regular season is officially in the books, so we can take a closer look at New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe’s final stat line.
Across just 70 games played, Volpe batted .245 with two home runs, 1 triple, and 12 doubles.
His OPS+ over 220 at-bats was 84. He also scored 24 runs and drove in 28 runs.
Yankees fans, do you agree with the decision to start Anthony Volpe in game one of this huge series with the Red Sox??

item.content:encoded:
Heliot Ramos, at least as far as the New York Yankees go, is not a household name.
He may have to become one for these 2026 Yankees to go on a deep run into the playoffs as they try to end a World Series drought dating back to 2009.
Ramos is batting third for the Yankees in their Wild Card Series opener against the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night at Yankee Stadium. He’s playing right field.
There are few more notable spots in sports than the 3-spot in the Yankees’ lineup, and so Ramos will have all eyes on him as these rivals clash in the Bronx.
Why is Heliot Ramos Hitting 3rd, Playing RF for Yankees?
The reality is that the Yankees were in need of a heart-of-the-order hitter and a right fielder once Aaron Judge went on the injured list.
Ramos wasn’t playing a ton with Judge back healthy. But with Judge hurt, Ramos becomes a crucial player for the Yanks.
The 3-spot on Tuesday is in part because the left-handed Payton Tolle is on the mound for the Red Sox.
It’s also, though, a vote of confidence in what Ramos can bring. Even once Tolle leaves the game, Ramos is still in that crucial lineup spot. The Yankees clearly believe he can deliver in a big spot, whether early in the game against a lefty or late in the game against a same-side righty.
Heliot Ramos the X-Factor
In a baseball playoff series, it’s always about more than one player. There are too many individual moments for a single guy to decide who advances.
But for the Yankees, Ramos is clearly going to be important.
Without Judge, the Yanks’ lineup is definitively worse. They need that “next man up” mentality that football teams embrace with injuries. They can’t do anything about the fact that Judge isn’t on the roster for the Wild Card Series. All they can do is count on the guys they do have to deliver when called upon.
That’s what Ramos is here for.
They traded for him from the San Francisco Giants before the summer deadline to add an outfielder who was previously an All-Star in the Bay Area.
He’s 27 years old and clearly in his prime.
Before being traded, Ramos had a .264 average in 74 games with the Giants this season with 13 doubles, three triples and nine home runs.
He has struggled with the Yanks a bit, a .198 average in 38 games with seven doubles, a triple and four homers.
But this is a guy who hit 22 and then 21 home runs in 2024 and then 2025, and he’s a career .253 hitter in an era when that’s above league average.
Ramos hadn’t gotten many big game opportunities in recent years as the Giants have slumped.
Now, he’s under the bright lights. The Yankees need Ramos to shine bright, too.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees are stacking their righties against left-hander Payton Tolle, which means Jazz Chisholm Jr. being out of the lineup for Game 1 of the AL wild-card series.
Anthony Volpe is starting at second base against Tolle, with Amed Rosario at third base, with the Yankees turning to both righty bats to give them a boost to begin the series against the Red Sox.
Chisholm said on Monday he expected to be in the lineup and indicated he would not be happy if he was out of it, which was the same case as last year when he did not start against lefty Garrett Crochet in Game 1.
Aaron Boone, though, hinted at this happening as he said playing the platoon game at second base was in play, after Volpe had looked the part at his new position after being called up earlier this month to replace the injured Chisholm (right thumb sprain).
Chisholm, a pending free agent who has had a mostly rough season despite getting hot before he got hurt, only played three games after coming off the IL.
Meanwhile, the Yankees are banking on Rosario’s track record crushing lefties compared to his numbers this season, when he hit just .208 with a .606 OPS in 160 plate appearances against them. They could have started José Caballero at third base, but they seem to prefer him as a 10th man off the bench to pinch run as needed and offer defensive versatility.
Yankees lineup
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B
Ben Rice, DH
Heliot Ramos, RF
Cody Bellinger, LF
George Lombard, SS
Amed Rosario, 3B
Anthony Volpe, 2B
Spencer Jones, CF
Austin Wells, C

item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the New York Yankees will open up their three-game playoff series with the Boston Red Sox (in the Bronx).
Last week, the franchise honored legendary pitcher CC Sabathia.
MLB wrote (on September 25): “The Yankees honor CC Sabathia with a plaque in Monument Park and retire his No. 52 👏”
Derek Jeter’s Sister Sends Out Heartfelt Post
Following the big day, Derek Jeter’s sister (Sharlee) made a heartfelt post to Instagram.
She wrote: “My heart is overflowing with pride. So happy for you, CC! Your LegaCCy is cemented in history. And Amber…you already know! Thanks for including me and my guy! 🖤🖤🖤🖤 #TillTheWheelsFallOff #52”
Comments On Her Post
Here’s what people were saying in the comments:
CC Sabathia: “Family 🙏🏾❤️”
Amber Sabathia: “💙💙💙”
@ginnydantonio: “Beautiful pictures of amazing people! Congratulations! 👏🏽🎊👏🙌🔥”
Derek Jeter, Hannah Jeter, Jorge Posada and Andruw Jones were among the people to like Sharlee’s post.
Looking At CC
Sabathia had an incredible 19-year MLB career.
He spent the first nine seasons of his career with the Cleveland Guardians and Milwaukee Brewers.
The Hall of Famer then played his final 11 seasons for the Yankees.
In 2009, they won the World Series title (which is their most recent).
New York Yankees wrote (via X) on September 25: “CC Sabathia learned to play baseball by playing catch in the backyard with his mom Margie. Now, he passes his love of the game to his son, Carsten Charles Sabathia III, who was drafted by the Brewers in this year’s MLB Draft 💙 @CC_Sabathia continued the Sabathia Legacy as he threw today’s ceremonial first pitch to his son Carsten ⚾”

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will face the Boston Red Sox in the American League Wild Card Series without their captain, Aaron Judge. Multiple sources report that Judge was left off the roster due to a calf injury sustained two weeks ago. The 34-year-old outfielder had been working hard to return, even taking live batting practice on Monday (September 28) to demonstrate his readiness.
Judge, who has been sidelined since September 16 with a strained right calf, received a platelet-poor plasma injection on September 21. Despite his efforts to convince the team of his fitness, Yankees manager Aaron Boone indicated that Judge's return for the Wild Card Series was unlikely. Boone mentioned, "We’re planning on him not being a part of that series," according to Big Country Homepage.
Judge's absence is a significant blow for the Yankees, who have struggled without him this season. He played in only 66 games, hitting .241 with 18 homers and 41 RBIs. Despite the setback, Boone expressed confidence in the team's ability to perform, stating, "We’ve played much of the year without him and for the most part, we’ve done a pretty good job," as reported by QC Online.
Judge himself remains hopeful for a quick recovery and return, emphasizing the short window of opportunity to play baseball. He remarked, "The time I get to be a Yankee and play this game of baseball is a very short window," according to AP News.

item.content:encoded:
How Jazz Chisholm Jr. can salvage lofty free agent demands during Yankees' postseason originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
There are a few players on this New York Yankees team who are about to hit free agency once the 2026 MLB postseason comes to an end.
While David Bednar is in good shape to land a new deal, Trent Grisham and Jazz Chisholm Jr. are facing some real questions about how much they should get on the open market. For Chisholm, the question is a lot more interesting.
He's had a decent 2026 season, but not close to being good enough to land a top-of-the-market deal. However, MLB.com's Mark Feinsand believes a strong postseason could help salvage his free-agent value.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. can salvage FA value with strong postseason
"Chisholm recently returned from the injured list after missing two weeks, and while his season hasn't been as productive as he had hoped heading into free agency, a big showing in the postseason -- something he hasn't had in his previous four trips to October -- would help him in his pursuit of a new contract," Feinsand writes.
While the questions about Chisholm's production in 2026 are warranted, if he can thrive in the postseason and be one of the best hitters in the Yankees' lineup, then he could salvage his free agent value a bit.
Coming off a strong 2025 season, it was looking like Chisholm was on the cusp of a massive new deal, one potentially reaching the $300 million mark.
That's not going to happen now after a 1.7 bWAR season in 2026, but he could still land something well north of $100 million, especially with a strong playoff run.
Chisholm's postseason success in 24 games, hitting .170 with a .543 OPS, is something teams will worry about, and for good reason.
But if he can thrive during this year's playoffs for the Yankees, not only could he finish his contract year strong, but he could prove to MLB clubs that he's capable of thriving in the playoffs.
That extra feather in his cap might make enough of a difference to help him land a massive deal this offseason. A team will have to believe in him beyond a small sample size, but the upside he's shown as a power-hitting, base-stealing infielder is enough.
Add in postseason success, and that he's only 28 years old, and Chisholm could be en route to a massive contract this upcoming offseason.

item.content:encoded:
Injured Yankees captain Aaron Judge was left off New York's roster for its AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox starting Tuesday night.
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 because of strained calf muscles in both legs, was included. So was center fielder Trent Grisham.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge took live batting practice on the field Monday, a day ahead of the series opener, in an effort to persuade manager Aaron Boone and the medical staff. He walked twice, hit a comebacker to the mound and took a called third strike against teammates Ryan Weathers and Elmer Rodríguez.
The three-time AL MVP had a platelet-poor plasma injection Sept. 21. The 34-year-old was sidelined by a fractured rib from May 31 to Sept. 8 and played in just seven games before the latest injury.
Judge was limited to 66 games this season. He hit .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs in September.
Stanton started the season with a .256 batting average, three homers and 14 RBIs in 24 games. The 36-year-old, acquired after winning NL MVP in 2017, had 38 homers and 100 RBIs in his first season with New York but has missed 500 of 1,194 games since (41.9%).
Grisham had been sidelined since straining his right hamstring on Sept. 4. He was among New York’s 15 position players.
Left-hander Garrett Crochet, who won last season’s WCS opener against the Yankees by allowing one run and four hits in 7 2/3 innings, will be available in the bullpen. The two-time All-Star has not pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation.
“He’s worked very hard to get everything back strong the way it needs to be, but we’re still going to be evaluating him daily to see where he’s at,” manager Chad Tracy said.
Second baseman Luis Arraez, a three-time batting champion, is out for the series against Atlanta after spraining his left ankle last Thursday.
Left-hander Brooks Raley, like Arraez acquired ahead of the trade deadline, also was left off.
Right-hander Jonathan Bowlan and infielder Otto Kemp were included as the Phillies went with 14 position players.
Philadelphia did not include any players it acquired at the trade deadline.
Infielders Rowdy Tellez and Luke Williams were included on the roster by Atlanta, which has 15 position players.

We’ve already got goosebumps.
For the seventh time in MLB history, the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox are meeting in the playoffs.
This time around, the Bronx Bombers and BoSox will go toe-to-toe in the Wild Card round in a best-of-three series that determines who gets to take on the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The trio of games will all take place at the Bronx’s Yankee Stadium. They’re slated go down:
Game 1
Tuesday, Sept. 29
8 p.m.
Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA) vs. Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA)
Game 2
Wednesday, Sept. 30
8 p.m.
Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA) vs. Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA)
Game 3
Thursday, Oct. 1
8 p.m.
Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA) vs. Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA)
If you’d like to be there, the lowest price we could find on tickets for any one games was $129 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $131 and $135 including fees for the other two contests.
Over the course of the regular season, New York and Boston met 13 times; the Yankees took seven of those showdowns. In their final battle, the Yankees walloped the Sox 16-1 on Aug. 30. Heliot Ramos, Paul Goldschmidt, José Caballero and Austin Wells all homered for the Bombers that afternoon.
Both teams went 5-5 in their last ten games of the regular season.
As for this series, manager Aaron Boone left Aaron Judge off the Wild Card round roster but activated Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham after both have been inactive for months and weeks at a time, respectively.
“[I’m] real confident if we play our game and pitch like we’re capable of, we got a chance to move on,” Boone said. “We got to play our best starting Tuesday.”

Levy stays up-to-date on all the latest tour announcements from your favorite musical artists and comedians, as well as Broadway openings, sporting events and more live shows – and finds great ticket prices online. Since he started his tenure at the Post in 2022, Levy has reviewed a Bruce Springsteen concert and interviewed Melissa Villaseñor of SNL fame, to name a few. Please note that deals can expire, and all prices are subject to change.

item.title: [heavy.com] Yankees Predicted to Sign $75 Million Infielder to Replace Star
item.dc:creator: Christopher Moore
item.description: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman is expected to be busy this winter. While the Bronx Bombers are set to begin their playoff push after winning 93 games in 2026, the roster could certainly improve. Third base is a clear area for Cashman to target in the offseason.
