He also stole 41 bases, tied for fourth in the majors, to deliver the first 40-4
item.content:encoded:
A year after Cal Raleigh’s 2025 season for the ages, another Major League Baseball star was born this season in Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong.
The presumptive National League MVP hit 21 homers over the final two months of the season to finish tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the major league home run lead with 45, leading Chicago to its second postseason appearance in the last six years.
He also stole 41 bases, tied for fourth in the majors, to deliver the first 40-40 season in Cubs franchise history.
Schwarber, who led the NL but not the majors last season with 56 homers, claimed the co-homer lead while also leading the NL in strikeouts (220).
On the American League side, Pete Alonso made a splash in his first season in Baltimore, leading the AL in homers (43, one ahead of Houston’s Yordan Alvarez and Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero) and RBIs (113).
Alonso entered the final day of the season within range of the major league RBI lead, but the Orioles’ finale was canceled due to weather while Alec Burleson was not in the St. Louis Cardinals’ lineup on Sunday and finished with an MLB-best 116 RBIs.
Alvarez, a runaway favorite to win his first AL MVP honor, led the majors with a .316 batting average, coming one homer and seven RBIs from the AL triple crown and the first in the majors with the achievement since Detroit’s Miguel Cabrera in 2012.
Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno narrowly won the NL batting title, beating Philadelphia’s Luis Arraez by one point (.311 to .310) to deny the journeyman his fourth batting title. Arraez missed the entire final weekend due to a sprained left ankle.
Nationals infielder Nasim Nunez led the majors with 49 stolen bases.
On the negative side, White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery struck out a major league-record 227 times, breaking Mark Reynolds’ mark of 223 set in 2009 for Arizona.
On the pitching front, Cy Young favorites Jacob Misiorowski (Milwaukee) and Cam Schlittler (Yankees) were No. 1 and No. 2 in ERA at 1.80 and 1.95, respectively. Misiorowski started Sunday and struck out five batters to also finish atop the major league strikeout leaderboard with 252 after entering the day one behind Cleveland’s Gavin Williams and also led the league in WHIP (0.80).
Boston’s Sonny Gray and Philadelphia’s Cristopher Sanchez shared the major league lead in wins (18). At the other end of the spectrum, Baltimore’s Shane Baz, Cleveland’s Tanner Bibee and Cincinnati’s Brady Singer were tied for the league lead with 15 losses.
A pair of unlikely closers in Bryan Baker of the Rays and Cade Smith of the Guardians shared the major league saves lead with 41. For context, Baker began this season with seven career saves while Smith had 17 before the 2026 campaign. A less surprising name, San Diego’s Mason Miller, tied with the Cardinals’ Riley O’Brien for the NL lead with 38 saves.
On the team side, the Milwaukee Brewers (103-59) set a franchise wins record for the second straight season, winning six more than the prior record (97) set last season.
The Los Angeles Angels (62-100) lost their last two games and five of their last seven to finish with 100 losses for the first time in franchise history. The Angels had previously been the only major league team to never lose 100 games in a season.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees’ new celebration feels like Oswaldo Cabrera tribute after Clarke Schmidt roster move
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: Baseball players can be an odd group at times. From bizarre pre-game rituals to over-the-top celebrations, things can get pretty weird on the diamond. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t meanings behind those idiosyncrasies. While Oswaldo Cabrera may no longer be a member of the New York Yankees, many people in the organization have not forgotten about him. This includes a couple of his former teammates who may have copied his signature celebration. When the Yankees activated Clarke Schmidt from
item.content:encoded:
Baseball players can be an odd group at times. From bizarre pre-game rituals to over-the-top celebrations, things can get pretty weird on the diamond. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t meanings behind those idiosyncrasies. While Oswaldo Cabrera may no longer be a member of the New York Yankees, many people in the organization have not forgotten about him. This includes a couple of his former teammates who may have copied his signature celebration.
When the Yankees activated Clarke Schmidt from the IL on September 16, they needed to make a corresponding move to free up space on the 40-man roster. With playing opportunities becoming more and more scarce for Cabrera, he was designated for assignment. Just a few days later, he was picked up by the Cincinnati Reds. But deep down, it almost feels as if Cabrera will always be considered a Yankee in everyone’s minds.
As first pointed out by Max Mannis of Jomboy Media, two players on the Yankees appeared to pay homage to Cabrera during the team’s 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on September 23. Mannis tweeted a clip of Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr. firing off a unique yet familiar celebration as they each rounded the bases following their home runs.
Both players hit the crowd with a grenade toss celebration, something first popularized by Cabrera when he debuted with the Yankees in 2022. During the famous roll call at Yankee Stadium, the super utility player would uncork an imaginary grenade and pretend to lob it at the Bleacher Creatures in the stands. Was the grenade toss from Rice and Lombard Jr. just a way to say hello to Cabrera?
Oswaldo Cabrera made his time with the Yankees count
Rice and Lombard Jr. have yet to confirm the exact meaning behind their own grenade toss celebrations. However, it would make sense for them to do something small to let Cabrera know that they still appreciate him. Rice had been a teammate of Cabrera on the Yankees since 2024 and Lombard Jr. spent a few months as his teammate in Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.
Cabrera first joined the Yankees organization back in 2016 when he signed as a 17-year-old out of Venezuela. However, he was never able to really light up the minor league system with impressive stats until 2021, when he caught the Yankees’ attention with an .863 OPS in 118 games.
The following season, he got his first taste of the majors and almost immediately became a fan favorite. Like with most things that Cabrera did, he always seemed to add his own brand of flair to spice it up a bit. This included his own way of acknowledging the fans at Yankee Stadium.
Just like his time in the Yankees’ minor league system, Cabrera never wowed anyone with elite ability on the field in the big leagues either. With a career .232/.292/.343 slash line in five seasons for the Yankees, Cabrera was passable on the field. Yet the excitement he brought to the game made him extremely popular in the clubhouse and among fans.
If the potential grenade toss tribute from Rice and Lombard Jr. was any indication, it appears that his popularity won’t be waning any time soon.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Yankees’ Carlos Rodon Lands Disappointing News Before Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Jake Rogers
item.description: The New York Yankees will open the American League Wild Card Series without Carlos Rodón on the mound as a starter, a decision that lands as disappointing news for the left-hander after a strong late-season stretch. Manager Aaron Boone confirmed the rotation Sunday after rain washed out the club’s regular-season finale against the Baltimore Orioles. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday night against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium. Max Fried is lined up for Game 2. Gerrit Cole would
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will open the American League Wild Card Series without Carlos Rodón on the mound as a starter, a decision that lands as disappointing news for the left-hander after a strong late-season stretch.
Manager Aaron Boone confirmed the rotation Sunday after rain washed out the club’s regular-season finale against the Baltimore Orioles. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday night against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium. Max Fried is lined up for Game 2. Gerrit Cole would pitch Game 3 if the series goes the distance.
That alignment leaves Rodón without a start in the best-of-three matchup. For a pitcher who has looked sharp since returning from injury, the news is a setback even if the team still plans to keep him on the roster.
Rodón finished the regular season 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA across 16 starts. Over his last seven outings he posted a 1.89 ERA, giving the Yankees a fourth starter performing at a high level just as October began.
Boone said he expects to have Carlos Rodon on the roster to pitch out of the bullpen in the Wild Card series. Will Warren will also move to relief duty for the short series.
The arrangement is practical. A best-of-three format only requires three starters, and the Yankees have four quality arms. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, earned the opener. Fried and Cole follow. Rodón becomes the odd man out for now.
That does not erase the disappointment. Starters typically want the ball in October, not a relief role after months of building toward a postseason start. Rodón has dealt with elbow issues this year, including surgery last offseason and a midsummer inflammation stint, yet he delivered when he returned.
Boone has described the group’s depth as the club’s greatest strength.
“It’s clearly our greatest strength this year and we haven’t had it all together at different times obviously, but I do feel like all four of those guys are throwing the ball incredibly well right now at the right time,” Boone said.
The Yankees still value that depth. If they advance past Boston, the next series would be best-of-five. In that case Rodón would be a strong candidate to return to the rotation, possibly as early as Game 1 or Game 4 of an AL Division Series.
For this first round, though, his assignment is different. The bullpen role could include multiple innings if a starter exits early or a game tightens late. It is useful work, but it is not the same as lining up for a start against a rival the Yankees just faced in last year’s Wild Card round.
Boston presents a familiar test. The Red Sox and Yankees meet again in the Bronx after New York eliminated them a year ago. Schlittler already has a strong playoff history against them. The rest of the staff will be asked to follow.
Rodón’s recent form made the choice harder, not easier. A 1.89 ERA over seven starts is the kind of run that usually locks in a postseason start. Instead, the short series and the presence of Schlittler, Fried and Cole pushed him to the side.
The Yankees have not framed the move as a demotion. Boone has said Rodón remains very much in the conversation. Still, conversation is not the same as a Game 1, 2 or 3 assignment.
Playoff baseball often rewards flexibility. A left-hander with Rodón’s stuff could help bridge innings or face a key stretch of Boston’s lineup. That value is real. It does not change the fact that he will watch the first two games from a different vantage point than he likely hoped.
If New York wins the series quickly, Cole might even be held for the next round and Rodón’s path back to starting could open sooner. If it goes three games, Cole takes the mound and Rodón stays in reserve.
Either way, the initial announcement is clear. Rodón will not start in the Wild Card Series. For a pitcher who finished the year pitching well, that is the disappointing part of Sunday’s news.
The focus now shifts to Tuesday. Schlittler takes the ball first. Fried and Cole wait behind him. Rodón waits in the bullpen, ready if needed, and hoping the series lasts long enough — or the next series arrives soon enough — for another chance to start.

Aaron Boone had nothing but good options to open the wild-card series Tuesday night. In the end, he went with his best — and the one that would cause the least second-guessing and noise. Carlos Rodón, who arguably outpitched them all down the stretch, will be in the pen.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — The regular-season finale between the Baltimore Orioles and New York Yankees on Sunday was canceled because of sustained rain.
New York will host Boston in an AL Wild Card Series starting Tuesday. Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 on Tuesday, followed by Max Fried and Gerrit Cole.
Aaron Judge appears doubtful for the Wild Card Series because of a calf injury. As of Sunday, Judge’s only activity has been plyometric exercises and running on the treadmill.
The Yankees finished 93-67. They were 94-67 in each of the prior two seasons and no team has finished with the same record in three straight seasons, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Baltimore finished 79-82 under first-year manager Craig Albernaz, up from 75-87 last year. The Orioles have had consecutive losing seasons after winning 275 games from 2022-24.
The Yankees drew drew 3,297,154 for 79 home dates, down from 3,392,659 in 80 dates last year. They had 12 home sellouts, a drop from 20 last season.
New York never announced its lineup, and the game was canceled about three hours after the scheduled 1:05 p.m. EDT start. This marked the first time since 2002 the Yankees didn't play all 162 games in a non-shortened season.

item.title: [MLB.com] Yanks turn to Cy favorite Schlittler to start G1 of Wild Card Series

Gerrit Cole would start Game 3, if necessary. “Who wouldn’t want to start the first game?” Schlittler said earlier this
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The Yankees’ braintrust spent days debating their rotation in the American League Wild Card Series, only to arrive at a logical conclusion: Just hand the ball to the guy who’s about to win the AL Cy Young Award.
Cam Schlittler will face the Red Sox in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET, the team announced, to be followed by Max Fried in Game 2. Gerrit Cole would start Game 3, if necessary.
“Who wouldn’t want to start the first game?” Schlittler said earlier this week. “I feel like this whole pitching staff kind of deserves it. We’re all competitors.”
Fried and Schlittler both tossed side sessions before Sunday's rainout at Yankee Stadium, and manager Aaron Boone said he would wait to announce his plans until both hurlers came through without incident.
Asked how Schlittler took the news, Boone replied: “He was half asleep on the training table.”
“He’ll be ready to go,” Boone added. “We talked a little bit about it a couple of days ago, having not made my decision yet. But he’s excited. He wants the ball, and he’s ready to go.”
The Yankees have been keeping close tabs on Schlittler’s workload. He’s coming off a 33-start campaign in which he posted a 14-6 record and 1.95 ERA in a career-high 193 2/3 innings.
Pitching coach Matt Blake said earlier this week that while Schlittler has “earned the right to pitch Game 1,” the righty’s health was among the items the team would consider.
Additionally, Blake noted that Schlittler has pitched on his regular day for three consecutive turns. The Yankees held Schlittler to 70 pitches in that start against Tampa Bay.
“Cam is going to win the Cy Young Award and has been the best pitcher in the league,” Boone said. “It was just working through, do we want him in a Game 2 scenario with a chance to move on and slam the door, or if your back is against the wall?
“ … It was something we debated. Different people had different stances on it. I kind of considered both things, but ultimately decided this was the way I wanted to go.”
Ultimately, common sense prevailed. Schlittler’s 1.95 ERA is the Yankees’ lowest since Ron Guidry’s 1.74 mark in 1978, and he’s in line to become the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young Award and the first since Cole in 2023.
“He’s a student of the game,” Blake said. “He understands who he’s facing and which [pitch] shapes are going to work better to hitters. I think that’s something he’s learned a lot about as the years have gone on.”
Neck and neck with the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease in the Cy Young conversation for much of the season, Schlittler separated himself with a strong finish. He pitched to a 1.17 ERA (10 runs, seven earned) over his final nine starts, spanning 54 innings.
“He just doubled down on what we saw last year,” Blake said. “The fact that he’s held velo the way he has, the fact that he’s thrown probably more strikes than he did in July and August – it’s a testament to the work that he put in over the course of 30-plus starts to put himself in this spot.”
Of course, Schlittler knows what a playoff start in the Bronx should feel like.
“The environment, it’s electric,” Schlittler said. “Being home is important. To be in front of these fans, it’s going to be special.”

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 of the New York Yankees’ Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night and be followed in the rotation by Max Fried and Gerrit Cole in the best-of-three matchup.
New York made the announcement Sunday, the last day of the regular season.
Schlittler struck out 12 over eight innings in the Yankees’ 4-0 win over the Red Sox in last year’s Wild Card Series. He allowed five hits, all singles, and walked none. Schlittler threw 11 pitches 100 mph or faster, including six in the first inning.
Schlittler was 14-6 with an AL-best 1.95 ERA and 239 strikeouts this year, the first full season for the 25-year-old right-hander. Schlittler also allowed one earned run or fewer in his final nine starts, matching Whitey Ford in 1963 for the longest streak in Yankees history.
A native of Walpole Massachusetts, Schlittler went 2-1 with an 0.74 ERA in four starts against Boston this year. He struck out 27 in 24 1/3 innings and held hitters to a .174 average.
If the Yankees advance to a best-of-five AL Division Series against Tampa Bay, Schlittler would be lined up to start Game 2 and, if necessary, Game 5.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
Larry Fleisher, The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Aaron Boone makes Bob Nightengale look silly with final playoff decision on Cam Schlittler, Max Fried appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are set to take on the Boston Red Sox in the playoffs in the Wild Card round. MLB insider Bob Nightengale initially reported that the club was planning on starting Max Fried in Game 1 of the series, with Cam Schlittler getting the start in Game 2. However, manager Aaron Boone decided to do the exact opposite hours after Nightengale's claims.
Reports indicate that the Yankees officially announced that Schlittler will start in Game 1, while Fried will start in Game 2, according to Jorge Castillo of ESPN. It's also said that if the Wild Card series gets to Game 3, then Gerrit Cole will start that contest.
"Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series for the Yankees. Max Fried will start Game 2. Gerrit Cole would get Game 3 if there is one."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schlittler last took the mound in the Yankees' 6-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on September 24. The 25-year-old right-hander only pitched three innings in that contest. He enters the postseason with an American League-best 1.95 ERA and 0.919 WHIP with 239 strikeouts. He also led MLB in starts with 33.
As for Max Fried, he hasn't played since the club's 6-1 loss to the Rays on September 22. While that outing wasn't his best, the 10-year veteran has been consistent throughout the 2026 campaign. He'll play Game 2 of the Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox with a 2.80 ERA and 0.994 WHIP with 104 strikeouts.
The Yankees have one more regular season game against the Baltimore Orioles before the playoffs begin. That contest is currently on a rain delay. The Game 1 postseason matchup agaisnt Boston will take place on Tuesday, September 29.
Related: Ex-player makes feelings clear on Yankees Cam Schlittler MVP argument

item.title: [Claro Sports] Los Yankees aprendieron a jugar sin su capitán
item.dc:creator: Enrique Ballesteros
item.description: A pesar de las lesiones recurrentes de Aaron Judge, los Yankees han logrado asegurar su lugar en la postemporada y se preparan para enfrentar a Boston en la Serie de Comodines que comenzará el próximo 29 de septiembre. item.content:encoded:
A pesar de las lesiones recurrentes de Aaron Judge, los Yankees han logrado asegurar su lugar en la postemporada y se preparan para enfrentar a Boston en la Serie de Comodines que comenzará el próximo 29 de septiembre.
La historia de los Yankees en 2026 no comenzó en septiembre, cuando aseguraron su boleto a los playoffs. Comenzó mucho antes, cuando tuvieron que aprender a jugar sin Aaron Judge. El capitán pasó más de tres meses en la lista de lesionados por una fractura por estrés en la primera costilla derecha. Regresó el 8 de septiembre, después de exactamente 100 días fuera, y parecía que Nueva York finalmente podía afrontar el cierre de temporada con su principal figura disponible. Duró poco.
El 19 de septiembre, Judge volvió a la lista de lesionados, esta vez por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. El manager Aaron Boone describió posteriormente la lesión como de grado moderado. Los Yankees comenzaron a prepararse para la posibilidad de disputar la Serie de Comodines sin su capitán.
Judge, sin embargo, no ha cerrado la puerta a octubre. El jugador mantiene la intención de estar disponible para el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines, que comenzará el martes 29 de septiembre en Yankee Stadium. Boone, por su parte, ha señalado que el equipo se prepara para iniciar la postemporada sin él, aunque tampoco ha descartado por completo su regreso.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Parte médico de Luis Arráez: la lesión que podría condicionar los playoffs de Philadelphia
Una temporada construida en la ausencia
Cuando Judge se perdió tres meses, Nueva York no tuvo la posibilidad de simplemente esperar. La organización tuvo que encontrar otras respuestas. Spencer Jones ganó protagonismo y George Lombard Jr., un novato de 21 años, terminó convirtiéndose en una de las historias del cierre de temporada.
Lombard fue llamado a las Grandes Ligas el 4 de agosto y rápidamente comenzó a aportar. El prospecto número uno de la organización conectó un cuadrangular en su debut y posteriormente siguió ganando espacio dentro del equipo.
El 23 de septiembre conectó su sexto cuadrangular de la temporada ante Tampa Bay y el 25 volvió a aparecer en un momento decisivo, con un cuadrangular que puso a los Yankees arriba en la octava entrada. Nueva York terminó remontando para vencer 6-4 a los Rays.
No significa que los Yankees hayan reemplazado a Judge. No hay una sustitución individual para un jugador de sus características. Significa algo distinto: el equipo desarrolló una manera de competir en la que la ausencia de Judge dejó de ser una explicación suficiente para cada resultado.
Nueva York tuvo que mantenerse a flote sin su capitán mientras enfrentaba otras lesiones importantes y atravesó una racha de 4-14 entre finales de junio y principios de julio. Aun así, consiguió mantenerse dentro de la carrera por la postemporada.
El 14 de septiembre llegó la confirmación. Los Yankees aseguraron su presencia en octubre por tercera temporada consecutiva. Judge estaba en el terreno y había conectado un cuadrangular el día anterior ante Minnesota. Parecía el regreso perfecto. Cinco días después, volvió a la lista de lesionados.
El equipo encontró otras respuestas
La ausencia de Judge no explica por sí sola el camino de Nueva York hacia octubre. Tampoco lo hace un solo jugador. El pitcheo terminó siendo una de las principales razones de la estabilidad del equipo. Según estadísticas de la liga, desde el 28 de julio, los abridores de los Yankees habían permitido dos carreras limpias o menos en 40 de 51 aperturas y habían registrado una efectividad de 2.50 en ese periodo.
La ofensiva también encontró producción en otros lugares. Ben Rice llegó a 41 cuadrangulares el 23 de septiembre y empató entonces el liderato de jonrones de la Liga Americana. Los dos cuadrangulares llegaron en la victoria 9-2 sobre Tampa Bay.
Jugadores como Spencer Jones y George Lombard Jr. también asumieron una mayor responsabilidad durante una temporada en la que los Yankees tuvieron que redistribuir buena parte de la producción que esperaban de Judge.
Eso ayuda a entender por qué el regreso de Judge no es simplemente la solución a todos los problemas de Nueva York. El equipo ya desarrolló otras formas de ganar. Ahora tiene que demostrar que esas respuestas pueden funcionar en octubre.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Los mexicanos que dirán presente en los playoffs de MLB 2026: la legión azteca va por octubre
El capitán puede volver, pero el equipo ya cambió
La pregunta ya no es solamente cuándo regresará Judge. También es qué Yankees encontrará cuando vuelva. El equipo que comenzó la temporada tenía una estructura. La novena que atravesó buena parte del calendario sin su capitán tuvo que desarrollar otra. Y ese proceso también explica por qué la clasificación no puede reducirse a la ausencia del jugador más reconocido de la plantilla.
El admirado Judge disputó 66 partidos antes de su segunda lesión y, aun así, Nueva York aseguró el cuarto puesto de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees serán el primer comodín y tendrán ventaja de local durante toda la Serie de Comodines.
Boston aseguró el quinto puesto de la Liga Americana el 25 de septiembre, por lo que será el rival de Nueva York en una serie al mejor de tres partidos que comenzará el martes 29 de septiembre en Yankee Stadium. En una serie corta, la ausencia de Judge adquiere otra dimensión.
Durante seis meses, los Yankees pudieron repartir ese vacío entre cientos de turnos, entradas y partidos. En octubre ya no existe ese margen. Pero tampoco existe la misma versión de los Yankees que perdió a Judge en primavera. Ahora tienen un equipo que sabe cómo jugar sin él.

The matchup against the Boston Red Sox could be more challenging than many expect, especially with Aaron Boone not viewing Aaron Judge as fully ready for his return. According to what The New York Post Sports’ Greg Joyce revealed on X, the manager said that Judge has been doing some plyos and has been on the treadmill, but “not a whole lot yet.” It appears that No. 99 still does not have
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are nearing the end of the 2026 MLB regular season as they await their postseason debut. The matchup against the Boston Red Sox could be more challenging than many expect, especially with Aaron Boone not viewing Aaron Judge as fully ready for his return.
According to what The New York Post Sports’ Greg Joyce revealed on X, the manager said that Judge has been doing some plyos and has been on the treadmill, but “not a whole lot yet.” It appears that No. 99 still does not have a guaranteed return in the near future.
The Bronx Bombers face a tough Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox, a historic rival who the Yankees know very well from their battles in the AL East. Having Judge back on the field could potentially tip the scales in Boone’s favor, but not at any cost.
Judge’s injury struggles this season
It’s been a brutal, injury-plagued 2026 campaign for Aaron Judge. After missing more than three months with a fractured right rib that kept him sidelined from late May until early September, he barely got seven games under his belt before getting bit by the injury bug again.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees looks on.
This time, a moderate right calf strain landed him right back on the injured list, requiring a plasma injection and leaving Aaron Boone uncertain about whether he will be able to count on his star player at the start of the playoffs.
The Yankees have their eyes on the playoffs
The Yankees are closing out the 2026 regular season today, September 27, hosting the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium. Once Game 162 is in the books, all eyes turn directly to October baseball: New York secured the #4 seed and will host the rival Boston Red Sox in a high-stakes, best-of-three Wild Card clash right in the Bronx.
That series kicks off on Tuesday, September 29, with Game 2 on Wednesday, September 30, and a deciding Game 3 on Thursday, October 1 if necessary. If Aaron Boone’s men manage to advance past Boston, they’ll move on to the American League Division Series to square off against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays.
Key takeaways
- Aaron Boone indicated Aaron Judge is doing treadmill work but is not fully ready.
- The star slugger missed more than three months with a fractured right rib.
- The Yankees secured the #4 seed and will host the Red Sox on Tuesday, September 29.

item.title: [amNewYork] Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card preview: Big questions looming for both NY, Boston | amNewYork
item.dc:creator: Joe Pantorno; Amnewyork
item.description: Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night. Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Ale
item.content:encoded:
Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night.
Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Alex Cora, in April following a miserable start, then caught fire in the summer behind a historic 15-game winning streak to grasp onto the No. 2 Wild Card spot and never let go.
The Yankees will hope that history repeats itself in 2026 and that they can find a way to get past their bitter rivals at home, but there are a remarkable number of huge questions looming over this series for both teams that can turn the tide before a single pitch is even thrown.
Let’s take a look.
Will the Judge preside over his court?
The Yankees’ captain and two-time-defending American League MVP missed three months earlier this summer due to a fractured rib, then lasted just seven days before suffering a “moderate” calf strain, as described by manager Aaron Boone.
All signs point to Judge not being a part of New York’s Wild Card roster, which in part was fueled by Boone last week when he said that the team was not planning on the 34-year-old slugger being available. But Judge pushed back on that, saying, “I’m doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go.”
Boone disclosed on Sunday that Judge has been doing plyometrics and treadmill work, but other than that, “not a whole lot yet.” That certainly does not bode well for his availability, as he would likely be significantly compromised even if he was available.
Who starts Game 1?
In a short, best-of-three series, it’s usually a no-brainer to go with your ace in an attempt to do everything possible to get the quickest advantage possible. That, in turn, would mean Cam Schlittler, who posted one of the greatest single-season stat lines ever by a Yankees pitcher (1.95 ERA, 239 strikeouts), would get the ball for Game 1 on Tuesday, right?
Not so fast, says Boone.
The Yankees’ skipper is considering starting southpaw Max Fried for Game 1, meaning Schlittler would start Game 2 to either clinch or keep his team’s season alive.
In fairness, Fried has been great since returning from the IL in late July. Over his last 10 starts, he has a 2.29 ERA with 54 strikeouts in 51 innings. He has also allowed just one earned run in 11.2 innings against the Red Sox this season.
Schlittler has had mixed results against Boston this year, but most recently went 5.2 shutout frames on Aug. 28 despite walking five. Still, it was his heroics in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series last year that put the young righty on the map, going eight scoreless innings and striking out 12 in what was a 4-0 win.
Carlos Rodon, who has been red-hot to end the season, to the tune of a 1.89 ERA over the last five weeks, should get the ball for a potential Game 3, meaning the struggling Gerrit Cole might not be in the Yankees’ equation until a possible ALDS matchup with the Rays.
Will the Sox be without their biggest bat?
Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras’ career-best season was cut short on Sept. 17 when he was hit on the right hand by a pitch. Not only has he not appeared in a game since, but he recently experienced a setback while taking swings, then divulged that he still cannot grip a bat.
“It’s really concerning,” Contreras told reporters on Thursday. “But at the same time, I’m putting all my effort, and everything I can do, I’m doing it. I don’t know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better, but I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It’s a really important series, and I’ll be completely honest with the team.”
The Red Sox are already going to be without Mickey Gasper, who suffered what Red Sox manager Chad Tracy described as a “significant biceps injury” on Friday. The 30-year-old first baseman/catcher/DH had been red-hot as of late, coming out of nowhere to hit 10 home runs with a 1.082 OPS over his last 33 games before the injury. He would have been the obvious Wild Card replacement for Contreras, who owned a .905 OPS with 27 home runs and 81 RBI in 129 games this season.
For more on the Yankees, visit AMNY.com

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Brian Cashman is once again learning the hard way about Yankees' annual trade deadline failures
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos. You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankee
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankees have been running arms like Brent Headrick and Fernando Cruz into the ground all season long.
Not surprisingly, Headrick is beginning to show signs of fatigue (he is human, after all), and Cruz is now injured. The Yankees are signing no-name arms to stay afloat, and Cashman deserves blame for this situation. At least New York Post's Joel Sherman is seeing things clearly.
Brian Cashman thought he could get away with Yankees current bullpen
Are Yankees really still hoping that arms like the untrustworthy Luis Gil or the recovering Clarke Schmidt will help make this crisis go away? That's where we're at entering October, and it's sad.
This roster has a ton of talent, and the American League is decidedly weak this season. But since Cashman ignored the pitching staff at the deadline, their World Series chances have no doubt taken a hit.
While the overachieving Tampa Bay Rays held off the Yankees and Red Sox, and New York deserves credit for emerging from the "grave danger zone" of losing ground to Boston, this front office oversight still doomed them to the Wild Card. Cruz's injury alone doesn't prove this, by the way — he'd been awful since the All-Star break. Anyone watching the Yankees has been able to see that their bullpen has slowly been breaking down. It was happening way before the deadline! It's a miracle things aren't much worse.
Fans can't be too shocked at Cashman's performance (or lack thereof). This has become an annual tradition. He makes false assumptions that the Yankees have enough depth in a certain area (oftentimes the pitching staff), and they never do. He hates purchasing insurance, despite evidence to the contrary that this team underachieves in August (almost every year) and enters the playoffs wounded and tired.
Getting to the postseason has never been a problem for the Yankees during the Cashman era. It's the whole advancing once they get there that's been consistently disappointing, and you can trace that back to Cashman's deadline every season.
Max Fried came back earlier than expected. Great! Schmidt vacillated between being close and injured. Splendid! None of that changes the fact that Cashman should have added reinforcements at the deadline and failed to do so. The script is so familiar at this point. Fans just want something different for once.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Ryan McMahon hasn't solved the Yankees' third-base problem yet

item.description: Ryan McMahon gave the Yankees a useful hit in Friday’s second game against Baltimore. His RBI double helped New York turn a split doubleheader into a 6-3 win, and he finished 2-for-4. Two days earlier, he hit a grand slam against Tampa Bay. You can see why fans want to believe he is heating up at exactly the right time. I would hold off on declaring third base fixed. Even with those swings, McMahon is hitting .200 with a .559 OPS in 18 September games. One homer and nine RBI for the month tell y
item.content:encoded:
Ryan McMahon gave the Yankees a useful hit in Friday’s second game against Baltimore. His RBI double helped New York turn a split doubleheader into a 6-3 win, and he finished 2-for-4. Two days earlier, he hit a grand slam against Tampa Bay. You can see why fans want to believe he is heating up at exactly the right time.
I would hold off on declaring third base fixed. Even with those swings, McMahon is hitting .200 with a .559 OPS in 18 September games. One homer and nine RBI for the month tell you how long the dry spell has been. A couple of timely hits matter, but the Yankees cannot treat them as proof that the whole month disappeared.
The Yankees have to judge the full September
McMahon’s glove gives him a reason to play. In a close postseason game, clean defense at third base has value, and Amed Rosario is another active option at the position. The question is how much offense New York can afford to lose if McMahon stays in the lineup every day. Rosario offers a different look with the bat; McMahon’s defense and left-handed power offer their own case. Neither answer should be automatic.
New York already has enough lineup decisions to make, including how to fit its young infielders. Third base has to be part of that discussion. If McMahon carries this better contact into the final games, he can make the decision easier. If Friday was an isolated night, the Yankees need to be willing to use the other option.
McMahon can still finish this argument himself
The recent extra-base hits are encouraging because the ball is finally getting hit with authority. I’d keep him in the lineup for now and watch the quality of his at-bats beyond the next box score. He has earned a chance to build on Friday. He has not earned a blank check for October.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
On Saturday, the New York Yankees have the day off.
They split two games against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday in the Bronx.
The two teams will finish their series on Sunday.
Alex Rodriguez Sends Message To Former Teammate
Ahead of Friday’s series, the Yankees honored legendary pitcher CC Sabathia.
MLB wrote: “The Yankees honor CC Sabathia with a plaque in Monument Park and retire his No. 52 👏”
On Saturday, Sabathia sent out a post (via X).
He wrote: “Still feels like a dream. 52 forever in Monument Park!!”
One person who reacted was Yankees legend Alex Rodriguez.
He wrote: “Congrats to my brother, and one of my favorite teammates of all time, the legend @CC_Sabathia on joining the legends that live on Monument Park.”
Looking At CC
Sabathia played 19 seasons at the MLB level for the Cleveland Guardians, Milwaukee Brewers (and Yankees).
He spent the final 11 years of his career with the Yankees (and won the 2009 World Series title).
Sabathia went 251-161 with a 3.74 ERA in 561 games.
The 46-year-old retired after the 2019 season.
Looking At Rodriguez
Rodriguez spent 22 seasons in the MLB with the Seattle Mariners, Texas Rangers (and Yankees).
He finished the final 12 years of his career in the Bronx.
The 51-year-old retired in 2016.
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with a 93-68 record in 161 games.
They have already clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs (and will host the Boston Red Sox next week).

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Will Warren Just Became a Lot More Important to Yankees’ World Series Hopes
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: The New York Yankees are running thin on bullpen options after injuries to Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers. There's even some uncertainty around Brent Headrick after a dip in velocity in his most recent outings. That is why it's important that whenever Aaron Boone calls for Will Warren to come out of the bullpen this October, he's ready. His position within the org has become even more important to the Yankees. So far, Warren has appeared in relief three times in 2026. He first appeared against
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are running thin on bullpen options after injuries to Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers. There's even some uncertainty around Brent Headrick after a dip in velocity in his most recent outings.
That is why it's important that whenever Aaron Boone calls for Will Warren to come out of the bullpen this October, he's ready. His position within the org has become even more important to the Yankees.
So far, Warren has appeared in relief three times in 2026. He first appeared against the Pittsburgh Pirates in July. Warren then pitched in relief against the San Diego Padres and again this week against the Baltimore Orioles.
This outing against the Orioles was his most dominant, too, and that lines up well with the playoffs beginning next week. He went 3.2 IP, struck out seven, allowed no runs or walks, and allowed just three hits. This came just hours after the Orioles wore down the Yankees' staff in game one of their day-night doubleheader.
"It's obviously something new, so I want to get used to it," Warren said, according to MLB.com's Bryan Hoch. "In San Diego, I ran in and was a little bit gassed. We wanted to repeat that and just get our feet wet. I felt good, a little less blackout this time."
Warren's potential as a reliever
If you gave Boone truth serum about who he would rather see come in relief between Warren and Weathers, the answer would likely be Weathers. Weathers not only has the ability to get the strikeout, but he is also above average at generating groundballs.
Warren, on the other hand, has been spotty. He's always had a propensity to give up the big inning, and the grand slam he allowed in relief in the last ALDS ultimately killed that series. The Yankees will need better from him now, though.
If there's one thing the Yankees are hoping for, it's that the swing-and-miss stuff he had against the Orioles shows up this postseason. He had 13 swings and misses against Baltimore's lineup. Four came off the fastball, five off his sweeper, and two off his changeup. He has had swings and misses off of his curveball and slider.
It will be interesting to see how the Yankees use Warren. When Boone called him in relief against Baltimore, he came out after Yarbrough. This could be his role in the postseason as well, where a starter leaves the game early, and he bridges the gap into the sixth inning and potentially beyond.
If the Yankees are going to do anything this postseason, it might hinge on Warren getting important outs, whether it's the Rays, the Red Sox, or anyone else if they move on. This is why it's a shame that they weren't more active on the trade front this deadline. It feels like, while this bullpen has been solid statistically, it's hard to feel confident in the unit as a whole.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card Series is only four days away, and there are still so many lineup questions on both sides. Entering the weekend, it wasn't even certain that New York and Boston would be the ALWC matchup! There remained a slim chance that these two clubs would avoid each other in the first round entirely. But, with things settled after Game 1 against the Cubs on Friday, we've now got some very interesting personnel narratives to dive into.
On the Red Sox side of things, Willson Contreras' availability for the Wild Card Series is in serious doubt. Since being struck on the hand with a fastball on September 17, Contreras has been doing everything he can to heal, but his body might simply need more time. Luckily for Boston, X-rays revealed no fracture for Contreras, but there's still significant inflammation and a deep bone bruise.
As of Thursday, Contreras wasn't able to swing without pain. There were reports of him choking up at his locker as he dealt with the reality of not being available for the ALWC. So yes -- there seems to be a very real chance that Contreras doesn't play in the series, which leads us to the Yankees side of the equation.
Yankees rumored to be considering Max Fried in Game 1 of ALWC against a Red Sox lineup missing Willson Contreras
If Contreras is out of the picture, the Red Sox's lineup is suddenly missing its most potent right-handed bat. This would ostensibly give the Yankees a greater advantage with a left-handed starter on the mound in Game 1 (in the event that Contreras decides to play later in the series). And according to fresh rumors, New York is indeed considering leaning into that advantage and putting lefty Max Fried on the mound for Game 1.
Jimmy "Jomboy" O'Brien even characterized the Fried-Game 1 plan as "seemingly locked into place", adding that Cam Schlittler would be slated for Game 2 as part of the plan. Jomboy also relayed that he's heard that Giancarlo Stanton will be on the playoff roster, which makes one re-consider the veracity of all of these rumors. Even so, the Fried part in all of this makes sense, especially considering Contreras.
So what do Boone and Matt Blake actually have in mind for Game 1? It's worth noting that Fried has been historically dominant against the Red Sox, boasting a 1.10 ERA in five starts against Boston since he's been with the Yankees.
Schlittler is New York's undeniable ace at the moment and the imminent AL Cy Young, but the Yankees might seriously mess with the Red Sox by throwing Fried out there for Game 1 instead. Doing so would force Boston to employ their iffy platoon depth against a pitcher who has owned the Red Sox every time he's put on his cleats in recent memory.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge playing isn't just about Aaron Judge. It's about making the whole roster work around him.
Judge is most effective in right field, and since he's dealing with a calf strain, that could be problematic if the New York Yankees toss him out there. Whether he plays or not, that leaves Aaron Boone with one of his tougher decisions, and since it feels more likely that Judge won't play unless he can somehow force his way in, right field could get a little messy.
Right field is a major Yankees concern ahead of first playoff series
Lately, Boone's best option in right field has been Heliot Ramos, who's mostly been a bust since the trade deadline, aside from a few moments. For the last two nights, his glove has been an adventure—not in a good way—and it's clear outfield depth is needed right about now.
Unfortunately, there aren't many remedies unless Ramos suddenly turns it around defensively. Based on this week, though, it probably isn't happening.
On Wednesday night, Ramos was late to a ball, and not only did it fall in front of him, but he also bobbled it. This allowed the runner Jonny DeLuca to reach second base on a ball that went all of 202 feet.
Ramos had another gaffe on Thursday night. Taylor Walls was rounding second after a Yandy Diaz single, and when Ramos got to it, he attempted to gun Walls down at third. Instead, the ball sailed on him, went past Amed Rosario, and Walls scored.
Right field at Yankee Stadium isn't the most complex outfield situation. Hence why, when they acquired Juan Soto, who has never been a good outfielder by any defensive metric, they stuck him out there.
If Ramos can't handle it, they have a problem, and since they probably don't want to hinder Judge's calf any more than it already is, they might have to go with somebody out of position.
José Caballero is one name. He has had experience in right field, too.
Last season he had 2 Outs Above Average and 6 Defensive Runs Saved in right in 210.2 innings. This year, he's played just 60.1 innings and has been a neutral defender there, with 0 OAA and 0 DRS. A neutral defender feels like they're sporting Judge's defensive prowess out there, seeing as Ramos has a -4 OAA and -1 DRS in right.
Another name they can go with is Trent Grisham. Grisham, unfortunately, has been compromised due to a hamstring issue, but at this point, he might not have the mobility for center, so right field could be the way to go for him. It's much less ground for him to cover, and if he plays right, that could let Caballero play more of a position of need, like third base.
In this case, it's a matter of who they trust to hit against Boston's lefties more: Ryan McMahon or Grisham, who is fresh off the IL without a rehab assignment. This one, of course, is more outside the box, and the Caballero one feels more likely than Grisham covering right.
That isn't even something Boone has broached in his daily meetings with reporters. At the same time, Caballero has had some outfield experience over the last week, playing center field against the Diamondbacks.
In a perfect world, it would just be Judge out there in right field. Since they're thin on outfielders, and Ramos hasn't been any good out there, they might have to get resourceful defensively as they head into the Wild Card round. These are things you wish the Yankees had figured out earlier, but Boone will have to navigate what's happening.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [roundtable.io] New York Yankees' Gerrit Cole Has a Demon In His Way
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: New York Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole is surely motivated as ever to conquer this demon. And how could he be? You all know why. The Yankees were leading the Dodgers 5-0 in Game 5 with the chance to send the series back to Los Angeles for a Game 6. It was the fifth inning, and the bases were loaded with two outs. item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole is surely motivated as ever to conquer this demon.
And how could he be?
You all know why.
The Yankees were leading the Dodgers 5-0 in Game 5 with the chance to send the series back to Los Angeles for a Game 6. It was the fifth inning, and the bases were loaded with two outs. Cole then got the ground ball he wanted from Mookie Betts.
Except he failed to cover first base.
Instead of darting over to the bag like he should have, Cole furiously pointed to Anthony Rizzo, whom he apparently expected to make the play on his own. This even though everyone knows it's the pitcher's job to break to first.
Things then unraveled for New York in an embarrassing loss at Yankee Stadium.
Cole was then sidelined for all of 2025 due to Tommy John surgery, missing his chance at a getback.
But now, he finally has the opportunity to conquer the demon that has haunted him since October 2024.
It hasn't been an easy road back for Cole. He missed most of the first two months of 2026 while still recovering from surgery. Once he returned, he didn't seem to skip a beat, but then went through a brutal stretch over the last month where he surrendered 11 home runs over his final seven starts. That included seven over a span of two games.
Cole ended his regular season with a 3.61 ERA, averaging 9.3 strikeouts per nine innings while recording a 5.24 K/BB ratio. Not bad for a 36-year-old coming off of Tommy John.
However, his hiccups down the stretch have many worried about his playoff prospects.
Will Cole be able to deliver? Is he still a frontline starter capable of winning a pivotal postseason game? Or is he just not that guy anymore?
If anyone should be more motivated than ever to have the best October of his life, it's Cole.
Did Cole cost the Yankees the 2024 World Series? No. Chances are, they would have lost the series even if Cole covered first base and led them to a Game 5 victory. That Dodgers team was unstoppable.
But you can bet that there is still a very sour taste in Cole's mouth even to this day.
Cole is on a mission, and there is a holdover demon from 2024 standing in his way. We'll see if the wily veteran can eradicate it starting next week.

They had Volpe start at the hot corner Friday for the first time in his big league career, and by the end of the 10-2 loss to the Orioles in the opener of a doubleheader, he was still waiting for his first real chance.

If the Yankees want to ensure they do not have a ball hit to third base against them in the playoffs, perhaps they should just put Anthony Volpe there.
They had Volpe start at the hot corner Friday for the first time in his big league career, and by the end of the 10-2 loss to the Orioles in the opener of a doubleheader, he was still waiting for his first real chance.

Try it free
A ball was finally hit to third base in the ninth inning, except it hit the bag and flew over Volpe’s head, giving him no shot to make a play.
Otherwise, nothing came his way, and while he could start there again Sunday if the Yankees are not washed out, Aaron Boone still considered the game valuable for Volpe.
“Not a lot of action over there, but there’s something to be said for being in there and thinking through the situations and moving and setting up how you’re supposed to,” said Boone, who started Volpe at shortstop in the nightcap.
Volpe seems unlikely to start at third base in the playoffs, but he played there Friday so he could at least have it in his back pocket, which would give him even more positional flexibility after making the transition from shortstop to second base at Triple-A.
Having that versatility could allow the Yankees to get more aggressive in using pinch hitters and pinch runners in the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“I felt comfortable,” said Volpe, who credited third baseman Ryan McMahon, infield coach Dan Fiorito, Triple-A infield coach Gil Velasquez and former teammate Oswaldo Cabrera for helping him get up to speed at the position.
“No matter where you play, you got to anticipate and know where you got to be. I feel like I’ve picked it up.”
Before Friday’s doubleheader, the Yankees held the equivalent of postseason tryouts — or perhaps prove-its — as Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham faced Ryan Weathers, with all three trying to show they are healthy enough and ready to be on the wild-card roster.
Weathers, throwing one inning and about 20 pitches, was facing hitters for the first time suffering a left forearm flexor strain last month. Doing so Friday leaves the door open for him to be on the roster next week, which would give the bullpen a power lefty.
“He looks healthy, that’s what I took away,” Boone said. “Looks like Ryan stuff-wise. He was up to 96 [mph] with the velo[city]. A little scattered there in his inning, but just from my vantage point on the side, stuff looked good. … Whether [he’s an option for the] first round or not, that’ll be the conversation we have here in the next day or two.”
Stanton and Grisham, meanwhile, were facing live pitching for the second time in three days (and faced minor league lefty Xavier Rivas for more at-bats around Weathers’ inning). Despite not having played in a game for five months because of three calf strains, Stanton is in consideration to make the roster as a pinch hitter depending on how many position players the Yankees carry.
“Obviously we’ll talk to G, see where he’s at, mentally, physically, all that,” Boone said. “But having the threat there is real, and if we feel like he’s up to it and ready for it, the threat that we all know G is, we got to weigh that.”
Grisham has been sidelined for three weeks with a hamstring strain but could make the roster as a fourth outfielder (and potentially start in center against righties, with Spencer Jones moving to right).
- CHECK OUT THE LATEST MLB STANDINGS AND YANKEES STATS
“He’s knocking on that door too,” Boone said. “He’s checked a lot of the boxes and gone through his running progressions and things like that. So he’s very much in play and in the conversation too.”
The Yankees had 18 innings to cover Friday, but Carlos Lagrange was not called up to throw any of them. Across the two games, they promoted Brendan Beck, Yerry de los Santos and Alexander Cornielle to eat innings (Beck starting Game 1), allowing them to protect the rest of their pitching staff ahead of the postseason.
Lagrange, meanwhile, was not going to be available to pitch Friday after throwing live on Wednesday in Somerset, N.J., as part of the Yankees’ stay-ready group. The hard-throwing 23-year-old is still not far removed from a shoulder sprain, so the Yankees are being cautious with him even while keeping him in play to potentially be an option for a postseason roster.
“He had an injury, and he’s just started throwing lives again,” Boone said. “He threw live two days ago, so he’s not in play right now. Could be down the road, but he’s not in play yet.”
With Sunday’s regular-season finale in jeopardy because of the nor’easter — and the Yankees planning to call up Elmer Rodríguez for length if they play that game — Lagrange seems doubtful to appear in a regular-season game.

item.title: [New York Post] Will Warren delivers in relief in final act of regular season as Yankees playoff role comes into view
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
For a bullpen that has three (heavily used) sure things and a whole lot of question marks behind them entering the playoffs, Will Warren is trying to become one of the answers the Yankees will need to find. The right-handed starter made his final regular-season appearance out of the bullpen Friday and delivered 3 ¹/₃ scoreless innings in the Yankees’ 6-3 win over the Orioles to split the doubleheader, as he prepares for a relief role in the AL Wild Card Series and beyond.

item.content:encoded:
For a bullpen that has three (heavily used) sure things and a whole lot of question marks behind them entering the playoffs, Will Warren is trying to become one of the answers the Yankees will need to find.
The right-handed starter made his final regular-season appearance out of the bullpen Friday and delivered 3 ¹/₃ scoreless innings in the Yankees’ 6-3 win over the Orioles to split the doubleheader, as he prepares for a relief role in the AL Wild Card Series and beyond.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Warren recorded seven of his 11 outs via the strikeout, racking up 13 whiffs on 28 swings and flashing the kind of swing-and-miss stuff that could be valuable in the Yankees bullpen.
“He can be big for us moving forward in the postseason, and in different roles,” manager Aaron Boone said.
The Yankees know they have workhorses Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn to form the bridge to David Bednar in the ninth inning, but they could certainly use more help. Warren has a chance to offer it, especially as his velocity and stuff has ticked up over the past month.
“I feel like as a starter, you’re supposed to get both sides of the plate out, so I think that would be pretty big for us,” said Warren, who finished the season with a 3.92 ERA. “You see Blackburn do it, you see Headrick do it, so whenever my name’s called, I’ll be ready to go.”
The club kept Warren to 54 pitches Friday in his third relief appearance of the season, ensuring he will be available on Tuesday for Game 1 against the Red Sox while also offering some length if needed.
“I felt good — a little less blackout this time,” Warren joked, referring to his bullpen cameo earlier this month against the Padres.
On a day when the wind from the incoming nor’easter wreaked some havoc, the Yankees (93-68) dropped the first game of the doubleheader 10-2 before taking the nightcap. Whether they actually play Game 162 on Sunday remains to be seen, with the forecast iffy, but their bats came alive in the second half of the twin bill, including a two-run double from Anthony Volpe and two hits apiece from Ben Rice and Ryan McMahon.
Former Met Pete Alonso crushed a pair of home runs for the Orioles (79-82) in Game 1 — including a 471-foot shot that cut through the wind blowing in — to move into sole possession of the American League lead with 43 on the year.
The Yankees also had some questionable outfield defense in both ends of the doubleheader, windy or not. In Game 1, Spencer Jones could not track down a fly ball to center field, as it hit off his glove and turned into an inside-the-park home run for Jeremiah Jackson. In Game 2, right fielder Heliot Ramos simply dropped a fly ball to right field.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – A los Yankees les quedan un par de días de calendario, pero los partidos que determinarán cómo se juzga esta temporada no llegarán hasta la próxima semana. Todo lo que ocurra de aquí a entonces es simplemente preparación para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana.
Con su próximo enfrentamiento de comodines contra los Medias Rojas ya confirmado oficialmente, los Yankees completaron el viernes otras 18 entradas de temporada regular, logrando dividir honores en una doble cartelera tras vencer 6-3 a los Orioles en el Yankee Stadium.
La victoria de Boston sobre los Cachorros en el primer partido de su doble cartelera aseguró el quinto puesto de clasificación y confirmó el duelo contra los Yankees, quienes se quedaron con el cuarto puesto. Será una reedición exacta de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana del año pasado, que los Yankees ganaron en tres partidos.
"Prefiero mil veces que sea aquí. Lo quiero en el Bronx", dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. "Lo quiero con nuestros aficionados. Creo que, sin duda, existe esa ventaja".
Tras recuperarse de una derrota por 10-2 —sufrida justo después de la ceremonia de homenaje a CC Sabathia en el Monument Park—, Ryan McMahon, Spencer Jones, Anthony Volpe, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos y Luis García Jr. impulsaron carreras para los Yankees, que además contaron con una alentadora actuación de relevo de tres entradas y 2/3 por parte de Will Warren.
Los Yankees aún no han anunciado quién abrirá el partido de Comodin del martes contra los Medias Rojas; el coach de lanzadores, Matt Blake, señaló que están evaluando si utilizar a Max Fried con descanso adicional o a Cam Schlittler —principal candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana—, quien llegaría con su descanso habitual para el primer encuentro.
Sin embargo, dado que Gerrit Cole y Carlos Rodón también figuran como posibles abridores para la postemporada, está previsto que Warren pase a desempeñar un papel en el bullpen durante octubre. Como era de esperar, el repertorio de Warren lució mejor desde el bullpen, incluyendo una recta de cuatro costuras que promedió 94.5 mph (0.8 mph más que su promedio de temporada). Warren permitió tres imparables y no otorgó bases por bolas, además de ponchar a siete bateadores.
McMahon inauguró el marcador en la quinta entrada con un doble impulsador ante el abridor de los Orioles, Brandon Young, quien lanzó cinco episodios. Jones conectó un sencillo productor frente a Josh Walker en el sexto inning, y más tarde en esa misma entrada, Volpe bateó un doble de terreno que impulsó dos carreras ante Anthony Núñez.
Ramos y García conectaron sencillos productores en la séptima entrada.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The Yankees have a couple of days left on the schedule, but the ones that will determine how this season is judged won’t happen until next week. Everything that transpires between now and then is simply preparation for the American League Wild Card Series.
With their upcoming Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox officially locked in, the Yankees crossed off another 18 innings of regular-season action on Friday, securing a split of a single-admission doubleheader with a 6-3 victory over the Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
Boston’s victory over the Cubs in Game 1 of their doubleheader secured the No. 5 seed and confirmed a matchup with the Yankees, who claimed the No. 4 seed. It will be an exact rematch of last year’s AL Wild Card Series, which the Yankees won in three games.
“I’d much rather have it here. I want it in the Bronx,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “I want it with our fans. I think there’s certainly that advantage.”
Bouncing back after they followed CC Sabathia’s Monument Park enshrinement with a 10-2 loss, Ryan McMahon, Spencer Jones, Anthony Volpe, Heliot Ramos and Luis García Jr. all drove in runs for the Yankees, who logged an encouraging 3 2/3-inning relief outing from Will Warren.
The Yankees have yet to announce who will start Tuesday’s AL Wild Card Game against the Red Sox, with pitching coach Matt Blake saying that they are weighing Max Fried on extra rest against AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler, who would be on normal rest for the opener.
But with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón also in line as potential playoff starters, Warren is slated to transition to a bullpen role in October. Not surprisingly, Warren’s stuff played up out of the bullpen, including a four-seam fastball that averaged 94.5 mph – 0.8 mph more than his season average. Warren permitted three hits without a walk, striking out seven.
McMahon opened the scoring with a fifth-inning RBI double off Orioles starter Brandon Young, who worked five frames. Jones touched Josh Walker for a sixth-inning RBI single, and Volpe found the seats for a two-run ground-rule double facing Anthony Nunez later that inning.
Ramos and García each had an RBI single in the seventh.

item.title: [Independent en Español] Yankees retiran el número 52 de CC Sabathia y lo honran en Monument Park
item.dc:creator: Larry Fleisher
item.description: CC Sabathia vio muchas ceremonias en honor a exjugadores durante 11 temporadas con los Yankees de Nueva York y nunca imaginó que él sería uno de los homenajeados. Sabathia se convirtió el viernes en el 24.º jugador o mánager en ver retirado su número, y el zurdo miembro del Salón de la Fama fue homenajeado con una placa en Monument Park durante una ceremonia previa al primer juego de una doble cartelera contra Baltimore. Sabathia se unió a Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Andy Pettitte y Jorge Posad
item.content:encoded:
CC Sabathia vio muchas ceremonias en honor a exjugadores durante 11 temporadas con los Yankees de Nueva York y nunca imaginó que él sería uno de los homenajeados.
Sabathia se convirtió el viernes en el 24.º jugador o mánager en ver retirado su número, y el zurdo miembro del Salón de la Fama fue homenajeado con una placa en Monument Park durante una ceremonia previa al primer juego de una doble cartelera contra Baltimore.
Sabathia se unió a Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Andy Pettitte y Jorge Posada como el quinto integrante de los Yankees campeones de la Serie Mundial de 2009 con un número retirado y una placa.
"Nunca me imaginé entrando a Monument Park y creo que esa fue la razón por la que tenía tanto miedo de venir aquí, porque uno nunca piensa que va a ganarse a la afición de los Yankees o a la ciudad. Así que poder estar sentado aquí ahora, haber jugado aquí 11 años, es una sensación increíble, y por eso he dicho en las últimas semanas que esto se siente más grande para mí que el Salón de la Fama, porque sé lo que estaba en juego cuando vine aquí”, señaló Sabathia.
Con 46 años, Sabathia firmó un contrato de 161 millones de dólares por siete años antes de la temporada 2009, después de que el gerente general Brian Cashman lo convenciera tras una reunión inicial en diciembre de 2008. El contrato fue el más grande en ese momento para un lanzador agente libre.
Sabathia tuvo marca de 19-8 con efectividad de 3,37 en 34 aperturas con los Yankees en su primera temporada. Ganó el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, con marca de 2-0 y efectividad de 1,13 en una victoria en seis juegos sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles, y abrió los Juegos 1 y 4 cuando los Yankees vencieron a Filadelfia para conquistar su 27.º título.
Sabathia terminó con marca de 251-161, efectividad de 3,74 y 3.093 ponches —tercero entre los zurdos detrás de Randy Johnson y Steve Carlton— durante 19 temporadas con Cleveland (2001-08), Milwaukee (2008) y los Yankees (2009-19).
Durante 11 temporadas en Nueva York, Sabathia tuvo marca de 134-88 con efectividad de 3,81 y 1.700 ponches. Ocupa el cuarto lugar en la historia de la franquicia en ponches, el séptimo en aperturas, el décimo en victorias y el 11.º en entradas lanzadas.
Sabathia fue elegido al Salón de la Fama en su primera aparición en la boleta en 2025, al recibir el 86,8% de los votos. Fue exaltado junto con Billy Wagner e Ichiro Suzuki, excompañero suyo en los Yankees de 2012 a 2014.
“Esa ceremonia fue increíble, surrealista. Estaba diciendo allá afuera que tengo tantos compañeros famosos, ya sea Mo, Derek, Andy. Así que he estado en la ceremonia muchas veces, pero que esa ceremonia fuera para mí es especial, y que mi familia estuviera ahí fue genial”, comentó Sabathia.
La ceremonia de los Yankees comenzó con mensajes en video de Jeter, Paul O’Neill, Jorge Posada y Bernie Williams, y Sabathia develó la placa junto con su esposa Amber, dos de sus hijos, dos amigos y su madre, Margie.
Después de los momentos destacados en video, Sabathia saludó a los aficionados desde un carrito de golf a lo largo de la pista de advertencia. Recibió un saco azul, una versión enmarcada de su placa y del número retirado, además de un anillo conmemorativo de su carrera, de manos del gerente general Brian Cashman, quien fue abucheado por los aficionados.
Tras la ceremonia, Sabathia realizó el lanzamiento ceremonial de la primera bola a su hijo Carsten, primera base de ligas menores de Milwaukee.

item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Let's get this out of the way right away: Anthony Volpe isn't Derek Jeter. Sure, it's pointing out the obvious about the New York Yankees legend compared to their current infielder. But it's also to say that yes, different standards applied to Jeter than currently apply to Volpe. Still, it makes for a fascinating contrast when you consider what Volpe is doing right now. item.content:encoded:
Let's get this out of the way right away: Anthony Volpe isn't Derek Jeter.
Sure, it's pointing out the obvious about the New York Yankees legend compared to their current infielder. But it's also to say that yes, different standards applied to Jeter than currently apply to Volpe.
Still, it makes for a fascinating contrast when you consider what Volpe is doing right now.
On Friday, Volpe made his first career start at third base.
This is a guy who came up as a shortstop, and has also played some second base. But he's never played third until working out there recently to prepare for this opportunity.
Because the Yankees have George Lombard Jr. at shortstop, and usually have Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second base, this may be Volpe's best chance to play at the moment — particularly given the ongoing struggles of Ryan McMahon.
So the narrative is different than the Jeter history we're about to dig into.
It is interesting, though: Volpe has made a move that Jeter never did.
Derek Jeter's History With Third Base
Jeter, for all his highlight-reel jump throws and catches falling into the stands, wasn't a great defensive shortstop. By the back half of his career, he graded out below average.
Despite that, the Yankees never moved him off the position.
Jeter was a shortstop, and so he remained a shortstop. When you're the Captain, that's what you get to do.
But there was an obvious inflection point for that position and Jeter that could've changed the story.
When the Yankees signed Alex Rodriguez, A-Rod was still playing shortstop for the Texas Rangers, and he was good at that spot, a true five-tool player.
Jeter didn't budge, though.
A-Rod went to third base.
On some of the most loaded teams of the '00s, the Yankees had their best defensive option for shortstop playing third base.
Volpe is Different
Of course Volpe is different. He's not in a position to refuse to move to a different position.
But there's something about shortstop in the Bronx that draws added attention. When it was Volpe's turn, people wondered, very under-their-breath, whether he could be the heir to Jeter. It's the pressure that comes at that spot.
Lombard will soon feel much the same pressure, and it'll be up to him to handle it.
Volpe had plenty of positive moments, but also some miscues, particularly with the glove. It has led to his training at other spots in hopes of lasting in the big leagues.
Jeter never had to worry about losing his job. He could just be Jeter.
But there's merit to moving a shortstop to another position. The Yankees are hoping it pays off with Volpe.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees' Anthony Volpe Doing What Derek Jeter Refused To Do appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
CC Sabathia es homenajeado por los Yankees al retirar el número 52 que utilizó en Nueva York por 11 años
NUEVA YORK — CC Sabathia presenció muchas ceremonias en honor a exjugadores durante sus 11 temporadas con los Yankees de Nueva York y nunca imaginó que él sería uno de los homenajeados.
Sabathia se convirtió en el vigésimo cuarto jugador o entrenador en ver retirado su número, y el lanzador zurdo miembro del Salón de la Fama fue homenajeado con una placa en Monument Park durante una ceremonia previa al primer partido de una doble jornada contra Baltimore el viernes.
Sabathia se unió a Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Andy Pettitte y Jorge Posada como el quinto miembro de los Yankees campeones de la Serie Mundial de 2009 en tener un número y una placa retirados.
“Nunca me imaginé entrando al Monument Park y creo que esa fue la razón por la que tenía tanto miedo de venir aquí, porque uno nunca piensa que va a ganarse a los fanáticos de los Yankees ni a la ciudad”, dijo Sabathia. “Así que poder estar aquí ahora, después de jugar aquí durante 11 años, es una sensación increíble, y por eso he dicho en las últimas semanas que esto es más importante para mí que el Salón de la Fama, porque sé lo que estaba en juego cuando llegué aquí”.
Sabathia, que ahora tiene 46 años, firmó un contrato de 161 millones de dólares por siete años antes de la temporada 2009, tras ser convencido por el gerente general Brian Cashman después de una reunión inicial en diciembre de 2008. En aquel momento, fue el contrato más cuantioso para un lanzador agente libre.
Sabathia tuvo una marca de 19-8 con una efectividad de 3.37 en 34 aperturas con los Yankees en su primera temporada. Ganó el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, con una marca de 2-0 y una efectividad de 1.13 en una victoria de seis juegos sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles, y fue abridor en los Juegos 1 y 4 cuando los Yankees vencieron a Filadelfia para obtener su 27º título.
Sabathia tuvo un récord de 251-161 con una efectividad de 3.74 y 3,093 ponches, tercero entre los lanzadores zurdos detrás de Randy Johnson y Steve Carlton, durante 19 temporadas con Cleveland (2001-08), Milwaukee (2008) y los Yankees (2009-19).
Durante sus 11 temporadas en Nueva York, Sabathia registró un récord de 134 victorias y 88 derrotas, con una efectividad de 3.81 y 1700 ponches. Ocupa el cuarto lugar en la historia de la franquicia en ponches, el séptimo en aperturas, el décimo en victorias y el undécimo en entradas lanzadas.
Sabathia fue elegido para el Salón de la Fama en su primer año de elegibilidad en 2025, recibiendo el 86,8% de los votos. Fue incorporado junto con Billy Wagner e Ichiro Suzuki, excompañero de los Yankees entre 2012 y 2014.
“Esa ceremonia fue increíble, surrealista”, dijo Sabathia. “Estaba comentando que tengo muchos compañeros famosos, como Mo, Derek y Andy. He asistido a la ceremonia muchas veces, pero que esta fuera solo para mí es especial, y tener a mi familia allí fue genial”.
La ceremonia de los Yankees comenzó con mensajes en vídeo de Jeter, Paul O'Neill, Jorge Posada y Bernie Williams, y Sabathia develó la placa junto a su esposa Amber, dos de sus hijos, dos amigos y su madre, Margie.
Tras la proyección de un vídeo con los mejores momentos, Sabathia saludó a los aficionados desde un carrito de golf junto a la pista de advertencia. El gerente general, Brian Cashman, le entregó una chaqueta azul, una placa enmarcada con su número retirado y un anillo que conmemoraba su trayectoria, lo cual fue abucheado por los aficionados.
Tras la ceremonia, Sabathia realizó el lanzamiento ceremonial de honor a su hijo Carsten, primera base de las ligas menores de Milwaukee.
