item.content:encoded:
By Field Level Media
Sep 24 (Field Level Media) – Manny Machado homered and drove in three runs as the San Diego Padres moved to the brink of their third consecutive playoff appearance with a 5-1 road victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday.
Fernando Tatis Jr. had three hits as the Padres reduced their magic number for clinching a National League wild-card spot to one. San Diego sits in the top NL wild-card position, one game ahead of both the Chicago Cubs and the Philadelphia Phillies.
San Diego won for the 14th time in its past 16 games while coming out on top for just the fourth time in 12 games against Los Angeles this season. The Padres have never reached the playoffs in three consecutive seasons.
In his return to the roster after recovering from knee and biceps injuries, Shohei Ohtani went 1-for-4 with a walk as the Dodgers saw their 11-game home winning streak end. Andy Pages and Teoscar Hernandez each had three hits while Los Angeles ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9) gave up four runs (two earned) on five hits over six innings.
Brewers 4, Phillies 1
Brice Turang and Christian Yelich hit early home runs as visiting Milwaukee topped Philadelphia.
William Contreras knocked in two runs for the Brewers, who extended their franchise-record win total. Milwaukee needs to capture one of its final four games to reach 100 victories for the first time in team history. Logan Henderson (11-3) allowed one run in five innings.
Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola (7-11) permitted four runs and four hits in six innings. Bryson Stott doubled twice for the Phillies, who have a magic number of two to clinch a playoff berth.
Marlins 3, Cubs 2
Esteury Ruiz’s hustle enabled visiting Miami to score the go-ahead run in the seventh inning, leading to a win over Chicago.
After a video review, Ruiz was declared safe at second base on what was originally ruled an inning-ending double play, with Agustin Ramirez scoring to break a 2-2 tie. Cade Gibson (6-2) threw one perfect inning, and ace Sandy Alcantara recorded his second save.
Cubs starter Kevin Gausman allowed two runs in 5 2/3 innings, exiting after hurting his left shoulder while diving to make a tag at third base. Dansby Swanson hit a two-run single in the bottom of the sixth after Kyle Stowers socked a two-run homer in the top of the frame.
Diamondbacks 5, Rockies 3
Tim Tawa homered, Gabriel Moreno had three hits and Arizona continued its drive for a postseason berth with a win over Colorado in Denver.
The Diamondbacks have won four straight to move within three games of the Phillies and the Cubs in the chase for the last two NL wild-card positions with four games to play. Arizona starter Merrill Kelly (10-14) allowed two runs on four hits in 5 1/3 innings.
Ezequiel Tovar homered and finished with two hits for the Rockies, who lost for the 14th time in 16 games. Rookie Mason Adams (0-2) struck out a career- high eight over a career-best six innings. He yielded four runs, all unearned, on five hits.
Mariners 6, Astros 5 (10 innings)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as Seattle kept its slim playoff hopes alive with a victory against visiting Houston.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners, whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston and Texas, who are tied atop the American League West. Julio Rodriguez’s bases-loaded walk tied the game before Naylor’s winning hit.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier belting a two-run homer for the Astros. Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2) took the loss.
Mets 7, Rangers 2
Marcus Semien damaged his former team’s playoff hopes when he hit a tiebreaking solo homer in the eighth inning to help New York prevail in Arlington, Texas.
Juan Soto socked a two-run homer in the third and Brett Baty added insurance with a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth for the Mets. New York starter Nolan McLean (12-10) gave up two runs in seven innings.
The Rangers managed just four hits while losing their third game in a row. Jacob Latz (3-4) served up Semien’s homer.
Red Sox 1, Guardians 0
Andruw Monasterio’s sixth-inning RBI single and Sonny Gray’s six shutout innings propelled Boston past visiting Cleveland.
The Red Sox managed the lone run on 12 hits, all singles. They went 1-for-9 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base through five innings before Monasterio’s run-scoring single broke the deadlock. Gray (18-5), who allowed four hits, increased his AL-leading win total.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) worked six frames, allowing one run on 10 hits. The Guardians remained tied with the White Sox atop the AL Central.
Royals 5, White Sox 4
Maikel Garcia’s tiebreaking double in the seventh inning capped a three-hit, three-RBI night as Kansas City beat visiting Chicago.
While the Royals snapped a five-game skid, the White Sox missed a chance to regain control of the AL Central and clinch a playoff berth.
Connor Thomas (2-1) tossed two shutout innings for the win, and Steven Cruz recorded his eighth save. Kansas City’s Carter Jensen and Chicago’s Braden Montgomery each had three hits and a run.
Braves 3, Reds 2 (10 innings)
Mauricio Dubon’s infield chopper to the mound in the 10th inning gave host Atlanta a walk-off victory over Cincinnati.
Braves starter Chris Sale pitched 5 2/3 innings and allowed one run while striking out 10, reaching 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career. Matt Olson and Austin Riley homered for Atlanta, and Brent Suter (3-2) tossed a perfect top of the 10th.
Juan Brito led off the game with a home run, and he and Matt McLain each had two hits for the Reds. Cincinnati starter Andrew Abbott fired a season-high seven innings and allowed two runs.
Orioles 4, Blue Jays 2 (Game 1)
Baltimore’s Pete Alonso hit another home run and the Orioles eliminated visiting Toronto from playoff contention by winning in the first game of a doubleheader.
The Blue Jays were the reigning American League champions, but they won’t have a chance to return to the World Series.
Chris Bassitt (9-5) pitched five-plus innings to notch a victory in his third consecutive start. He gave up two runs on seven hits. Max Scherzer (3-9) surrendered four runs and four hits in five innings.
Orioles 4, Blue Jays 2 (Game 2)
Christian Encarnacion-Strand homered and drove in three runs and Trey Gibson took a shutout into the seventh inning as Baltimore completed a doubleheader sweep of visiting Toronto to stay in playoff contention.
Baltimore must win its remaining three games and have the White Sox lose their remaining four in order to have a chance for an AL wild-card spot. Gibson (2-3), a rookie who hadn’t pitched in the major leagues since June 30, gave up three hits in 6 2/3 innings.
Davis Schneider hit a two-run ninth-inning homer off Felix Bautista in the nightcap for the Blue Jays. Toronto rookie starter CJ Van Eyk (0-2) allowed four runs on four hits in five innings.
Yankees 9, Rays 2
Ryan McMahon hit a third-inning grand slam and tied a career high with five RBIs while Ben Rice hit a pair of solo homers as host New York rolled past Tampa Bay.
McMahon drove in five runs for the fourth time in his career. Rice homered on the first pitch of the contest to become the 13th Yankee with 40 homers in a season. He later hit his 41st. Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs on three hits in 5 2/3 innings.
Jonny DeLuca hit an RBI double and Cedric Mullins homered for the Rays. Mason Englert (0-4) allowed eight runs on nine hits over 3 2/3 innings.
Nationals 4, Tigers 2
Yohandy Morales hit a two-run homer and visiting Washington held on for a victory over Detroit as the Nationals won the three-game series 2-1.
Brady House had two hits and scored a run while CJ Abrams, who homered twice on Tuesday, reached base three times and knocked in a run for Washington. Will Dion (2-2) tossed two innings of one-run relief, and Yovanny Cruz got four outs for his first career save.
Detroit starter Framber Valdez (10-12) gave up two runs and four hits over 5 1/3 innings. Ben Malgeri homered and drove in both of the Tigers’ runs, and Kevin McGonigle added three hits.
Twins 4, Giants 2
Pinch hitter Walker Jenkins broke a seventh-inning tie with an RBI single as Minnesota completed a 4-3 road trip with a win over San Francisco.
Luke Keaschall drove in two runs with a homer and a sacrifice fly while Josh Bell added an RBI single for the Twins. Yoendrys Gomez (3-4) threw 1 2/3 innings of scoreless relief, and Andrew Morris escaped a ninth-inning jam for his fifth save.
Shay Whitcomb had two hits for the Giants, who have lost five out of six. Reliever Dylan Smith (0-6) yielded two runs while getting just two outs.
Cardinals 5, Pirates 1
Matthew Liberatore struck out six over 5 2/3 innings and JJ Wetherholt had three hits and an RBI to lead St. Louis to a victory at Pittsburgh.
Liberatore (6-14) allowed only one run — on a solo homer by Brandon Lowe — as the Cardinals snapped the Pirates’ season-high-tying five-game winning streak. St. Louis’ Jose Fermin went 2-for-4.
Lowe had two hits and Ryan O’Hearn added two doubles for Pittsburgh. Pirates reliever Brandon Eisert (3-3) gave up three runs in two-thirds of an inning.
Athletics 7, Angels 3
Rookie Henry Bolte recorded the first four-hit game of his career and Donovan Walton hit a three-run homer to help the Athletics top Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
Shea Langeliers had a two-run double and Bolte scored twice, had two doubles and drove in one run for the A’s, who assured they will avoid a 100-loss season. Geoff Hartlieb (2-1) threw 1 2/3 innings of scoreless relief.
Mike Trout and Vaughn Grissom homered for the Angels, who are two losses shy of the first 100-loss season in franchise history. Walbert Urena (9-11) allowed five runs and seven hits over four innings.
(–Field Level Media)

item.title: [arkansasonline.com] Brewers postpone Phillies’ celebration with win | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: PHILADELPHIA -- Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia's potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night. The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next sea
item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia's potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night.
The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next season and are coming off consecutive NL East titles.
The Phillies have to settle for a wild-card berth this season and are likely to open the playoffs next week on the road. The Phillies, Chicago and San Diego hold the three NL wild cards headed into the final games of the season.
The Phillies went 0 for 12 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers and left 10 runners on base.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said ahead of the game the team was willing to wait at Citizens Bank Park until after the Padres game ended, if necessary, to celebrate. No need to hang around.
Aaron Nola (7-11) had turned around a miserable season and posted a 1.86 ERA over his past eight starts as the longest-tenured Phillie got the chance to clinch. With a playoff party looming, he instead surrendered Turang's 20th homer of the season in the first inning and Yelich's 12th of the year in the second.
The Phillies scored their only run in the second inning after loading the bases with no outs against Brewers starter Logan Henderson (11-3). Henderson allowed four hits and one run over five innings to help the NL Central champion Brewers win their 99th game of the season.
MARLINS 3, CUBS 2 Kyle Stowers homered and Miami denied host Chicago a chance to clinch a playoff berth for the second straight night with a victory. Dansby Swanson drove in both runs for the Cubs, who needed a win or an Arizona loss to Colorado to secure an NL wild-card berth. Joe Mack's groundout brought home Augustin Ramirez with the go-ahead run in the seventh and the Marlins retired the next nine Chicago batters to win their second straight game after dropping three in San Diego.
DIAMONDBACKS 5, ROCKIES 3 Corbin Carroll had a two-run triple to cap a four-run first inning and visiting Arizona kept its playoff hopes alive with a victory over Colorado. Gabriel Moreno drove in the first run and finished with three hits to help Arizona (84-74) close within three games of the Phillies and Cubs for an NL wild card.
CARDINALS 5, PIRATES 1 Matthew Liberatore ended an 11-start winless stretch and Alec Burleson got his major league-best 112th RBI as St. Louis defeated host Pittsburgh. Liberatore (6-14) gave up 1 run and 6 hits in 5 2/3 innings with 6 strikeouts and no walks.
BRAVES 3, REDS 2 (10) Chris Sale struck out 10 and reached 200 strikeouts for the season, Mauricio Dubon delivered a winning RBI single in the 10th inning, and host Atlanta defeated Cincinnati.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
ORIOLES 4-4, BLUE JAYS 2-2 Pitcher Trey Gibson was strong into the seventh inning and host Baltimore beat Toronto to sweep a doubleheader and at least temporarily stay alive in the American League playoff race. One more loss by the Orioles -- or a win by the Chicago White Sox, who lost at Kansas City on Wednesday night -- would eliminate Baltimore. The Orioles also won the opener 4-2. The 24-year-old Gibson (2-3) allowed 3 hits in 6 2/3 scoreless innings with 7 strikeouts and 2 walks in his eighth career start
ROYALS 5, WHITE SOX 4 Maikel Garcia had three hits and three RBI, including a tiebreaking, run-scoring double in the seventh inning, as host Kansas City beat the White Sox and delayed Chicago's bid for a postseason berth.
RED SOX 1, GUARDIANS 0 Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single and host Boston edged Cleveland to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak. Gray (18-5) allowed 4 singles, struck out 3, walked 1 and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
YANKEES 9, RAYS 2 Ben Rice hit his 40th and 41st home runs, Ryan McMahon added a grand slam while matching his career high with five RBI and host New York beat Tampa Bay. Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed 2 runs and 3 hits in 5 2/3 innings with 8 strikeouts and 3 walks for the Yanks.
INTERLEAGUE
NATIONALS 4, TIGERS 2 Yohandy Morales homered for the second time in three games and Washington beat host Detroit. Washington has won eight of its past 11 games. Detroit has lost six of eight.
TWINS 4, GIANTS 2 Pinch-hitter Walker Jenkins hit an RBI single in the seventh inning allowed visiting Minnesota to win its second straight over San Francisco.
METS 7, RANGERS 2 Marcus Semien hit a tiebreaking homer in the eighth inning against his former team and Brett Baty added a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth as New York beat host Texas. Rookie right-hander Nolan McLean (12-10) allowed 2 runs and 3 hits over 7 innings for the last-place Mets, who have won both games in Texas since ex-interim manager Andy Green was given the full-time position Tuesday.

item.content:encoded:
Clarke Schmidt Injury: May be shut down
Schmidt could be shut down for the season if he's unable to pitch Thursday, MLB.com reports.
After completing his recovery from an internal brace procedure he underwent in July of 2025, Schmidt returned to the Yankees and pitched a scoreless two-thirds of an inning against Minnesota on Sept. 16. However, he suffered a biceps injury while warming up in the bullpen four days later. The right-hander reportedly had a "better" day Tuesday, but it's still unclear if he'll be able to return before the end of the season. Should Schmidt not be feeling well enough to pitch by Thursday, the Yankees may decide that he's better off being held out of pitching until 2027.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Diamondbacks’ Corbin Carroll Joins Lou Gehrig in Baseball History
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Those in the desert know. item.content:encoded:
Those in the desert know.
They know just how special Arizona Diamondbacks outfielder Corbin Carroll is, and they've known it from pretty much the moment he arrived in the major leagues.
For those from elsewhere, though, it's stats and milestones like the one Carroll achieved on Wednesday night that really drive the point home:
Carroll is keeping the company of some of the greatest players to ever play this magnificent game.
Often, his record achievements include Willie Mays, because Carroll hits triples at a rate that no one else in modern baseball does.
This time, it's Lou Gehrig.
That's right — Carroll just joined an MLB club that was previously a one-man show, occupied just by the New York Yankees' all-time great.
There's now room for two, with Carroll joining Gehrig a century later.
Corbin Carroll Joins Lou Gehrig
Carroll is part of a two-player historical club with Gehrig thanks to the triple he hit in the first inning on Wednesday night.
Batting against the Colorado Rockies with two on, Carroll turned on a ball down the line and took off.
There aren't a ton of active hitters who pull a ball and you immediately think triple. Carroll is one of those dudes.
It ended up being a no-doubter. He coasted into third.
It was the 60th triple of his career:
That brought along an awesome stat by MLB Network's Sarah Langs: Carroll is just the second player in MLB history with at least 60 triples and 100 home runs through his first 640 career games.
Gehrig was the first.
Gehrig isn't necessarily remembered for his athleticism, but he was a tremendous athlete who played college football and sprayed line drives all over the ballpark. He was going to get his triples, too.
Corbin Carroll Triples
Carroll was playing in his 640th game of his career on Wednesday night. He's up to 104 homers and 60 triples after that three-bagger in the first inning.
It marked Carroll's 17th triple of this season. That ties his career-high, which he set last season.
It's going to be the third year in a row that Carroll leads all of MLB in triples. It's the fourth year in a row he's atop the National League.
Carroll hit two triples in 32 games in 2022, then hit 10 in 155 games in 2023.
He upped it to 14 in 158 games in 2024, then 17 in 143 games last year.
Now he's got 17 again this year in his 152nd game.
Carroll hits doubles and homers, too, making him one of the most dangerous hitters in the sport.
And still just 26 years old, Carroll has a long way to go in continuing to build a special career.
But now that he's next to Gehrig in the history books? That's pretty epic.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Diamondbacks' Corbin Carroll Joins Lou Gehrig in Baseball History appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

24 Sep 2026, 07:55 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Ryan McMahon hit a third-inning grand slam and tied a career high with five RBIs, while Ben Rice hit a pair of solo homers as the host New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night.
McMahon drove in five runs for the fourth time in his career and started his big night with a two-strike single off Tampa Bay spot starter Mason Englert (0-4) for a 2-0 lead in the second.
After George Lombard Jr. started the third with a homer to right-center field, McMahon lifted a full-count offering down the right field line for a 7-0 lead.
It was the third baseman's third career grand slam, and McMahon went deep after Anthony Volpe took ground balls at third before the game.
Rice homered on the first pitch of the contest from Englert to become the 13th Yankee with 40 homers in a season. After hitting his fourth career leadoff homer, Rice homered again into the right field seats for an 8-1 lead in the fourth.
Rice had his fifth career multi-homer game and became the seventh player to reach 40 homers this season. Rice also added a single and reached base four times.
The Yankees (91-67) won for the 10th time in 15 games. Rookie Spencer Jones doubled and scored on McMahon's RBI single in the second, while Heliot Ramos chipped in a sacrifice fly.
New York's Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs on three hits in 5 2/3 innings in a postseason tuneup. Cole struck out eight, walked three and reached double-digit victories for the 10th time in his career.
Jonny DeLuca hit an RBI double, and Cedric Mullins homered for the Rays (96-62), who fell three games behind Milwaukee for the best record in baseball.
After clinching their fifth AL East title on Tuesday, the Rays rested AL hits leader Yandy Diaz and played Junior Caminero for five innings.
Englert allowed eight runs on nine hits over 3 2/3 innings after Ian Seymour was originally slated to start for Tampa Bay. Seymour is expected to pitch in Thursday's series finale.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Bronx Pinstripes] Schlittler Makes Franchise History, Yankees Bury Angels With Five-Run…
item.dc:creator: Jimmy Spiro
item.description: Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th. Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. item.content:encoded:
Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th.
Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. By the time the inning was over, the Yankees had scored five runs on four straight singles and taken the rubber match of the series, 2-1.
The Turning Point
Extra innings started with Amed Rosario parked on second, the automatic runner, and it took a while to cash him in. José Caballero singled to send him to third. Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked to load the bases. Luis García Jr. popped out for the second out, and for a second it looked like the Yankees might strand the whole mess (they'd left 14 men on base by night's end, which tells you something about how stubborn this offense had been all night).
Then Wells got to Murphy. Two runs scored, Chisholm to third. Cody Bellinger singled him home. Trent Grisham singled Wells home. Ben Rice singled in Bellinger. Four hitters, four singles, five runs, and the Angels never got the third out they needed to escape it.
Star of the Game: Schlittler Rewrites the Record Book
Before any of that happened, Schlittler spent eight innings quietly making history. Two hits. One run. Nine strikeouts. Zero walks. Ninety-nine pitches, 71 of them strikes -- the kind of start where you check the line twice because it doesn't look real for a guy facing a lineup with Mike Trout in it.
That was the 19th time this season Schlittler has allowed a run or fewer in a start. That's a new Yankees single-season record, passing the mark of 18 shared by Ron Guidry's 1978 Cy Young season, Whitey Ford in 1964, and Jack Chesbro all the way back in 1904. Good company. Better yet, Schlittler's still adding to it.
He didn't get the win (no decision, if you're scoring at home), because the Yankees' bats needed extra innings to back him up. He also didn't seem to care. That's usually the sign of the right kind of pitcher.
Detmers Made Him Earn It
Give the Angels' Reid Detmers his due, too. Seven innings, six hits, one earned run, eight strikeouts of his own -- the only damage against him a ground-rule double by Rosario in the fourth that scored Bellinger. For seven innings, this was a legitimate pitchers' duel between two guys who deserved a better final line than "no decision."
Vaughn Grissom's solo homer off Schlittler in the seventh tied it at 1-1 and set up the standoff that lasted until the 10th blew it open.
Boone's Bullpen Math Worked, Barely
David Bednar came in for a scoreless ninth -- one hit, three strikeouts -- and got the win when the Yankees broke through an inning later, which is how it works even if Bednar didn't throw a single pitch in the inning that decided it. Michael Fulmer took the 10th with a five-run lead and made it interesting, giving up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros that scored the Angels' own automatic runner, Wade Meckler. Fulmer got the next two outs anyway. A laugher stayed a win, which is really all that matters in the box score.
Yankees take the series 2-1 after dropping the opener 1-10 on Monday, and they move to 80-60, three and a half back of the Rays with a month to play. San Diego's up next.
Jimmy writes the Bronx Pinstripes game recap after every Yankees game. Beat-reporter pacing, fan's heartbeat. He calls opposing players by last name and has no patience for dead-air innings.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees (91-67) defeated the Tampa Bay Rays (96-62) 9-2 on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium to take a 2-1 lead in the four-game series.
The win comes a day after the Rays clinched the American League East championship. Ben Rice hit his 40th home run for the Yankees in the first inning, and his 41st homer in the fourth. After New York added a single run in the second, they broke through with five in the third, thanks in part to a grand slam from Ryan McMahon.
The Rays offense came from Jonny DeLuca, who hit a RBI double in the fourth, and Cedric Mullins who hit a solo homer in the fifth. Mason Englert (0-4, 5.95) took the loss for the Rays, allowing eight earned runs on nine hits in three and two-third innings in which he struck out six and walked one.
The Rays will now try to split the four-game series when they meet in the finale on Thursday night. Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38) is scheduled to start for the Rays and face Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94) for New York. First pitch Thursday is scheduled for 7:05 PM - pregame coverage begins with Ronnie Lane hosting Inside Pitch at 6:00 PM on 95.7 WDAE & AM 620, your Home of Rays Baseball.
COVER PHOTO COURTESY GETTY IMAGES

item.content:encoded:
Cole (10-9) earned the win Wednesday over the Rays, allowing two runs on three hits and three walks over 5.2 innings. He struck out eight.
Cole ended his regular season on a high note, allowing just four runs over 11.2 innings while striking out 17 in his last two starts -- he had struggled to a 5.96 ERA in his previous four outings. The right-hander held Tampa Bay scoreless Wednesday until Jonny DeLuca's two-out RBI double in the fourth inning before Cedric Mullins added a solo home run in the fifth. Cole will finish the regular season with a 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and 131:25 K:BB across 22 starts (127 innings).

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – Han pasado cuatro días desde que Aaron Judge afirmó que el plan era "definitivamente" regresar a tiempo para la postemporada. Aunque los Yankees están planificando asumiendo que no estará disponible, la mentalidad del capitán no ha cambiado.
Judge declaró a ESPN el miércoles que tiene la intención de estar listo para el primer partido de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana, programado para el 29 de septiembre en el Yankee Stadium.
"Ese es el plan", dijo Judge a ESPN. "Tratar de preparar mi cuerpo para estar listo para jugar".
Al preguntársele sobre la situación de Judge antes del partido del miércoles, el manager Aaron Boone señaló que "el proceso ha comenzado y está en marcha".
"No sé cómo se desarrollarán los próximos días", comentó Boone. "Esperamos que se recupere lo más rápido posible y que sea una opción cuanto antes".
El martes, Boone informó que Judge sufre una distensión de "grado moderado" en la pantorrilla derecha, lesión que probablemente lo dejaría fuera de la Serie de Comodines.
"Estamos planificando contando con que no participe en ella", dijo Boone el martes. "Pero también estamos en una época del año en la que... obviamente forzaríamos un poco la situación si fuera una posibilidad real. Sin embargo, falta una semana. No cuento con ello, pero tampoco lo descarto".
Judge fue colocado en la lista de lesionados de 10 días el sábado, con efecto retroactivo al 17 de septiembre.
El jugador recibió una inyección de plasma en plaquetas (PPP) en la pantorrilla derecha durante el día de descanso del lunes y realizará actividades limitadas durante los próximos días.
Judge dijo a ESPN que ha conversado con los responsables de la toma de decisiones de la organización sobre su pronóstico.
"Hemos hablado mucho, pero no puedo controlar lo que dice la gente", dijo Judge. "Así que tendrán que hablar con ellos sobre eso".
Durante la serie del equipo el fin de semana en Phoenix, Judge y Boone se mostraron imprecisos respecto a la gravedad de la lesión, que Judge sufrió la semana pasada en la serie contra los Mellizos.
Judge reveló que se trata de una distensión en el músculo sóleo de la pantorrilla derecha, una zona que, según señaló, "es un poco más crítica para correr y batear".
"Ya he lidiado con distensiones antes y he jugado a pesar de ellas, pero esta vez la lesión estaba en una zona distinta, lo que lo hacía un poco más difícil", comentó Judge.
Por lo general, la recuperación de una distensión de grado 2 en la pantorrilla requiere al menos tres semanas.
"Si está en condiciones de jugar, le daremos la oportunidad", dijo Boone.
Judge se perdió gran parte del verano debido a una fractura en una costilla derecha, sufrida aparentemente el 26 de abril en Houston. Jugó con la lesión antes de ser incluido en la lista de lesionados a principios de junio.
Tras ser reactivado en septiembre sin pasar por un periodo de rehabilitación en ligas menores, Judge disputó solo siete partidos y bateó de 23-4 (.174) con un jonrón.
En total, Judge registró una línea ofensiva de .241/.360/.511, con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos esta temporada.
"Tenemos partidos que ganar", dijo Judge. "Me pagan por jugar con los Yankees de Nueva York, así que volveré tan pronto como pueda".

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK –- Durante el reciente viaje de los Yankees a Phoenix, Aaron Boone se reclinó detrás del escritorio de una oficina, claramente satisfecho con su capacidad para hacer pronósticos. Meses atrás, había predicho que Ben Rice terminaría con 39 jonrones, una cifra que le pareció baja a uno de los interesados.
“Ya sabes lo que está tratando de hacer”, dijo Rice entonces. “Estaba tratando de provocarme un poco. Le gusta quedarse una o dos por debajo de lo que quizás sería tu meta”.
Rice debería apreciar más esta cifra: Su actuación de dos cuadrangulares la noche del miércoles le permitió compartir el liderato de jonrones de la Liga Americana. Ryan McMahon conectó un grand slam y George Lombard Jr. también se voló la cerca, impulsando a los Yankees a una victoria por 9-2 sobre los Rays en el Yankee Stadium.
Con 41 vuelacercas, la mayor cantidad del equipo, Rice igualó a Pete Alonso, de los Orioles, Yordan Álvarez, de los Astros, y Junior Caminero, de Tampa Bay, con la mayor cantidad en la Liga Americana. La cifra representa un récord personal para Rice, quien recibió su primer llamado al Juego de Estrellas este verano y se perfila como una pieza integral de la producción ofensiva de los Yankees en los playoffs.
Rice se unió a Aaron Judge (cuatro veces) como los únicos jugadores seleccionados por los Yankees en el Draft que han conectado al menos 40 bambinazos en una temporada. Judge (2017), Rice (2026) y Joe DiMaggio (1937) son los únicos jugadores de los Yankees que han tenido una campaña de 40 jonrones dentro de sus primeros tres años de carrera.
McMahon remolcó cinco carreras y los Yankees ganaron por décima ocasión en 14 juegos.
Gerrit Cole limitó a Tampa Bay a dos anotaciones y tres hits en 5.2 innings, realizando 105 pitcheos, 63 de ellos strikes, su mayor cantidad de la temporada, en su última apertura de la campaña regular. El derecho se prepara para una esperada asignación en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Cole otorgó tres bases por bolas y ponchó a ocho, permitiendo un cuadrangular de Cedric Mullins en la quinta entrada. Cole terminó el año con récord de 10-9 y efectividad de 3.61 en 22 aperturas, luego de regresar a finales de mayo de una cirugía Tommy John a la que se sometió en marzo del 2025.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Ben Rice hit his 40th and 41st home runs, Ryan McMahon added a grand slam while matching his career high with five RBIs and the New York Yankees beat the Tampa Bay Rays 9-2 on Wednesday night.
Gerrit Cole (10-9) allowed two runs and three hits in 5 2/3 innings and a season-high 105 pitches with eight strikeouts and three walks. The 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner had a 3.61 ERA and 131 strikeouts over 22 starts and 127 innings following his return in May from Tommy John surgery.
A day after Tampa Bay clinched the AL East title, Rice hit the first pitch of the first inning from Mason Englert (0-4) into the right-field second deck for his fourth career leadoff homer and second this season.
Rice added a solo drive in the fourth for his fifth career multihomer game and finished with three hits. He is tied for the AL home run lead with Baltimore's Pete Alonso, the Rays' Junior Caminero and Houston's Yordan Alvarez.
George Lombard Jr. also homered for the Yankees and Cedric Mullins went deep for the Rays.
New York is assured of hosting a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series starting Tuesday, likely against Boston. The winner will face the Rays in a best-of-five Division Series.
McMahon had an RBI single in the second and boosted the lead to 7-0 in the third with his third career slam.
Englert, brought up to allow Rays starters extra rest ahead of the playoffs, allowed eight runs and nine hits in 4 2/3 innings.
Rays manager Kevin Cash said left-hander Shane McClanahan won't recover in time for the Division Series but left-hander Garrett Cleavinger and right-hander Tyler Wells are possibilities. All three have forearm tightness.
Up next
Yankees RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94 ERA) and Rays RHP Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.56) start Thursday night's series finale.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – During the Yankees’ recent trip to Phoenix, Aaron Boone leaned back behind an office desk, clearly pleased by his prognostication ability. Months ago, he’d forecast that Ben Rice would finish with 39 home runs, a tally that seemed light to one interested party.
“You know what he’s trying to do,” Rice said then. “He was trying to get under my skin a little bit there. He likes to just short you one or two of maybe what your goal would be.”
Rice should appreciate this number more: His two-homer performance on Wednesday evening earned a share of the American League home run lead. Ryan McMahon hit a grand slam and George Lombard Jr. also went deep, powering a 9-2 victory over the Rays at Yankee Stadium.
With a team-leading 41 home runs, Rice tied the Orioles' Pete Alonso, Yordan Alvarez of the Astros and Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero for the most in the AL. The mark is a career high for Rice, who earned his first All-Star selection this past summer and projects to be an integral part of the Yanks’ playoff production.
Rice joined Aaron Judge (four times) as the only Yankees Draft picks to hit at least 40 home runs in a season. Judge (2017), Rice (‘26) and Joe DiMaggio (1937) are the only Yanks to have a 40-homer season within the first three years of his career.
McMahon drove in five runs as the Yankees won for the 10th time in 14 games.
Gerrit Cole limited Tampa Bay to two runs and three hits over 5 2/3 innings, throwing a season-high 105 pitches (63 strikes) in his final start of the regular season. The right-hander is preparing for an expected assignment in the AL Wild Card Series.
Cole walked three and struck out eight, surrendering a fifth-inning homer to Cedric Mullins. Cole finished the year with a 10-9 record and 3.61 ERA in 22 starts, having returned in late May from Tommy John surgery performed in March 2025.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Giancarlo Stanton, Carlos Lagrange, Game 1 starter among Yankees’ many playoff puzzle pieces
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while. “There’s a lot
item.content:encoded:
The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while.
“There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days,” the manager said before the Yankees played the division-winning Rays on Wednesday. “Hopefully, we have a lot of options to choose from.”
THE RETURN OF STANTON (AND GRISHAM)?
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 due to three separate calf strains (two right, one left), and Trent Grisham, sidelined by his second right hamstring strain of the season, took live at-bats in Somerset on Wednesday. Both ran the bases, and Boone said Stanton homered while getting six or seven at-bats.
“They’re knocking on the door,” Boone said, but he wasn’t sure if Stanton, a decorated postseason performer, could be ready for the Wild Card round.
The manager previously said that Grisham could be in play, though he wasn’t expected to be activated before the final five games of the regular season.
Asked what he would need to see from Stanton after a five-month layoff, Boone earnestly said, “I’m not sure.”
“I don’t know that answer,” he continued. “Obviously, there’ll be conversations with him. Does he fit on the roster? Is it realistic? All those things, and I can’t answer that right now.”
With the Yankees already log-jammed with first-base/DH types — Stanton can’t play the outfield anymore — Boone added that the former MVP would probably be used as a pinch-hitter, if anything. While not a big role, Stanton’s right-handed bat could be helpful off the bench if the Yankees face the lefty-heavy Red Sox, their likeliest opponent, in the Wild Card round.
Grisham, meanwhile, would give the Yankees an interesting choice in center field with Spencer Jones handling the position in his absence. Jones has outperformed Grisham at the plate, but both are shaky defenders, and the latter has postseason experience that the rookie does not.
LAGRANGE TO DEBUT?
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said of flamethrowing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange, who threw live batting practice on Wednesday.
But the skipper noted that a lot of “unknown” comes with righty, who has yet to make his major league debut, only recently returned from a shoulder sprain, and has just eight relief appearances under his belt this season. If the Yankees were to use Lagrange and his 100-plus-mph fastball, it would be out of the bullpen.
Asked why the Yankees don’t just promote Lagrange now, Boone said that they still have to cover innings over the last few games of the regular season. They would also have to clear space for him on the 40-man and active rosters.
While Lagrange is 23 and Stanton is 36, both are in similar positions in that they offer the Yankees an intriguing combination of upside, mystery and risk. Asked how Boone might personally weigh all that as the Yankees prepare to make their postseason roster, he said the club will “make the best decision possible” “if those guys are truly pushing into the conversation.”
“Carlos is in the stay ready [phase]. G [got] at-bats today,” Boone said. “All, at least, putting them on the outskirts of the conversation, if nothing else.”
WHO STARTS GAME 1?
Cam Schlittler is the clear frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award. So he’s obviously going to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round, right?
“Not necessarily,” Boone said. “We’ll see. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 doesn’t affect the next series. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 can pitch Game 2 and Game 5 in the next series, for example. We’ll decide what makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games.”
Gerrit Cole, who totaled two earned runs, three walks and eight strikeouts over 5.2 innings and 105 pitches on Wednesday against the Rays, is currently lined up for Game 1 of the Wild Card round on extra rest. The 2023 Cy Young winner, now 22 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, has struggled to get swing-and-miss this season. He’s also faltered against the Red Sox throughout his career. With Max Fried and Carlos Rodón also in the rotation, the case can be made that Cole has been the Yankees’ fourth-best starter lately.
Schlittler, who dominated Boston in last year’s Wild Card series, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1. He is scheduled to make his final start of the regular season on Thursday.
VOLPE AT THIRD? MCMAHON OFF THE ROSTER?
With the lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon putting the finishing touches on an abysmal offensive season and taking a step back defensively, the righty-hitting Anthony Volpe did some pregame work at third base on Wednesday. Boone expects the shortstop turned second baseman to play the hot corner in one or two games before the regular season ends.
“Good to go,” Volpe, who played a few games at third in the minors this year, said of his comfort level at the position.
Meanwhile, José Caballero, another righty, has already gotten some starts at third over McMahon against right-handed pitching. If Volpe shows that he can handle third, it could increase the odds of the Yankees leaving McMahon off their Wild Card roster.
Boone said that he still sees McMahon as a “top-shelf” defender, but he entered Wednesday’s game with -2 Defensive Runs Saved and one Out Above Average, numbers well below career norms. Couple that with a 73 wRC+, and the $16 million man has not been a quality player, though he did hit a grand slam on Wednesday.
“I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I want him in the game and the ball hit to him in a big spot,” Boone said. “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half and lately getting it going. But through his struggles that he’s had offensively, he’s gotten a lot of big hits for us, too, along the way.”
On the subject of third base, Boone also said that he hasn’t given much thought to Jazz Chisholm Jr. trying the position again. However, he’s not ruling it out.
WHAT ABOUT OTHER INJURED ARMS?
Fernando Cruz made a rather adamant appearance in the Yankees’ clubhouse on Wednesday. The reliever, out with a partially torn UCL, repeatedly said that he refused to “accept” the diagnosis.
“I had real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” said Cruz, who isn’t considering surgery right now. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart, it’s not a partial tear.”
While it seems rather improbable that Cruz will pitch again this season, he said that that is his goal, and Boone didn’t rule out the possibility. The righty threw a touch-and-feel bullpen three days ago, and he plans to throw another bullpen on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Clarke Schmidt felt better playing catch on Wednesday than he did on Tuesday after experiencing some biceps cramping over the weekend. However, if the recently returned Tommy John patient is not a viable option by Thursday, “then we’ll probably go a different way,” Boone said, referring to the Yankees’ postseason roster plans.
Finally, Ryan Weathers isn’t expected to throw live batting practice until sometime during the Wild Card series, so he won’t be an option.
With Weathers ruled out and Schmidt’s status uncertain, it will be interesting to see how the Yankees fill out their Wild Card bullpen. On a related note, Boone said that he sees “no scenario” in which the team carries 13 pitchers for the series. They may not even roster 12, he said with so many balls up in the air.
“It depends who’s available and who’s not,” Boone said.

item.content:encoded:
- MLB. La interpretación del himno en la MLB se vuelve incómoda tras fallar una trompeta
- MLB. Gran preocupación por Aaron Judge: “Existe una fuerte posibilidad de que no vuelva a jugar esta temporada”
Tras un día en el que parecía descartada su presencia en la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana, Aaron Judge se niega a quedarse fuera y ahora tiene como objetivo ayudar a los New York Yankees en la primera ronda de los playoffs.
Aaron Judge mantiene la esperanza de regresar con los Yankees
Un día después de que el manager Aaron Boone reconociera que la organización se preparaba para disputar la serie sin su capitán, Judge ofreció una perspectiva mucho más positiva sobre su recuperación.
El toletero le dijo a ESPN que su objetivo es estar disponible para el Juego 1 del próximo martes, mientras continúa trabajando para superar una distensión muscular de grado moderado en la pantorrilla derecha.
“Ese es el plan. Intentar preparar mi cuerpo para estar listo y poder jugar”, afirmó Judge.
Las palabras del tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana contrastan con el mensaje que Boone había enviado apenas un día antes.
“Estamos planeando que él no sea parte de eso”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, aunque dejó abierta la posibilidad de un regreso si la recuperación del jugador avanza favorablemente.
Judge fue colocado en la lista de lesionados el sábado, con efecto retroactivo al 17 de septiembre, poniendo fin temporalmente a otra temporada regular marcada por problemas físicos.
El capitán de Nueva York recibió una inyección de plasma pobre en plaquetas el lunes y ha tenido restricciones en sus actividades mientras espera autorización para aumentar la carga de trabajo.
Aunque el tiempo es limitado, Judge todavía confía en sus posibilidades. Sin embargo, reconoció que estar en buenas condiciones físicas no garantiza automáticamente su inclusión en el roster, ya que la decisión final dependerá de los Yankees.
Por ahora, Nueva York se prepara para el escenario de disputar la postemporada sin su principal figura ofensiva, pero la puerta para el regreso de Judge sigue completamente abierta.
Si finalmente no logra recuperarse a tiempo o únicamente puede participar en algunos encuentros, los Yankees tendrán que encontrar la fórmula para avanzar en los playoffs sin el bate más peligroso de su alineación.

item.title: [el-balad.com] Rays clinch AL East title for the first time since 2021 as Yankees head to the wild-card round — Rays Vs Yankees now has a very different edge - El-Balad.com

item.description: This was the kind of Tuesday that changes the entire shape of a postseason race. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East, secured a first-round bye, and suddenly made the Yankees’ path look a lot harder than it did 24 hours earlier. For New York, the comfort of having already locked up a postseason berth now comes with a much less comfortable reality: the wild-card round is next. The Rays finishing on top of the division is not a small footnote. It is the difference between waiting
item.content:encoded:
This was the kind of Tuesday that changes the entire shape of a postseason race. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East, secured a first-round bye, and suddenly made the Yankees’ path look a lot harder than it did 24 hours earlier. For New York, the comfort of having already locked up a postseason berth now comes with a much less comfortable reality: the wild-card round is next.
The Rays finishing on top of the division is not a small footnote. It is the difference between waiting with an advantage and scrambling for survival. Tampa Bay had not won the American League East since 2021, and now it has done it again with the sort of timing that makes the whole thing feel like a statement. The Rays are not just in the playoff picture. They are positioned to matter immediately.
New York got the result, but Tampa Bay got the prize
The Yankees did win Game 1 of the doubleheader, 2-0, behind eight shutout innings from Carlos Rodon, and that should not be ignored. This is still a team that can point to its starting pitching and say, with some justification, that it remains a dangerous opponent in the American League. But that is the problem with baseball’s playoff ladder: one good result does not erase the bigger picture.
Because while New York was grinding through nearly 13 hours at Yankee Stadium, the Rays were doing the one thing that actually mattered most. They beat Max Fried in the nightcap and then walked away as AL East champions. That changes everything. Tampa Bay gets the first-round bye and the cleaner route. New York gets a tougher road and less margin for error.
Jose Caballero summed up the mood perfectly after the clinch. “The 162 first games, it doesn’t matter,” he said. “Now, the clock starts.” That is exactly the point. The regular season can fill the calendar, build the record and create the noise, but once the division is decided, all of that fades. What matters now is who gets the privilege of choosing a better route and who has to fight through the mess.
For the Yankees, the answer is simple enough: they have work to do, and they will have to do it without Aaron Judge for at least the AL wild card series against the Boston Red Sox. That is not a detail. That is a major complication. It leaves New York leaning even more heavily on the very thing that has kept them in the conversation all along: the starting pitching.
So yes, the Yankees can still be taken seriously as a possible team to beat in the American League. But the Rays have made the bigger move, and in October that is often the only move that really counts. Tampa Bay are AL East champions. New York are in the wild-card round. That is the difference between control and uncertainty, and on Tuesday the Rays grabbed all of it.

But Ryan McMahon was back there again against the Rays as the Yankees try to get him right before the playoffs.
And Aaron Boone insisted it’s still possible.
Boone professed his confidence that McMahon remains a viable option, even as the long-slumping player has also regressed on defense.
“Defensively, I have tremendous faith in him moving forward,” Boone said Wednesday. “I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I view it as, ‘I want him in the game with the ball hit to him in a big spot.’ ”
That may be the case, but McMahon’s issues with his glove don’t just come down to a few recent errors.
According to FanGraphs, his defensive runs saved have dropped from 10 last season to -2 this year.
And scouts who have watched McMahon have noted a drop-off in his range, glove and overall fielding throughout the season.
“I get why they’re still trying to make it work,’’ one American League scout said. “The other options [at third] aren’t great, especially as you’re staring at the playoffs. But if he’s not going to be not just reliable, but stellar, then the issues with his bat are even worse.”
As Boone noted, “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half.”
Complicating matters are the lefty-swinging McMahon’s issues against left-handed pitching, which could open the door for Caballero or Amed Rosario, especially if they face a Red Sox team that’s filled with southpaws.
Caballero has done well at third but is valued for his ability to come off the bench, while the Yankees have continued to believe that Rosario, who has hit lefties well in recent years, will get back to that after having a hard time against them this season.
McMahon entered Wednesday with a .614 OPS, which ranked 224th out of 232 players with at least 350 plate appearances.
And versus lefties, McMahon has an OPS of .518, also among the lowest in the majors.
That doesn’t figure to lead to too many good matchups for McMahon.
Boone, though, said McMahon has “gotten a lot of big hits for us along the way. Defensively, not much has changed in that I view him as top-shelf over there.”
A year ago against Boston in the wild card, McMahon started just one of the three games, but then had a solid series in the ALDS against Toronto.
“We’ll try to get more out of him offensively,’’ Boone said. “Last year, he went into the postseason and right away had some big hits for us. You never know how that can switch, especially when a guy has the ability like [McMahon] does.”
As for the Volpe experiment, Boone said he wanted to get the converted shortstop over to third “a time or two” before the end of the regular season.
Volpe played three games at third with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre this season and would be “ready to go” if called upon.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Reveal Cam Schlittler May Not Be Game 1 Starter In Postseason
item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: The New York Yankees will start the postseason with a Wild Card Series on Tuesday, most likely facing the Boston Red Sox. The Yankees have the probable American League Cy Young Award winner, but are not committing to having him start Game 1. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will start the postseason with a Wild Card Series on Tuesday, most likely facing the Boston Red Sox.
The Yankees have the probable American League Cy Young Award winner, but are not committing to having him start Game 1. Cam Schlittler has been arguably the second-best pitcher in all of baseball this year, and has a strong case to say his season has been better than Jacob Misiorowski's. Schlittler is scheduled to pitch on Thursday, putting him on four days of rest for Game 1 of the Wild Card Series.
"We'll see," Boone said when asked if Schlittler would start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, per MLB.com's Bryan Hoch. "Not necessarily."
Schlittler has worked on four days of rest 14 times this season. He has a 2.19 ERA in those 14 starts and has worked 82 1/3 innings. He is very capable of thriving on four days of rest, but Aaron Boone is not saying he will start Game 1. The reasoning has to do with how it lines the team up for the next series.
"Whoever goes 1 or 2 doesn't affect the next series," explained Boone. "So whoever goes 1 or 2 can pitch 2 and 5 in the next series, for example. So we'll decide what kind of makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games."
Schlitter is a lock to start one of the first two games. If he starts Game 1, he would be on five days of rest for Game 2 of the American League Division Series. That would also have him available for a Game 5 on four days of rest. If Schlittler starts Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, he would be on four days of rest for Game 2 of the ALDS, and then available for Game 5 on four days of rest again.
The Yankees' decision will come down to whether they want Schlittler to have an extra day or not before Game 2 of the next series.
More MLB: Yankees' Aaron Judge Says He Plans To Be Ready For Wild Card Series

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice is in the process of wrapping up a breakout season for the New York Yankees. That included making some history on Wednesday.
Facing the Tampa Bay Rays, the All-Star first baseman opened the scoring in the first inning with his 40th homer of the season. It was a second-deck no-doubter off a first-pitche sinker from Rays starter Mason Englert.
Then he hit another in the fourth inning, putting him in a four-way tie for the AL lead at 41 homers with Pete Alonso, Yordan Álvarez and Junior Caminero.
By reaching 40 homers in a season, Rice has entered rare territory. As MLB.com's Sarah Langs notes, he joins teammate Aaron Judge as the second Yankees draft pick to post a 40-homer season.
Yes, only the second.
Obviously, the Yankees have more than fair share of elite sluggers in history. It's just that many of the homegrown ones entered the league before 1965, when the MLB Draft was first instituted. Others began their careers with other teams before joining the Yankees.
Here is the complete list of Yankees players to post a 40-homer season and how they joined New York, with pre-draft players italicized:
- Aaron Judge (draft pick)
- Roger Maris (trade)
- Mickey Mantle (signed)
- Lou Gehrig (signed)
- Joe DiMaggio (signed)
- Tino Martinez (trade)
- Reggie Jackson (free agent)
- Ben Rice (draft pick)
There are other Yankees draft picks who have come close, with Fred McGriff, Steve Balboni and Don Mattingly all posting a season with at least 35 homers.
McGriff, a ninth-round Yankees pick in 1981, came closest to 40 among that group with 37 in a 1993 season split between the Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres. He never played a game for New York, having been traded as minor leaguer in a now-infamous deal for Dale Murray and Tom Dodd.
As for some other famous names, Derek Jeter never hit more than 24 and Bernie Williams never hit more than 30.
It's all a fun little quirk of history, created by the flow of both the Yankees and the MLB rulebook through the time. It actually requires quite a lot to go right for a draft pick to hit 40 homers in even a single season.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – Consider it a long shot, but Giancarlo Stanton has entered the Yankees’ playoff conversation.
Down at Somerset, the slugging DH – on the injured list since April 25 – is batting against live pitching and even running the bases.
“I heard G went deep over there,’’ manager Aaron Boone said of Stanton’s “six or seven’’ at-bats Wednesday, with at least one home run.
Boone described both Stanton (calf) and Trent Grisham (hamstring) as “knocking on the door’’ in their Somerset rehab, with the lefty-hitting center fielder also hitting and running the bases.
But are they really in consideration for a Wild Card series roster spot?
“I don’t know. Anything’s possible. We’ll see,’’ Boone said Wednesday at Yankee Stadium, with his club already locked into hosting a best-of-three playoff beginning Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a day after Boone said that the Yankees weren't planning on having Aaron Judge ready for the Wild Card series due to a "moderate'' grade right calf strain, the captain told ESPN that he's planning otherwise.
Judge told reporter Jorge Castillo that he's trying "to get my body ready so I'm ready to go'' by Tuesday.
On Monday, Judge had a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection, limiting his activity.
Judge was asked by ESPN if he expected to be on the first round playoff roster replied: "I don't make the roster. I've got no idea."
Giancarlo Stanton's lengthy absence
It’s been five months since Stanton last appeared in Boone’s lineup, due to three separate calf strains – including his current right calf issue.
Due to Stanton’s DH-only status, and the makeup of the Yanks’ current roster, “you’re looking more in a pinch-hit scenario,’’ Boone said of his potential role.
“We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option,’’ said Boone. “I don’t know yet.’’
But it’s an interesting development, and something to watch if the Yanks advance deeper in October.
Again, Judge isn’t in the Yankees’ first-round playoff plans due to a calf strain that might cast him as doubtful to return this year.
Stanton’s finest moments as a Yankee have come during postseason, which adds to his intrigue; as a looming option, he’d at least give an opposing manager something else to weigh.
Advertisement
On the IL since Sept. 5, Grisham might stand a better chance at activation, given the Yanks’ lack of outfield depth.
Hard-throwing righty Carlos Lagrange is pitching at the Yanks’ Somerset camp for potential playoff roster additions, coming back from a capsular (right shoulder) strain.
Lagrange’s big arm and his potential for transitioning to an impact bullpen role was an exciting prospect for the Yanks, until his injury in late July.
As of now, “he’s in the conversation for something,’’ Boone said of Lagrange, the rookie who has yet to make a big-league appearance.
Speaking of both Stanton and Lagrange, specifically, Boone said their recent activity puts them “on the outskirts of the conversation’’ about the postseason “if nothing else.’’
Clarke Schmidt, Fernando Cruz updates
After a recent bout of biceps cramping, Clarke Schmidt’s throwing session Wednesday was “better’’ than Tuesday’s effort, per Boone.
However, “if he’s not a real viable option by (Thursday), we’ll probably go a different way,’’ Boone said of Schmidt’s diminishing chances of being on a Wild Card series roster.
Though apparently minor, this is Schmidt’s second setback since his rehab from Tommy John surgery in July 2025.
Meanwhile, right-hander Fernando Cruz (partial torn UCL) threw a bullpen session Sunday, and plans to throw again Thursday.
Cruz opted against surgery and is trying to be a postseason bullpen option.
“That’s what we’re shooting for…to be back in the next couple of weeks,’’ said Cruz, adding that, in his mind, he’s not dealing with a partial tear.
“I’m going through inflammation and real chronic irritation,’’ said Cruz, determined to pitch through his condition.
Anthony Volpe will get a look at third base
Over these next few games, Boone plans to give Anthony Volpe some playing time a third base.
It's a position he's played briefly in the minors but never in the majors, though Volpe says he feels "pretty comfortable'' in his limited experience at the hot corner.
Volpe has so far made a successful transition from shortstop to second base, and "I'll just try to be prepared'' for whatever the team needs from him defensively.
This article originally appeared on NorthJersey.com: Giancarlo Stanton a Yankees playoff option again? Latest rehab update

item.title: [Boston Herald] Yankees’ Aaron Judge contradicts manager’s Wild Card roster announcement
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: If New York Yankees captain Aaron Judge gets his way, he’ll be back in his team’s lineup for next week’s Wild Card series. One day after Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters, “We’re planning on him not being part of that (round),” his star slugger told ESPN the opposite on Wednesday. “That’s what the plan is,” said Judge, who went on the injured list Saturday with a right calf strain (soleus muscle) and received a Platelet-Poor Plasma injection (PPP) on Tuesday. “Try to get my body ready s
item.content:encoded:
If New York Yankees captain Aaron Judge gets his way, he’ll be back in his team’s lineup for next week’s Wild Card series.
One day after Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters, “We’re planning on him not being part of that (round),” his star slugger told ESPN the opposite on Wednesday.
“That’s what the plan is,” said Judge, who went on the injured list Saturday with a right calf strain (soleus muscle) and received a Platelet-Poor Plasma injection (PPP) on Tuesday. “Try to get my body ready so I’m ready to go. … I’ll get back as soon as I can.”
Judge, who is coming off back-to-back American League MVP seasons and three in the last four years, said he had “no idea” if he will make the Yankees’ Wild Card roster. Including him would be a gamble; if the Yankees put Judge on the roster only to need to replace him mid-series due to injury, he will be ineligible for the next round of the postseason as well.
Injuries limited Judge to 66 games this season; a rib injury cost him all of June, July, and August. He returned on Sept. 8 for seven games before the leg ailment sidelined him again. He hit .241 with a .871 OPS, 18 home runs, 43 walks and 85 strikeouts.
The Red Sox and Yankees are likely to face off in a rematch of last year’s Wild Card round at Yankee Stadium, but the matchups are not yet finalized. Judge went 4 for 11 (.364) with an RBI and two strikeouts in their 2025 series, which the Yankees took by winning the final two games.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge says he plans to be ready for Yankees' wild-card series, disputing comments from manager Aaron Boone
item.dc:creator: Jack Baer

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Tuesday that franchise star Aaron Judge will not play in the team's wild-card series next week. Judge himself had a different story a day later.
The three-time AL MVP told ESPN that he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.
"That's what the plan is," Judge said. "Try to get my body ready so I'm ready to go."
Judge has been on the injured list since Saturday due to a right calf strain, the latest blow in the worst season of his career. He reportedly received a platelet-poor plasma injection in the knee on Monday and is waiting for clearance to resume activity with his injured leg.
The Yankees can technically activate Judge on the final day of the regular season, but his potential return date is unclear. While addressing Judge's health with reporters, Boone said, "We're planning on him not being a part of that," seemingly ruling Judge out until at least the ALDS if the Yankees advance.
Judge reportedly said he has had discussions with the Yankees' decision-makers about his prognosis, but he doesn't know if he will be on the club's wild-card roster:
"We've done a lot of talks, but I can't control what people say," Judge said. "So you'll have to talk to them about that."
If the season ended Wednesday, the Yankees would face the Boston Red Sox in the wild-card series for a second straight season. They have already clinched the top wild-card spot in the AL, with the Red Sox three games ahead of the Chicago White Sox for the second spot.
A healthy Judge would be a boon to the Yankees, but there's no telling what they will get from him even if he's on the roster. This season has been a trying one for the 34-year-old, who has played only 66 games due to that calf injury and a stress fracture in his ribs. That's the fewest games he has played in a season outside of his cup of coffee in 2016 and the COVID-shortened 2020 season.
Judge has also underperformed even when playing, slashing .241/.360/.511 with a 141 OPS+ that ranks, again, as the worst of his career outside of 2016.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge's latest injury offers a glimpse of a rapidly approaching Yankees future
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are locked in.
Their doubleheader split with the Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday ensured that the Bombers will enter the postseason as the top wild card in the American League. (The Rays clinched the AL East and the No. 1 seed). That means, barring a major surprise over the next few days, New York is set to host its forever rivals, the Boston Red Sox, in a best-of-three series starting Tuesday in the Bronx.
But while the schedule and the opponent offer a dose of certainty, there's one enormous unknown swirling around YankeeLand: the health of three-time MVP Aaron Judge.
It has been an injury-riddled season for the Yankees' captain, who missed more than three months due to a stress fracture on his first rib. He returned Sept. 8 and appeared in seven games, tallying four hits and one homer, before landing back on the shelf due to a calf strain suffered Sept. 16. Predictably, the Yankees have been quite mum about Judge's status. Skipper Aaron Boone first declined to disclose the severity of the strain but eventually described it as "moderate."
Before Tuesday's doubleheader, Boone told reporters that Judge won't return during the regular season and that the Yankees are "planning on him not being a part" of the team's wild-card exploits. On Wednesday, Judge reversed course, telling reporters that he intends to be ready for wild-card Game 1. So while the door remains open on a heroic comeback from the goliath slugger, the possibility of Judge taking in October's opening act from the dugout still looms large.
In the event that he does return next week, it's difficult to envision Judge doing so at full strength. Notably, the calf issue is on his right leg — his rear or plant leg. Judge's swing mechanics are particularly reliant on his having explosiveness and stability in his right hip and right leg. Without that, he could be a shell of his best self. Still, players are famously more willing to use certain medications and numbing agents in the postseason, things that could help push Judge onto the roster.
His not being able to play in the outfield is another consideration. Even after the lengthy layoff, Judge slotted immediately back into right field, in part because the Yankees' roster is overloaded with designated hitter types. A more cautious course of action might've saved Judge's calf from giving out, though it's impossible to know for sure.
But now, given the glut of DHs on New York's roster, it's hard to imagine a super-reduced version of Judge being the optimal choice in the lineup over Ben Rice or Paul Goldschmidt. As such, how Boone slots Judge back into the mix if he's able to play will be one of the more fascinating storylines to follow.
Otherwise, the Yanks might need to soldier on, a man — one very large man — down.
This era of Yankees baseball has simultaneously been shaped by Judge and shaped around him. Critics have argued the current roster is overly dependent on the future Hall of Famer — a ridiculous proposition. Wouldn't anyone build a team around one of the world's best hitters? Still, entering October without a world-beating Judge is a bizarre new possibility and, at the same time, one the Yankees, given Judge's age, might need to acquaint themselves with.
New York has not played a postseason contest without Judge since the 2015 winner-take-all wild-card game. A 40-year-old Alex Rodriguez hit fourth for the Yanks that day. Dallas Keuchel threw six shutout innings for a plucky, likable Houston Astros team yet to villainize themselves in the baseball world. Colby Rasmus and Carlos Gómez each ripped solo homers in Houston's victory. Since then, Judge has appeared in all 65 of New York's playoff games, the most over that span by a non-Dodger or non-Astro.
Of course, Judge's physical woes this season do not necessarily portend the beginning of the end. Playing through pain and in a small sample, the 6-foot-7 Californian still posted an impressive .871 OPS. He was, less than a year ago, the American League MVP. He surely has more magical moments to conjure, more souvenirs to crank into the seats. And yet, the clock is undeniably ticking. Father Time, you see, has never been defeated.
The Yankees' captain will turn 35 in April. There have been only 22 individual MLB seasons since integration (1947) in which a qualified player 35 or older finished with an OPS over 1.000. Seven of those years — five from Barry Bonds, one from Mark McGwire and one from Manny Ramírez — were likely aided by performance enhancers. The list, understandably, grows only smaller as the age ticks closer to 40. It's hard to be elite; it's even harder as your body decays.
Judge could certainly ward off Father Time and his sinister ways and remain otherworldly for a few more years. Ted Williams did it. So did Henry Aaron and Chipper Jones and David Ortiz. Some folks age like fine wine. Judge is disciplined, driven and athletic enough to make it work. Modern medical and training technology make it easier for the best to stay healthy for longer. Nobody would be shocked if Judge has another MVP season in him.
But the opposite is also true. Even if his production doesn't tumble off a cliff, there's reason to be wary about the future. Judge cannot carry this franchise around on his broad shoulders forever. Eventually, the Yankees will need to pivot, grow, change, chart a new course. And given the club's institutional smarts and financial might, chances are they'll find another aircraft carrier on which to center the franchise.
Besides, the Yankees' pitching-driven success this year is a reminder that such a path is possible, even fruitful. The 2026 New York Yankees have won a lot of games without Judge. They might need to continue doing so in October.

item.title: [bolavip.com] Aaron Judge challenges NY Yankees, Aaron Boone’s Wild Card plan with unexpected injury update
item.dc:creator: Federico O'donnell
item.description: After the New York Yankees and Aaron Boone offered a grim update on Aaron Judge, most MLB fans thought the writing was on the wall and No. 99 would miss the upcoming AL Wild Card Series. The Yankees had even tested Giancarlo Stanton after seemingly ruling Judge out. There’s a reason they say not to count your chickens before they hatch, though, and all hope may not yet be lost. Not after Judge’s recent injury update, which leaves the door wide open for a return, perhaps sooner than anybody expec
item.content:encoded:
After the New York Yankees and Aaron Boone offered a grim update on Aaron Judge, most MLB fans thought the writing was on the wall and No. 99 would miss the upcoming AL Wild Card Series. The Yankees had even tested Giancarlo Stanton after seemingly ruling Judge out. There’s a reason they say not to count your chickens before they hatch, though, and all hope may not yet be lost.
Not after Judge’s recent injury update, which leaves the door wide open for a return, perhaps sooner than anybody expected, including manager Boone and the rest of the Bronx Bombers. After receiving tough news on top of tough news, such an unexpected surprise must feel nice for a change.
“That’s what the plan is [to be ready for Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series]. Try to get my body ready so I’m ready to go,” Judge admitted during an interview with ESPN’s Jorge Castillo.
Boone reacts to Judge’s update
Asked about Judge’s recent comments, Boone wasn’t caught off guard by the change of plans, and his answer may hint that this was actually New York’s doing. In the end, keeping their cards close to the vest may work out just fine for the Yankees and Judge.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees at Globe Life Field
“The process has started and is ongoing,” Boone said, per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. “I don’t know [how] the next day or two unfolds. We’ll hopefully get healed as quickly as possible and be an option as soon as possible.”
Judge defies NY Yankees’ original timeline
Judge’s latest update on his calf strain took fans by surprise, especially because Judge’s plan is one that goes directly against that of Boone and the Yankees. That’s not to say Judge is defying his coach and team’s orders, but that he doesn’t want to sit idly by with his arms crossed and settle for the initial timeline, which had him missing—at least—the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Postseason.
Instead, Judge is taking matters into his own hands and remains hopeful he might complete a Phoenix-like rise to be back in the batting order come the postseason. Whether he will actually make the Yankees’ postseason roster or not, that he can’t tell, nor does he know.
“I don’t make the roster,” Judge admitted. “I’ve got no idea. We’ve done a lot of talks, but I can’t control what people say. So you’ll have to talk to them about that.”
When does MLB Postseason start?
To say Judge has now entered a race against the clock would be an understatement. The AL Wild Card Series, which New York will host, will be held at Yankee Stadium from Sep. 29-Oct. 1.
Even if Judge considers himself healthy enough to play, it remains to be seen what Boone and company might decide. Perhaps they will be extra cautious, even if it means risking an early playoff elimination and all the drama that would stir up in the Bronx.
Key takeaways
- Aaron Judge stated he plans to be ready for Game 1 of the Wild Card series.
- Aaron Boone indicated the Yankees are hoping he heals quickly to become an option.
- The AL Wild Card Series will take place from Sep. 29-Oct. 1 at Yankee Stadium.
