While the Yankees are planning as though he won’t be available, the captain’s mindset has not shifted. Judge told ESPN on Wednesday that he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series, which is scheduled for Sept. 29 at Yankee Stadium. “That’s what the plan is,” Judge told ESPN. “Try to get my body ready so I’m ready to go.” Asked about Judge’s sta
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – It has been four days since Aaron Judge said it was “definitely the plan” to return in time for the postseason. While the Yankees are planning as though he won’t be available, the captain’s mindset has not shifted.
Judge told ESPN on Wednesday that he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series, which is scheduled for Sept. 29 at Yankee Stadium.
“That’s what the plan is,” Judge told ESPN. “Try to get my body ready so I’m ready to go.”
Asked about Judge’s status before Wednesday’s game, manager Aaron Boone said that “the process has started and is ongoing.”
“I don’t know [how] the next day or two unfolds,” Boone said. “We’ll hopefully get healed as quickly as possible and be an option as soon as possible.”
On Tuesday, Boone said Judge has a “moderate grade” right calf strain that would likely keep him out for the Wild Card Series.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone said on Tuesday. “But we’re also at a time of the year where … obviously we’d push it a little bit if that was in play. But that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out, either.”
Judge was placed on the 10-day injured list Saturday, retroactive to Sept. 17.
He received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection in his right calf during Monday’s off-day and will have limited activities for the next several days.
Judge told ESPN he has spoken with organizational decision-makers about his prognosis.
“We’ve done a lot of talks, but I can’t control what people say,” Judge said. “So you’ll have to talk to them about that.”
During the club’s weekend series in Phoenix, Judge and Boone were vague about the severity of the injury, which Judge sustained during the club’s series last week against the Twins.
Judge revealed the strain is in the soleus muscle of his right calf, which he said “is a little more crucial with running and hitting.”
“I’ve dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was kind of in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult,” Judge said.
Generally, a Grade 2 calf strain takes at least three weeks for recovery.
“If he’s able to play, then we’ll give him that opportunity,” Boone said.
Judge missed most of the summer with a fractured right rib, believed to have been sustained on April 26 in Houston. He played with the injury before landing on the injured list in early June.
Activated in September without a Minor League rehab assignment, Judge played just seven games after his reinstatement, going 4-for-23 (.174) with a homer.
Overall, Judge batted .241/.360/.511 with 18 homers and 41 RBIs in 66 games this season.
“We’ve got games to win,” Judge said. “I’m getting paid to play games for the New York Yankees, so I’ll get back as soon as I can.”

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees split their doubleheader against the Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday.
With one of those losses, the Rays officially clinched the AL East division and the No. 1 overall seed in the American League postseason.
This now places the Yankees in the top Wild Card spot, meaning they'll host a best-of-three series next week in the Bronx against what seems like the Boston Red Sox if the current standings hold.
Yankees Announce Anthony Volpe Decision
With New York already locked into a playoff spot, manager Aaron Boone seems like he's going to experiment with his lineup over these final five games.
However, for the second straight night, he's electing to keep infielder Anthony Volpe out of the starting lineup.
Volpe was seen pregame Wednesday evening taking reps at third base after Boone mentioned that morning that he'll play some third base this week after Jazz Chisholm Jr. returned from the IL.
That seemingly won't happen in Game 3 of the series, though, unless Volpe enters the game off the bench at some point. Ryan McMahon will start at third base.
Here's the full Yankees lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: "Yankees 9/23 B. Rice DH G. Lombard Jr. SS L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF S. Jones CF J. Chisholm Jr. 2B J. Caballero LF R. McMahon 3B A. Sánchez C G. Cole SP."
Yankees 9/23
B. Rice DH
G. Lombard Jr. SS
L. García Jr. 1B
H. Ramos RF
S. Jones CF
J. Chisholm Jr. 2B
J. Caballero LF
R. McMahon 3B
A. Sánchez C
G. Cole SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 23, 2026
Volpe's Rocky 2026 Campaign
It's been a year of ups and downs for Volpe, who's in his fourth season with the Yankees.
He's appeared in 67 games at the major league level while also spending some time in Triple-A this year. He enters Wednesday hitting .244 with 51 hits, two home runs, and 26 RBIs while slugging .335 with a .655 OPS.

item.content:encoded:
Cody Bellinger is out of the New York Yankees lineup for Wednesday night's game against the Tampa Bay Rays, but no injury has been reported.
With the top American League wild-card spot secured and Aaron Judge sidelined, the open question is how many at-bats Bellinger takes into a best-of-three series that starts in six days, most likely against the Boston Red Sox.
José Caballero moves into left field against Rays right-hander Mason Englert, according to CBS Sports. The site found nothing pointing to a physical problem and characterized the absence as a pre-playoff day off.
The timing follows a cold stretch. Bellinger opened September by hitting .373 through his first 14 games of the month, then managed just three hits in his next 20 at-bats.
He managed to come through on Tuesday. His fourth-inning, two-run homer off Nick Martinez, his 17th of the season, was the only scoring in a 2-0 Game 1 win before Tampa Bay took the nightcap of a doubleheader 6-1 and clinched the American League East.
| NEW YORK YANKEES STARTING LINEUP | | | | |
| SP: Gerrit Cole (RHP #45) • 9-9, 3.63 ERA, 123 K | | | | |
| September 23, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 7:05 PM EDT • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | OPS |
| 1 | Ben Rice | DH | .260 | .884 |
| 2 | George Lombard Jr. | SS | .237 | .670 |
| 3 | Luis García Jr. | 1B | .277 | .832 |
| 4 | Heliot Ramos | RF | .239 | .707 |
| 5 | Spencer Jones | CF | .246 | .751 |
| 6 | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | 2B | .233 | .716 |
| 7 | José Caballero | LF | .236 | .666 |
| 8 | Ryan McMahon | 3B | .206 | .615 |
| 9 | Ali Sánchez | C | .241 | .569 |
| Season stats shown (AVG / OPS). Rays lineup not yet available. Lineups subject to change. | | | | |
Yankees Rest Plan Includes Cody Bellinger
After the doubleheader, manager Aaron Boone singled out Bellinger, catcher Austin Wells and outfielder Spencer Jones as regulars due for rest over the final week, according to Yankees beat writer Gary Phillips.
"As best we can, we'll get ourselves sharp. They're real games, so we're playing, but I definitely will pick some spots to get some guys down. Some of our leverage guys in the 'pen, we want them pitching, but we'll be very selective in how we do it," Boone said as quoted by MLB.com's Bryan Hoch.
Gerrit Cole starts Wednesday, and Cam Schlittler follows Thursday before a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles closes the schedule, according to Hoch.
At 90-67, New York holds the No. 4 seed and will host the No. 5 seed in the Wild Card Series opening Sept. 29, according to MLB.com. The Boston Red Sox, at 84-73, are the likeliest opponent.
Judge will not be part of it. Boone said the captain has a "moderate" right calf strain and is not expected back for that round, according to Hoch.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way," Bellinger said, as quoted by Hoch.
Bellinger Career Resume
Bellinger's September line sits at .338/.351/.581 with five homers and 14 RBI, according to Yardbarker. He has appeared in 76 playoff games, hitting 10 homers and driving in 37 runs.
Bellinger was born July 13, 1995, in Scottsdale, Arizona. The Los Angeles Dodgers drafted him in the fourth round in 2013, straight out of Chandler's Hamilton High School. He won National League Rookie of the Year in 2017 and NL MVP in 2019, when he hit .305 with 47 homers.
His path also runs through a 2020 World Series title with the Dodgers and two seasons with the Chicago Cubs. New York acquired him in a December 2024 trade and, after a 2025 season of 29 homers and 98 RBI, re-signed him in January to a five-year, $162.5 million contract that gives him two opt-out chances and full no-trade protection, according to Bronx Pinstripes.
Limited to 130 games by a 25-game injured-list stint for a left hamstring strain, Bellinger is hitting .268 this season with 17 homers, 73 RBI and 12 stolen bases. His career totals stand at 242 home runs and 768 RBI.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said yesterday that star Aaron Judge, who is on the injured list with a calf strain, is unlikely to participate in the Wild Card round next week.
However, Judge just made a statement that suggests otherwise.
New York Yankees Star Aaron Judge Announces Major Update Amid Tampa Bay Rays Series
Judge told ESPN’s Jorge Castillo on Wednesday that he intends to play in the Wild Card series after all.
From ESPN’s Jeff Passan on X: Yankees star Aaron Judge told @jorgecastillo today that he intends to play in the wild card series next week.
The Wild Card round will begin on Tuesday. The Yankees have already clinched the top seed among the AL Wild Card teams.
Unless something crazy happens before next week, the Yankees will host the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card series.
Looking at New York Yankees Star Outfielder Aaron Judge
The Yankees removed Judge from Wednesday’s loss to the Minnesota Twins at Target Field in the sixth inning due to his calf injury.
“I tried to play it off and see how long we can go because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “Talking it over I thought it’d be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepaths.”
Aaron Judge missed most of the season with a right rib stress fracture. New York placed him on the IL on June 2. He didn’t return until Sept. 7.
Judge struggled after returning from the IL, hitting just .190/.227/.333 with one home run and three RBI over six games.
Before being placed on the IL, Judge hit .248/.375/.533 with 17 home runs and 38 RBI over 59 games this season.
Since making his MLB debut in 2016, Judge has slashed 291/.410/.610 with 386 home runs and 871 RBI. He has won three AL MVP Awards.
The Yankees will finish their four-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday night.
After the Rays series, the Yankees will finish the regular season with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.

item.content:encoded:
Just ahead of the MLB Playoffs, the New York Yankees received rough injury news surrounding Aaron Judge, who suffered a calf strain, which is expected to sideline him through the Wild Card and possibly longer. Kalshi’s MLB market immediately cut Yankees futures prices
Prices dropped as soon as the injury hit. The Yankees' World Series price dropped from 12% to 9% while their AL Championship price went from 25% to 20%. A $10 trade profits $107.37 on their World Series price and $37.32 for the AL Championship.
New York Yankees futures prices - Kalshi
- World Series 9%
- AL Championship 20%
Aaron Judge injury update
On September 16 against the Minnesota Twins, Judge made a play in the outfield and suffered a calf strain. Doctors later called it a moderate strain. It fell short of a Grade 3 injury, which is a torn muscle. However, even a Grade 1 strain would require multiple weeks on the sidelines.
The Yankees placed Judge on the 10-day IL. He received a Platelet-Poor Plasma (PPP) injection to treat the injury and to speed healing.
This is Judge’s second major injury this season. In late April, he suffered a fractured right rib and played through the pain until the team shut him down on May 31. He returned to action on September 8 and played seven games before the calf strain.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said he does not expect Judge back for the Wild Card Series, but he did not rule it out:
"You hear all the time with injuries, we get ranges," Boone said. "Two to four weeks, four to six, all these things. There are ranges for a reason, and we're at a point in the year where obviously we push it a little bit if that was in play. But that's a week away so I'm not expecting it, but I'm not ruling it out either."
Judge has a major impact on the Yankees success. In games he’s missed this season, the Yankees are 48-41. They are 41-25 in games that he’s played. The Yankees are gearing up for the Wild Card round, which begins on Tuesday, September 29.

item.content:encoded:
This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more.
Ronald Acuña Jr. of the Braves may be hitting .259 with career lows in exit velocity and hard-hit rate, but don’t be fooled by the overall stats. If the star outfielder can fight through a left shin contusion he suffered Tuesday night on a foul ball at the plate—he’s currently considered day-to-day—he’ll be a force to be reckoned with in October. Ever since mid-August when Acuña began to knock off the rust from two IL stints, he’s been a dangerous, dynamic hitter.
The tell-tale sign is how Acuña is getting to high fastballs he used to miss.
| Acuna vs. 95+ MPH | No. | BA | SLG | HR | Attack Angle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Through Aug. 22 | 315 | .183 | .268 | 1 | 9° |
| Since | 119 | .393 | .857 | 4 | 7° |
Pitchers were dominating Acuña with velocity over his hands. No more. Acuña has made the adjustment. While his barrel had been working underneath the pitch plane, now he is flattening his attack angle, as you can see here:
Acuña heads my list of hitters who are most likely to cap a disappointing year with a strong finish.
Down Year but Primed for Big October
1. Ronald Acuña Jr., Braves
2. Mookie Betts, Dodgers
3. Will Smith, Dodgers
4. Trevor Story, Red Sox
5. José Ramírez, Guardians
Gerrit Cole, Game 2 Starter?
Yankees righthander Gerrit Cole broke through a late-season slump with an improved outing Friday in Arizona (six innings, two earned runs).
As I said last week here, Cole has been throwing too many strikes in the middle of the plate. His fix: tighten the delivery to be more compact and move almost six inches on the rubber toward the third base side.
A frequent tinkerer, Cole began the season toward the center of the rubber but after the Red Sox pounded him for four runs June 27, he moved to the first base side July 3 and stayed there for 13 starts. But after his poor start Sept. 12 against the Mets, which included a career high of hard hits, he returned to the center.
Here you can see his foot position change on the rubber in his past two starts:
It’s the quickest fix to a command issue. You don’t need to change mechanics, just the lane in which the ball leaves your hand.
How did it work? His command was much better. Look at his fastball heat maps and it’s clear he did a better job of keeping the ball out of the center lane:
Cole Fastball Heat Maps
This start moved Cole closer to getting the ball ahead of Max Fried or Carlos Rodon (or both) in a wild-card series against Boston.
As usual, Cole pounded the zone. He has not issued a walk among 71 batters faced in his past three starts. But still a concern: the swing-and-miss still has not returned to his game. He had only six swings-and-misses against Arizona. His September whiff rate is 17%, down from 22.4% entering the month.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have a difficult decision in choosing who starts after Schlittler, a decision that should be based on how Cole, Fried and Rodon are throwing the ball rather than sheer numbers or opponent trends. The Red Sox are slightly better against left-handed pitching (24–15, .746 OPS) than right-handed (60–55, .713 OPS), though the return of Roman Anthony changes that a bit.
📺 TV on TV This Week
Sunday, Sept. 27: Postseason Preview, 8 p.m. ET (MLB Network)
Up to 53 pressure-packed games in 33 days. The best month in all of sports is just about here.
I’ll’ll also be recording a playoff preview show on Monday along with MLB editor Will Laws and staff writer Ryan Phillips. Look out for that on our
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [heavy.com] Aaron Boone Drops Surprising Cam Schlittler Revelation Ahead of Yankees' Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: Zach Kaplan
item.description: Cam Schlittler may have the American League Cy Young locked up, but that doesn’t mean he’ll be toeing the slab in the first game of the Yankees’ upcoming Wild Card series. On Wednesday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone dropped a few surprising tidbits, including that ailing sluggers Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham might be back in pinstripes soon, and that the Yankees are considering adding top pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange to the postseason roster despite Lagrange not having made his debut y
item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler may have the American League Cy Young locked up, but that doesn’t mean he’ll be toeing the slab in the first game of the Yankees’ upcoming Wild Card series.
On Wednesday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone dropped a few surprising tidbits, including that ailing sluggers Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham might be back in pinstripes soon, and that the Yankees are considering adding top pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange to the postseason roster despite Lagrange not having made his debut yet.
Still, the most surprising part of Boone’s pregame press conference might have been his response to the question of which Yankees starter would start Game 1 of the American League Wild Card on Tuesday night.
“We’ll see. Not necessarily,” Boone said about Schlittler, noting that much of his decision around Schlittler’s first start will depend on how they feel about a potential ALDS pitching order.
Cam Schlittler’s Cy Young Caliber Season
Not only does it look Schlittler’s first full professional season will culminate in an American League Cy Young award, but it’s nothing short of historic. Earlier in the year, Schlittler posted a 1.14 ERA in his first 16 road starts of the season, which broke the all-time American League record. With a solid start against the Rays Thursday night, Schlittler would finish his season with a sub-2 ERA, and become the first Yankee to do so since Ron Guidry in his 1978 Cy Young season.
If the Yankees match up against the Red Sox next week, which seems more than likely, Schlittler will get another chance to draw ire from his childhood team after ending their season as a rookie in Game 3 of last year’s Wild Card.
Schlittler also has some history of his own that he can chase, with a little help from the rest of the team. He enters Thursday’s start with 22 straight road starts in which he has recorded more strikeouts than hits allowed, a streak that continued with his six strikeouts to three hits against the Diamondbacks. Only Randy Johnson has had more consecutive starts, doing so in 23 straight road appearances between 1999 and 2000.
Schlittler wouldn’t get another opportunity to do so unless he starts at Tropicana Field in a potential ALDS game with the Yankees. Being put in a group that includes Randy Johnson would be the icing on the cake to an elite first full campaign.
Aaron Boone’s Cam Schlittler Decision
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have his hands full deciding which order to send out his four top starters next week, as one wrong move could be what ends the Yankees’ season far short of their ultimate goal.
Max Fried and Schlittler will likely be the two choices for Game 1, and Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon would be the choices for an if-necessary Game 3 to decide the season. But for Boone, and all Yankee fans at home, the hope is that they won’t need to go there.
With a strong start from Fried or Schlittler, and a bullpen that looks even more formidable with a potential new, young back-end reliever in Lagrange, the Yankees could be well-positioned for a Wild Card triumph after Tuesday night.

item.content:encoded:
Hours before Wednesday’s meaningless game between the Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays, reporters swarmed Anthony Volpe’s locker as he was seen taking grounders at third base.
Volpe’s locker is positioned next to third baseman Ryan McMahon’s, who sat unnoticed right beside the former top prospect while he was swarmed with questions about potentially playing the hot corner.
It could be a sign of things to come, as the Yankees will be getting the infielder out there at third base — as they did during his time in the minors — at some point during the remaining five games of the regular season.
“I would say it just took a couple, like one session of earlier work, just to get used to it,” said Volpe. “And then I felt like it was pretty comfortable. … t’s definitely more similar to shortstop.”
The Bombers have nothing left to play for as the Rays celebrated winning the AL East on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium and their spot atop the Wild Card standings is locked in.
Therefore, the only value these games provide is trying new things. Volpe at third base is among the most intriguing options.
“Yeah, there’s a lot going on with things from our standpoint being settled as far as our playoff standing and position and everything,” said Boone. “There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days. Hopefully we have a lot of options to choose from, but we won’t know that until Saturday or Sunday and into Monday. …
“I’ll probably get [Volpe] in there a time or two. Just certainly want him working over there a little bit and again trying to be as flexible as possible. There’s a lot of different iterations and ways we can go going into the Wild Card series where if you went heavy position player [on the roster], you could have a lot of options throughout the game and the more position flexibility you have, the better.”
The Bombers’ left-handed heaviness has been well-documented. Boone values balance in the lineup and the Yanks haven’t had much of it.
McMahon has objectively been a weak bat since he’s arrived in New York last season. This season, the 31-year-old is slashing .209/.274/.341 with 10 homers and 35 RBI in 121 games.
Against lefties, it’s even worse.
McMahon is slashing .196/.286/.232 against southpaws this season. That doesn’t bode well entering October, while the book is out on the Yankees’ preference to face righties. Barring some crazy series of events during the final weekend of the regular season, the Yanks will likely be welcoming the Boston Red Sox into Yankee Stadium for a best-of-three Wild Card series.
The Sox are well equipped to potentially go with left-handed starters in all of three of those games. This is where Volpe could potentially come into play.
The 25-year-old has performed respectably since being recalled from Triple-A on Sept. 10. Volpe is slashing .263/.300/.395 with one homer, seven RBI and four stolen bases — reminder, the bar is very low offensively for these Yankees right now.
Against lefties on the whole in his 67 MLB games this season, Volpe owns a .680 OPS — it’s well below average, however, it’s a large improvement from McMahon. The one thing to consider, however, is the potential defensive downgrade to consider with McMahon ranking in the 80th percentile in Outs Above Average at third base.
There is certainly an October role available for Volpe to carve out this season. The third base situation is amongst the many unanswered questions for the Yanks entering the postseason.
McMahon is no shoo-in to make the postseason roster with his season-long struggles at the plate, Jose Caballero hasn’t separated himself — .666 OPS entering Wednesday — although he may be the leader in the clubhouse to get the start at the hot corner.
One could argue that far too many questions remain for the Yankees with the clock winding down this season, however, they hope to have many of them answered over these final few games.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees will play the third game of their series with the Tampa Bay Rays in the Bronx.
The Yankees most recently lost by a score of 6-1 on Tuesday night.
After starting at third base in Tuesday afternoon’s 2-0 victory, Jose Caballero was not in the lineup at night.
Yankees Announce Jose Caballero Change
For Wednesday’s game, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/23 B. Rice DH G. Lombard Jr. SS L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF S. Jones CF J. Chisholm Jr. 2B J. Caballero LF R. McMahon 3B A. Sánchez C G. Cole SP”
Caballero is hitting 7th (and starting in left field).
He comes into the night batting .236 with 95 hits, 14 home runs, 51 RBIs, 49 runs and 34 stolen bases in 133 games.
The 30-year-old is in the middle of his second season playing for New York.
Before the Yankees, Caballero had been with the Rays.
MLB.com wrote (on July 31, 2025): “Tampa Bay Rays traded SS José Caballero to New York Yankees for CF Everson Pereira and Future Considerations. Player To Be Named Later or Cash Considerations.”
Caballero has also spent time with the Tampa Bay Rays over four seasons at the MLB level.
Social Media Reacts
Here’s what people were saying about the team’s lineup:
Max Mannis: “First start in left field for Caballero since June”
@KevinConnelly24: “The Yankees are *officially* playing exhibitions for the remainder of the regular season. It’s incomprehensible Ryan McMahon is still playing third base”
@FungoMLB: “The #Yankees have just 5 games to test out new 3B options. Without Volpe/Jazz/Garcia winning that role, NYY will be starting the worst defender in the sport (Rosario) vs LHP or the worst batter (McMahon) vs Sonny. Shouldn’t they be desperate to see if someone else could do it?”

item.content:encoded:
BRONX, NY — New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone had a feeling that this was going to happen.
When asked about his club’s largest threats in the American League East, the Bronx Bombers’ skipper was sure to group in the Tampa Bay Rays with the rest of the pack — the defending pennant-winning Toronto Blue Jays, the reloading Baltimore Orioles, and the rival Boston Red Sox — despite a 77-85 finish last year and a fourth-place finish and many prognosticating a last-place finish this year.
He was spot on.
The Rays celebrated their fifth-ever AL East division title on Tuesday night at Yankee Stadium with a 6-1 win over Boone’s squad, picking up their 96th win of the season with a roster built around the young, homegrown superstar and AL MVP contender Junior Caminero, and a pitching staff that has exceeded all expectations, ranking seventh-best in MLB with a 3.76 ERA.
“That’s the area where I always respect the Rays, and what they’re capable of doing,” Boone said. “Certainly they’ve put it together… to be in the mid-90s wins is impressive.”
Don’t let the small-market designation fool you; the Rays have mastered the art of being a chameleon contender. They can morph their roster into a winner under a litany of circumstances. When they won the American League pennant six years ago and 100 games the following season, they were rife with bigger, more recognizable names: Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Willy Adames.
But, like most clubs of their designation, they’re forced to sell off their big-ticket items to keep their sustainability intact. Their 2026 roster does not look nearly as imposing as the ones from 2020 and 2021, yet here they are. Score one for the little guys, because you can, in fact, build a winning team and not break the bank — a testament to the talent evaluators and developers within the organization.
“I always hear that year after year with the Rays, year after year,” Boone said. “No, it’s different this year. They’ve had a great season, and it’s a different makeup team than in the 2020, 2021 Rays, which were a juggernaut. I mean, big arms, big pen, an outstanding roster. This year, they’ve done a really good job of winning games. Obviously, offensively they’re built around that big three of [Yandy] Diaz, Caminero, and [Jonathan] Aranda, and they’ve been healthy and gone to post. The support players they’ve got have had some good years, like Chandler Simpson. They’ve pitched well for the most part, rotation and pen, but this is a different makeup than what they’ve had in years past. They’ve taken advantage of their athleticism. They’re a very athletic team; they push the envelope on the bases, do a lot of different things in that regard. You’ve gotta give them credit. They’ve won a ton of games this year… and they’re always a challenge to play.”
They are a direct contrast to everything that the Yankees are and have represented for the last 100 years, so it’s somewhat amusing that it was them celebrating winning the AL East in the Bronx following a 6-1 win on Tuesday night.
But for Boone, it was no surprise. Now, the Yankees’ road to a pennant will likely have to run through Tampa.

item.content:encoded:
Gerrit Cole will take the mound Wednesday against the Rays in his continued effort to get right before October.
One of his toughest matchups will be waiting for him in the box.
Yandy Díaz has been ice cold lately, having gone without a hit in his past five games, but Cole offers a good opportunity for the Rays first baseman to break out of his slump.
The Tampa Bay slugger has consistently handled the Yankees right-hander throughout his career, batting .340 with a .520 slugging percentage and .909 OPS in 50 at-bats against him.
He has 17 hits in those meetings, including three doubles and two home runs.
Díaz has carried that success into this season as well, going 3-for-6 with a double against Cole in 2026.
Cole bounced back after a tough run of late in his last start, allowing two runs over six innings while striking out six against the Diamondbacks, but he hasn’t exactly been dominant down the stretch of the season.
Before his last outing, Cole surrendered nine earned runs and seven home runs over his previous two starts.
Cole, in fact, has been hit hard all season, allowing an average exit velocity (90.9 mph) and hard-hit percentage (45.2 percent) that rank in the bottom four percent of the league.
That gives Díaz a solid chance at doing some damage against a pitcher he has consistently seen well.

Now locked into the Wild Card Round, the New York Yankees are shifting their focus to the postseason, where starting pitcher Max Fried addressed the sting of watching a division rival celebrate on Bronx turf. “You don’t want anyone to be celebrating at your stadium,” Fried told the YES Network following the game. “Especially this morning, with the
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are the newly crowned American League East champions, clinching a first-round bye as they await the winner of the Wild Card Series. Now locked into the Wild Card Round, the New York Yankees are shifting their focus to the postseason, where starting pitcher Max Fried addressed the sting of watching a division rival celebrate on Bronx turf.
“You don’t want anyone to be celebrating at your stadium,” Fried told the YES Network following the game. “Especially this morning, with the way Carlos came out, we wanted to put some pressure on and win some games. Unfortunately, I wasn’t able to follow up what he did this afternoon.”
Fried was blunt about his own performance during the nightcap of Tuesday’s doubleheader. Though Carlos Rodon turned in a gem during his final regular-season start, the Yankees couldn’t complete the sweep, leaving the door open for Tampa Bay to seal the division title.
Looking ahead to the road to October, manager Aaron Boone outlined the team’s strategy for the remaining five games of the regular season. However, Boone also delivered a concerning injury update regarding Aaron Judge, clouding the captain’s availability for the upcoming Wild Card Series.
Max Fried #54 of the New York Yankees throws a live bullpen session.
Fried struggles against Rays’ offense
Tuesday presented a tale of two games for New York’s rotation. Game 1 saw Rodon deliver a dominant performance on the mound to reach the 100-strikeout mark for the season, but Fried was unable to replicate that command in the second matchup.
Fried allowed four earned runs on six hits over 6.2 innings as Tampa Bay pulled away for a 6-1 victory. The sub-par outing highlighted pressing questions about the rotation’s consistency, especially with no margin for error in a short Wild Card Series where a single loss can alter the entire series.
Fried maintains confidence in Yankees’ rotation
Despite his rough outing, Fried expressed full confidence in his fellow rotation members as the postseason approaches. “We’ve got great arms. We’ve got a guy who’s going to win the Cy Young. Anytime you have that guy in your rotation, it’s obviously a good thing. We’ve got a lot of guys throwing the ball really well right now,” Fried remarked.
Key takeaways
- The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East division title and celebrated at Yankee Stadium.
- Max Fried allowed four earned runs over 6.2 innings in a 6-1 defeat, and sounded off on Rays’ celebration.
- The starting pitcher expressed full confidence in New York’s rotation ahead of the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Alonso has spent much of the last week going viral, much to Baltimore Orioles fans’ pleasure and New York Mets fans’ … well, we’d call it dismay, but Citi Field viewed things far differently.
Alonso has since left New York in more ways than one, and the Orioles are back in Charm City for their final home series. The five-time All-Star hit his 39th and 40th homers in Monday’s 4-3 win over the Blue Jays, becoming only the ninth player in franchise history to join such a club.
Fans might dig the long ball, but Alonso has done far more than round the bases so frequently. He entered Tuesday leading the American League with 108 RBIs, and he's only three behind the Cardinals' Alec Burleson for the most in the majors. Despite a relatively slow start, the veteran first baseman has a healthy lead over the Astros' Yordan Alvarez (99) and Rays' Junior Caminero (97) with six games left.
All of that sounds great, but here’s the kicker: At his current pace, Alonso would become the first player in MLB history to lead the AL and NL in RBIs in two separate seasons; he and Aaron Judge tied for an MLB-high 131 RBIs in 2022.
Pete Alonso continues to further humiliate Steve Cohen’s New York Mets
First off, can we just appreciate the fact that no player has ever won the RBI title in separate leagues? You’d think Frank Robinson would have done it seeing as he became the first player to win the MVP in both the AL and NL, but apparently not. Our dark horse pick would have been Mark McGwire.
Alonso’s 4.6 bWAR is his highest since 2019, and he's on track to finish with career highs in on-base percentage (.359) and walk rate (11.4 percent). He cleared the 300-homer mark last week and is currently at 304, so he stands an excellent chance at reaching 400 within the coming years.
All of this follows the Mets allegedly not making Alonso — their all-time home run leader and one of the most beloved players in the post-David Wright era — a formal contract offer this past offseason. Steve Cohen and David Stearns instead opted for Jorge Polanco, who hit .148 with a .431 OPS and -1.4 bWAR over 37 games. Great job, all.
The concerns about how Alonso would age as a power-heavy first baseman were valid, but not offering him a contract easily ranks among the worst decisions in Mets history. You don’t let one of your all-time greats leave without a fight, especially not when he’s still playing at an All-Star level. It’s not like Alonso had a realistic chance to receive $300 million on the open market.
But “what could have been” is the story of the New York Mets’ existence. How far would they have gone in the postseason had they not collapsed in 2007, 2008, and 2025? Would Tom Seaver have helped the Mets return to form rather than join the Reds in the “Midnight Massacre?”
At least Alonso seemingly landed in a place where leadership respects him — and if they’re smart, they’ll consult him on any potential offseason moves. Here’s an idea: Do everything that the Mets wouldn’t do.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees now know that they will have to play in a best-of-three Wild Card Series in the Bronx starting on Tuesday.
Gerrit Cole is set to pitch on Wednesday against the Tampa Bay Rays, and that would put him on five days of rest before the Wild Card Series starts. Cam Schlittler will pitch on Thursday, giving him four days of rest if the Yankees plan to start him in Game 1.
Schlittler has had no problems working on four days of rest this season, so he should still draw the Game 1 start. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón both pitched on Tuesday, so assuming neither one makes another traditional start in the regular season, both would be available to pitch in the Wild Card Series with some extra rest.
Essentially the Yankees have to decide whether to start Cole or Rodón as the third starter in a Wild Card Series, assuming Fried and Schlittler both get starts. Aaron Boone has already noted that fans should expect Cole to get a start in the Wild Card Series, and judging by how things are lining up, that start could come in Game 1 or 2. He would be going into Game 1 with five days of rest, setting Schlittler up to pitch in Game 2 on five days of rest if the Yankees want to make sure he doesn't pitch on four days' rest.
Then, Fried or Rodón would start Game 3 with extended rest. It's safe to assume that if one of them starts in the regular season finale, the other would start Game 3 on extended rest. However, the reality is, starting Cole over either of them is a mistake.
Cole has a 5.34 ERA this month and also struggles against the Red Sox. Since 2020, when Cole joined the Yankees, he has had a 5.93 ERA against the Red Sox in the regular season. In his postseason career, he has faced the Red Sox twice, allowing seven runs in eight innings.
Fans already know how god Fried and Schlittler are, and they both deserve to start. However, Rodón should be the one getting the nod over Cole in a best-of-three series against the Red Sox. Rodón has a 1.89 ERA since returning from the injured list in August. He has delivered three straight quality starts, and the Yankees should ride the hot hand.

item.content:encoded:
It's not the trade that will have the most bearing on who wins the World Series this fall, but the Boston Red Sox' decision to dump former top prospect Marcelo Mayer onto the San Francisco Giants stands out as among the most quietly curious of this past deadline. Then again, hearing Mayer and his family speak about his time in Boston ahead of his debut with his new team, perhaps it was for the best all the way around.
Will Mayer be able to prove that the Red Sox got this one wrong? The latest round of MLB rumors has more on that as well as the Philadelphia Phillies' looming Don Mattingly decision and Alex Bregman on the mend for the Chicago Cubs.
Marcelo Mayer and his family sound relieved to be out of Boston
Not all that long ago, Mayer was a crucial part of the future for the Red Sox, as much a foundational prospect as Roman Anthony. But he struggled to stay healthy over the last two years, and struggled to hit even when he was in the lineup. Eventually, Boston decided they'd seen enough, flipping the young infielder to San Francisco at this year's trade deadline — and it seems as though Mayer is eager to prove that Craig Breslow was wrong to cut bait.
According to Susan Slusser of the San Francisco Chronicle, Mayer and his family "let the Red Sox front office know they'd be comfortable with a trade" as the atmosphere in Boston grew hostile toward the 23-year-old.
“Obviously, it didn’t go the way I wanted,” Mayer told Slusser, “and obviously, outside the lines, it’s a lot over there.”
Mayer's dad was willing to go even further, saying that he "jumped 30 feet in the air" when he heard the news that his son was headed back to his home state of California.
On the one hand, Mayer's offensive numbers over his first two big-league seasons are undeniably ugly, and he's missed time due to injury in each of the past four years. Then again, none those health issues seem to be of the chronic variety, and they undoubtedly hampered his development. You can understand why the Red Sox weren't willing to wait around for Mayer to maybe turn into a big-league second baseman, but you can also understand why the Giants were eager to give him a second chance — and why, given all the criticism he faced from fans and talk-radio types in Boston about whether he was soft, Mayer can't wait to get back on the field.
Phillies waiting until offseason to make a decision about Don Mattingly
It's been a big few days for interim managers, with both Chad Tracy in Boston and Andy Green with the Mets earning the full-time job moving forward. But no such vote of confidence has come for Phillies interim skipper Don Mattingly, who took over from Rob Thomson back in late April and has guided the team to the brink of a Wild Card spot. And from the sound of it, he shouldn't get his hopes up.
"[We] have felt it is better to wait until our season is complete," Phillies president Dave Dombrowski told reporters this week, per Scott Lauber of the Inquirer.
That seems to be a pretty clear warning: Take this team deep into October, or else. And really, despite Mattingly's 78-51 record at the helm this season, it's hard to fault Dombrowski too much here. The roster Mattingly inherited certainly has its flaws, with a thin bullpen and a lineup with multiple trouble spots. But Mattingly also hasn't helped matters at times, with some questionable decision-making that makes clear why his previous managerial stints ended unhappily.
Yes, he deserves credit for his role in Philly's turnaround. But it has much more to do with the players on the field than anything else, and the Phillies are wise not to tie themselves to a 65-year-old who could very well come back to bite the team in the postseason. And if Mattingly does prove himself next month, they can very easily revisit the matter.
Cubs appear to have dodged a bullet with Alex Bregman injury
The Cubs suffered a real scare in Cincinnati over the weekend, when star third baseman Alex Bregman took a line drive directly to the face while standing in the on-deck circle. Given the frightening nature of the injury and the timing just a week before the end of the regular season, it was hard not to fear that Chicago might have to at least begin its playoff journey without a guy who's been one of their very best players in the second half.
Thankfully, though, the Cubs appear to have gotten good news. Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures in the incident, but manager Craig Counsell told reporters on Tuesday that the veteran isn't expected to go on the IL — and that he might even be able to return to the lineup before the regular season concludes.
Will Bregman be the same guy he was prior to the injury? That remains to be seen. But as things stand right now, it seems like he'll at the very least be ready to go for the Cubs' first postseason game next week, and that's a huge sigh of relief.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why José Caballero Gives Yankees Better Chance at Third Base Than Ryan McMahon in MLB Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: For much of the New York Yankees' 2026 season, there was a constant conversation about who would be the everyday shortstop. item.content:encoded:
For much of the New York Yankees' 2026 season, there was a constant conversation about who would be the everyday shortstop. The debate surrounded Jose Caballero and Anthony Volpe for most of the year. In the end, the debate over who was better became irrelevant because George Lombard Jr. won the job.
While Caballero is currently without a position, that doesn't mean he doesn't have an opportunity to get everyday reps in the postseason. In fact, maybe the conversation of Caballero vs. Volpe could shift toward him vs. Ryan McMahon. At this point in the season, can the Yankees honestly say McMahon's defense is that much of a difference-maker when he is easily one of the worst everyday bats this organization has ever had?
It isn't hyperbole to mention that McMahon is that bad, either. According to Baseball Reference's Katie Sharp on X, 232 players have over 350 plate appearances this season. He is the only one with an OBP under .280 and a strikeout rate over 29%.
Beyond being a bad hitter, McMahon's defense has regressed. Last season, McMahon had a 7 OAA and 10 DRS. This year, he has a 1 OAA at third and -2 DRS. He can't hit, and apparently his defense — his only calling card as a player — is mediocre at best.
That is why, at this point, it wouldn't hurt to leave McMahon off the Wild Card roster. It isn't a secret that the Boston Red Sox are going to throw an amalgamation of lefties that entire series, and considering McMahon can't hit anybody no matter which side of the mound they're throwing from, Caballero makes the most sense to play every game in that series.
The difference between McMahon and Caballero
That said, Caballero hasn't been all that great this season, either. He has an 86 wRC+ and .666 OPS this year. The one thing he brings is athleticism, and he showed that against the Tampa Bay Rays. In the day game of their day-night doubleheader on Tuesday, Caballero stole second and third with ease.
The Yankees didn't score, unfortunately, but Caballero put them in the position to do so. The Yankees don't get that with McMahon.
Considering McMahon has also regressed defensively, it wouldn't be a downgrade at the hot corner anyway if the Yankees go with Caballero, who has a -1 OAA and 1 DRS at the position. It would just be one bad hitter replacing another, except Caballero is always a threat to steal and brings speed on the bases.
Going from Caballero to McMahon feels like one of the easiest decisions the Yankees have heading into the Wild Card series. At this point, McMahon does nothing better than Caballero, and given that Caballero is already one of the weakest bats in baseball, it's hard to find anything positive about his season.
That said, his ability to put pressure on the opposing teams' pitcher with his base-stealing prowess could be a differencemaker in the playoffs.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Yankees' Anthony Volpe Could Surprise Everyone in the Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: Is it possible the New York Yankees will have a larger playoff role for Anthony Volpe than expected? Things took a turn on Tuesday when Jazz Chisholm returned from the 10-day injured list after suffering a thumb injury earlier in the month, reclaiming his spot at second base. item.content:encoded:
Is it possible the New York Yankees will have a larger playoff role for Anthony Volpe than expected?
Things took a turn on Tuesday when Jazz Chisholm returned from the 10-day injured list after suffering a thumb injury earlier in the month, reclaiming his spot at second base.
But will Chisholm be a permanent fixture there in the playoffs? And is it possible Anthony Volpe could get more playing time than expected?
Chisholm had yet another mental lapse on Tuesday night, failing to cover first base on a bunt. Aaron Boone expressed clear frustration with Chisholm after the game and didn't rule out the possibility of Anthony Volpe playing some second base even with Chisholm back.
Chisholm does not hit lefties well. He is slashing .221/.268/.386 against them in 2026 and owns a lifetime .663 OSP versus southpaws.
Volpe hasn't exactly lit it up against left-handers, either (.719 OPS), but he does hit lefties slightly better than Chisholm, and given how frustrated Boone appears to be with Chisholm, there appears to be a chance Volpe gets some run.
The Boston Red Sox will be the Yankees' Wild Card Series opponent. They are absolutely loaded with left-handed pitching. It's basically Sonny Gray and then a bunch of southpaws. Does that mean Chisholm will be out of luck in that short series?
Of course, it's only a three-game set, but if it does go the full three, Volpe might get starts in two of them. That seemed unheard of in early August when Volpe was demoted to Triple-A, but now, it's a legitimate possibility for the 25-year-old.
It should also be noted that Volpe has shown some playoff chops in the past, particularly during New York's run to the World Series in 2024 when he slashed .286/.407/.408 with a home run and six RBI.
Is Volpe going to be anyone's favorite option? No, but he has demonstrated that he is not afraid of the bright October lights, and it's not like Chisholm has been good enough this season to warrant a guaranteed start every night.
It's also worth noting that Volpe has done a fine job defensively at second base, registering two defensive runs saved over 93.1 innings there thus far.
Just when Yankees fans thought they may have seen the last of Volpe, the former first-round pick may surprise them with potentially significant postseason playing time. And while that may not be preferable, New York may not have any other choice.

item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description:
The glaring Ryan McMahon playoff problem has the Yankees set to once again expand Anthony Volpe’s defensive repertoire. Volpe, now at second base after transitioning from shortstop, will “probably” play third base in the team’s final five games, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told Talkin’ Yanks.

item.content:encoded:
The glaring Ryan McMahon playoff problem has the Yankees set to once again expand Anthony Volpe’s defensive repertoire.
Volpe, now at second base after transitioning from shortstop, will “probably” play third base in the team’s final five games, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told Talkin’ Yanks.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
The team is not planning to do so with Jazz Chisholm, although Boone caveated that statement with a “we’ll see” during his usual midweek interview with the podcast.
The Yankees have six days before they likely welcome the Red Sox — or the AL Central runner-up — to The Bronx for a second straight AL wild-card series and they will use this time to figure out roster construction.
Boone said after the Rays clinched the AL East on Tuesday in the nightcap of the doubleheader that he would consider experimenting with players at certain positions.
The glaring roster question centers on third base.
McMahon has become virtually unplayable due to his shaky defense as of late and horrific offense.
The veteran is hitting just .143 in 15 games since returning from the injured list, going 6-for-42 with one extra-base hit and a .217 on-base percentage.
Against a Boston team filled with lefties, McMahon, who owns a .518 OPS against southpaws this year, becomes an easy fade.
The question is where the Yankees would turn and they have Amed Rosario and Jose Caballero as potential options, although there are flaws with both.
Rosario is a bad defender this year and has not hit lefties like usual, with just a .599 OPS, and Caballero can be rather streaky offensively.
Volpe has tallied just a .695 OPS in 11 games since being recalled, which doesn’t scream must-start, but his righty bat could be needed against potential southpaws.
He also has handled second base rather well since shifting to the position earlier this month with rookie George Lombard Jr. handling shortstop.
Boone added that Lombard will remain at shortstop amid these possible changes.
The complicating factor about Volpe’s postseason role is whether the Yankees trust Chisholm — who is slashing .221/.268/.386 versus lefties — against a southpaw in a three-game series.
If Chisholm is starting, the only other starting route would be third base.
Seeing how Volpe can handle third base opens up the possibility of starting at the hot corner — although that would appear a long shot since he would have, at most, five major-league games at the position before the postseason starts — or potentially entering or shifting in the late innings.
Volpe being able to handle the position could allow the Yankees to optimize their roster in a better fashion in the late innings, with one potential example being a game in which Rosario starts.

item.content:encoded:
Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

item.content:encoded:
¡Beso incluido! Jazz Chisholm alegra el día de una seguidora con una foto especial
This browser does not support the video element.
Hay días en los que nada puede arruinarte el buen humor.
El martes, según parece, fue uno de esos días para Jazz Chisholm Jr. Activado de la lista de lesionados de 10 días entre los partidos de la doble cartelera de los Yankees frente a los Rays, Chisholm vio sus primeros turnos de acción en dos semanas, y su buen ánimo simplemente no se podía contener.
Toma como ejemplo esta interacción particular con una seguidora.
Mientras Chisholm esperaba en el círculo de espera en la parte baja de la cuarta entrada, una aficionada aprovechó la oportunidad desde la primera fila para tomarse una rápida foto con el jugador de cuadro. Chisholm se dio cuenta y pausó su rutina para posar con ella. Pero un buen día, claramente, exige más que un selfie regular: para diversión de la fanática, Chisholm le dio un ligero beso en la cabeza a través de la red de protección.
De las miles —tal vez millones— de fotos entre peloteros y aficionados que existen, esta podría ser única en su clase.

item.title: [MLB.com] Cinco factores por los que los Yankees podrían ganar sin Judge
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch
item.description: NUEVA YORK – La noticia sobre el regreso de Aaron Judge a la lista de lesionados aún estaba fresca, habiendo sido anunciada menos de una hora antes, y ya Cody Bellinger estaba imaginando cómo los Yankees podían tener éxito en la postemporada sin su capitán. item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – La noticia sobre el regreso de Aaron Judge a la lista de lesionados aún estaba fresca, habiendo sido anunciada menos de una hora antes, y ya Cody Bellinger estaba imaginando cómo los Yankees podían tener éxito en la postemporada sin su capitán.
Desafortunadamente para Judge y su club, han tenido mucha práctica haciendo exactamente eso esta temporada. No han tenido otra opción.
"Falta Judge y duele", dijo Bellinger. "Todos sabemos que él es el mejor bateador del juego. Para nosotros aquí, nuestra mentalidad es que vamos a tener que encontrar la manera. Creo que el talento en este clubhouse habla por sí mismo. Estoy completamente seguro de que tenemos suficiente talento aquí para salir, ganar y vencer a cualquiera.
Ahora tendrán su oportunidad para demostrarlo.
El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, confirmó el martes que Judge está lidiando con un esguince "moderado" de la pantorrilla derecha y no se espera que esté listo para una posible Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana contra los Medias Rojas, que comenzaría el 29 de septiembre.
La disponibilidad de Judge para las rondas posteriores, especialmente la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, también está en duda. Pero los Yankees necesitan llegar allí primero. Aquí hay cinco motivos por los que los Yankees, elogiados como favoritos para ganar el banderín, aún pueden llegar a la Serie Mundial incluso si Judge no regresa:
Lanzadores abridores dominantes
**
Cuando Carlos Rodón lanzó ocho entradas sin permitir carreras en la **victoria por 2-0 del martes sobre los Rays, no sólo mantuvo el champán en el clubhouse de Tampa Bay (por el momento), sino que también sirvió como un recordatorio de la mayor fortaleza de los Yankees.
Rodón podría ni siquiera abrir un partido en una posible Serie de Comodines, quedando detrás de los favoritos al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole y Max Fried. En pocas palabras, la rotación los ha mantenido a flote.
Los abridores de los Yankees han permitido dos carreras limpias o menos en 40 de 51 aperturas desde el 28 de julio, incluyendo una carrera limpia o menos en 33 de esas aperturas, acumulando efectividad de 2.50 en ese período. En general, han permitido una carrera o menos en 65 encuentros, un récord de franquicia en una sola campaña.
"Venimos a ganar cada partido, sin importar quién esté en el terreno", dijo Rodón. "Obviamente, es difícil cuando no tienes al mejor jugador del mundo en el terreno contigo. Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva. Pero... se trata simplemente de ganar juegos para nosotros.
Hay otro trueno
Esto no es el 2022, cuando los 62 jonrones de Judge establecieron un récord de la Liga Americana para una sola temporada y sirvieron como el motor indiscutible de la ofensiva. Principalmente debido a la lesión en la costilla, Judge se limitó a un promedio de .241, 18 vuelacercas y 41 impulsadas en 66 encuentros. Ben Rice asumió gran parte de la carga este año, cumpliendo con la predicción de la primavera de Boone de 39 cuadrangulares.
Bellinger sigue siendo una fuerza impactante, mientras que el aumento de la velocidad del bate del dominicano Luis García Jr. sugiere que su producción es sostenible, a pesar de una reciente caída. Mientras tanto, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos ha mostrado poder después de un comienzo lento y se confiará en él en los playoffs contra lanzadores zurdos.
"Sabemos que somos capaces de ganar partidos", dijo Boone, quien señaló el récord de 36-24 del club desde el descanso del Juego de las Estrellas, la mayor parte del cual ocurrió sin Judge. "Nos hemos tenido que enfrentar a jugar sin muchas piezas clave en diferentes momentos y durante grandes tramos de esta campaña”.
**Los jóvenes pueden dar la cara
**
El cubano-estadounidense George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones llamaron la atención durante la reciente serie del club contra los Diamondbacks, cuando dieron jonrones con un total combinado de 872 pies calculados por Statcast contra Corbin Burnes – potentes batazos de 424 y 448 pies, respectivamente, que sugieren que se están sintiendo más cómodos en Grandes Ligas.
Ha habido algunos obstáculos durante sus primeros meses de actividad en las Mayores, con Lombard cometiendo errores en seis compromisos consecutivos en un período y Jones mostrando los swings en blanco que probablemente siempre sean parte de su juego. Pero el talento es real y nadie debería sorprenderse si alguno de los novatos brilla en un gran momento de octubre.
"Realmente sólo tenemos que jugar uno para el otro; apoyarnos mutuamente, pasar la batuta", dijo Bellinger. "Haces tu trabajo y controlas lo que puedes”.
Mejorando la salud
Mientras la situación de Judge no está clara, los Yankees están volviendo lentamente a estar completos.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue activado de la lista de lesionados entre los juego de la doble-jornada del martes, restaurando una presencia dinámica. Ha sido un año decepcionante en general, pero Chisholm estaba en racha en el momento de su lesión (de 46-18, .391). Los Yankees esperarán que retome eso.
Mientras tanto, Anthony Volpe aprovechó al máximo una oportunidad ante la ausencia de Chisholm, lo que podría haberle valido un lugar en el roster de playoffs, especialmente si los Yankees optan por contar con 11 lanzadores y 15 jugadores de posición en la primera ronda. Se cree que Trent Grisham está en la contienda para el roster.
"Con suerte, más personas podrán unirse y hacernos más formidables en el camino", dijo Boone.
Un bullpen reforzado
Los relevistas de los Yankees han estado entre los mejores de Grandes Ligas todo el año, pero ha habido señales preocupantes últimamente. Brent Headrick ocupa el segundo lugar en las Grandes Ligas con 79 presentaciones y ha mostrado una velocidad inconsistente. Mientras tanto, David Bednar y Paul Blackburn siguen en buena forma.
Debido a que los Yankees no tendrían por qué para a tener cinco abridores en octubre, la ayuda está en camino. Will Warren tiene programada una última apertura y luego pasará a un rol de relevista, dando al bullpen una opción intrigante de múltiples entradas. Clarke Schmidt y Ryan Weathers también están en consideración.
"Eso es lo bueno de la postemporada; los muchachos caen en diferentes roles y muchas veces pueden ser heroicos en papeles que no necesariamente imaginabas al inicio de la temporada", expresó Boone.

item.content:encoded:
With one six-foot-seven sized caveat, the biggest concern facing the New York Yankees as we prepare for October is third base. Ryan McMahon has proven to be too much of a liability at the plate to count on as he's sunk to a new low as the only player in the league (min. 350 plate appearances) to post a sub-.280 on-base percentage and a strikeout rate north of 29%.
Meanwhile, Amed Rosario's inability to do his one job, hit lefties, and porous glove make him an untenable alternative. It appeared as if the Yankees would just have to deal with a black hole in the lineup and/or a butcher in the field, but Aaron Boone's latest update might have a solution coming to the rescue in a strange way.
With Jazz Chisholm Jr. back in action, and apparently kissing fans, the skipper announced a new plan for Anthony Volpe: playing third base. Boone always uses qualifiers, so to be accurate, he said he'd "probably" send Volpe out the man the hot corner some time this week, so there's always a chance that the frustratingly opaque manager could change his mind. Still, it would be nice to have another option, and believe it or not, Volpe could be a decent one.
Anthony Volpe ironically could come full circle and become a Yankees savior with the proposed third base plan
There's some reason to be concerned about how Volpe can handle third base, especially due to questions about his arm. The greater fear is that if he struggles there, he'll bring those issues with him to the batter's box and scuffle on the offensive side of the ball as well.
However, the former can't-miss prospect got a decent amount of run at the hot corner during his last demotion to Scranton, and during the last month he was in Triple-A, he hit 10 homers and posted an eye-popping 1.023 OPS.
Since he's come back up, his bat hasn't been that hot, hitting .263/.300/.395. Still, that's an improvement over McMahon, and he's had a few big moments over the last few weeks, most notably his September 10 grand slam against the Colorado Rockies.
Getting him some big league reps at the position before the playoffs begin is a great way to test this out in a low-pressure environment now that New York has clinched home-field advantage against the Boston Red Sox for the upcoming AL Wild Card Series.
If it works, well, it sets up a world of possibilities. We don't want to get ahead of ourselves, but Volpe getting hot at a new position in the postseason could completely flip his career narrative. If he makes a positive impact, his confidence could soar, fueling more and more encouraging developments.
At the end of it all, he could prove to be a viable replacement for the struggling McMahon this offseason. That's huge because unless the Yankees pull off a blockbuster trade, the free agent market is barren at the hot corner. One step at a time, but this could serve as the jumping-off point for Volpe's rebirth, and we're 100% here for that.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees manager Aaron Boone provided some updates during his weekly appearance on the 'Talkin Yanks' podcast…
Volpe at the hot corner
Third base is one of the positions the Yanks still need to shore up before they kick off postseason play next week.
Ryan McMahon has struggled mightily, reaching a near unplayable level.
The Yanks will also likely face numerous lefties against the Red Sox in the Wild Card round, pushing the lefty-hitting McMahon to the bench.
In an effort to solve that problem, Boone said that he'll be testing out Anthony Volpe at the hot corner at some point over the next week.
In that scenario, George Lombard Jr. would stick at shortstop.
While Volpe has never played third in the majors, he did see some time there in the minors in an effort to increase his versatility this year.
The 25-year-old has looked much better at the plate of late, hitting .263 with a .300 OBP and seven RBI in 11 games since returning to the majors.
Cruz on the mend
Boone said that Fernando Cruz is doing "pretty well" in his recovery from a partially torn UCL.
Cruz was able to throw for the first time this week.
An MRI revealed the injury in late-August, but the righty is attempting to pitch through it and return down the stretch.
He'll likely have to undergo surgery at some point, but could play a factor with the Yanks as long as things continue progressing as planned.
The reliever pitched to a strong 3.13 ERA in 61 appearances before the injury.

item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Cody Bellinger hit the ball out in the fourth inning, and for a few hours the Yankees had exactly what they needed. His two-run shot was the entire offense in a 2-0 win over Tampa Bay. Carlos Rodon gave them eight scoreless innings. No one needed to discuss the lineup after that first game. The second game changed the conversation. New York lost 6-1, scored only three runs across the doubleheader and watched the Rays clinch the division. item.content:encoded:
Cody Bellinger hit the ball out in the fourth inning, and for a few hours the Yankees had exactly what they needed. His two-run shot was the entire offense in a 2-0 win over Tampa Bay. Carlos Rodon gave them eight scoreless innings. No one needed to discuss the lineup after that first game.
The second game changed the conversation. New York lost 6-1, scored only three runs across the doubleheader and watched the Rays clinch the division. Bellinger’s swing won a game; it did not make the Yankees’ scoring issue disappear.
The Yankees needed that homer from Bellinger
There is a difference between calling one swing a cure and appreciating what it did. Bellinger has 17 home runs and 73 RBI with a .268 average and .779 OPS after Tuesday. He does not need to hit 40 homers to help this club, but his power has to show up in the games where one mistake pitch can decide the result.
He got that pitch from Nick Martinez and did not miss it. The sight of Bellinger rounding the bases mattered more because the Yankees were playing without much margin for error. It was also a reminder that Ben Rice and the rest of the order cannot leave the run production to one man every afternoon.
Tuesday’s opener was a clean illustration of how this team wins when the bats are light: a dominant starter, one big hit and a quiet ninth inning. The evening loss was the other side of the same bet.
A good afternoon cannot carry the whole Yankees lineup
I liked the homer, especially against the club New York spent months chasing. I do not think it is fair to treat it as proof the offense is ready for three October games in a row. Drew Rasmussen held the Yankees down in the nightcap, and they did not find another answer until it was too late.
With Aaron Judge’s availability already under a microscope, the supporting bats have to contribute more than an occasional solo moment. Bellinger delivered on Tuesday. The Yankees still need several hitters to do the same when a short series starts.
